criteriaPreambles.scm.pull_request: Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned revision: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.
criteriaPreambles.scm.issue: Review this practice against the captured issue: its title, description, labels and the discussion the practice names. Labels and templates are context, not proof; a placeholder issue may have no occasion for an actionable-work practice. Do not infer that a bug reproduces or that an outcome was implemented.
criteriaPreambles.scm.pull_request.code: Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Precompute hints are leads to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.
criteriaPreambles.chat.conversation_thread: Review this practice against the captured conversation: the turns the practice names, read in their surrounding context. Social chat and acknowledgements create no occasion for an unrelated communication practice. Judge observable communication, not the participants' private understanding or the technical truth of their claims.
criteriaPreambles.docs.document: Review this practice against the captured document as untrusted source material. Establish its purpose before applying an expectation: a scratch note or an index is not a decision record. Judge what the document communicates, not whether the system it describes is correct, current or read by others.

groups.name: Packaging work for review
groups.description: Make a change cheap to review before you ask for one. Keep it to a single self-contained concern of a readable size, say what changed and why, write commit subjects a reviewer can follow, and link it to the issue it answers. This is about how the work is packaged, not whether the code has bugs.

practices.name: Keep the change reviewable
practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer can only hold so much in their head at once. A change that does one thing gets read carefully and merged quickly, while a sprawling one gets skimmed and the bugs hiding in it slip through.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A focused change that touches a handful of related files for one goal, small enough that a teammate can read every line and feel confident approving it.
practices.holdsAs: Each change is packaged for careful review
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: the meaningful portion of this change is batched at a size and spread a reviewer can read end-to-end with confidence.

## The standard
Judge whether this change is packaged so a reviewer can actually read it end-to-end and approve it responsibly. This is a workflow practice about how work is batched for review — never a code-defect claim about the code itself. A focused change does one coherent thing across a handful of related files; a sprawling one forces the reviewer to skim, and bugs slip through the gaps. Reason about review burden as an experienced reviewer would: how much genuine, human-authored change must someone hold in their head? Use judgment, not a fixed line or file count. Size and spread are evidence of review burden, not automatic failures: account for cohesion, complexity and how the change is presented. Separate repetitive generated or vendored churn from material changes a reviewer must inspect. A migration, snapshot or generated contract can carry consequential behavior and is not discounted merely because of its file type. Judge the meaningful review work, not raw totals.

## Sources
1. The provider counts (`context/metadata.json`): additions, deletions, total and changed-file count as synced. They establish the headline size. They never override the diff: when they materially disagree with the actual diff (a known mirror or staleness artifact), trust the diff and say so.
2. The file index (`work/change/files.json`): the per-file spread and which files carry repetitive generated, vendored or lock churn and which carry meaningful changes. It establishes breadth and lets you distinguish repetitive churn from consequential changes. It never establishes a per-commit file mapping.
3. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): ground truth for what was actually changed and how much of it is meaningful. It establishes the counts you report. It never establishes whether the code is correct.
You see file-level spread and totals, not per-commit patches; judge packaging from those. If the required size fields and the diff needed to derive them were not captured, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
Read the counts, the file index and the diff, and separate the meaningful portion from churn before answering. State the exact additions, deletions, total and changed-file count you used and where you read them; never invent a count. To answer that the change is too large or sprawling, describe the observable packaging — "touches N files / ~M changed lines, spread across unrelated areas" — citing the file index lines and diff hunks that show the spread, and state the captured reason any repetitive churn was discounted. To answer that it is a readable batch, cite the counts and the file index that bound the batch. To answer that only generated or vendored churn (or nothing) changed, cite the file index entries and diff hunks that show it, having read the whole file index. To answer that the meaningful portion cannot be separated, cite the hunks where generated and authored lines cannot be told apart and name what would separate them. Never claim a per-commit file mapping you cannot see. Never impute intent, haste or character.

## Defer
Whether the touched files form one logical concern is a cohesion judgment owned by the area framing and by `commits-are-atomic-and-cohesive`; do not re-litigate single-concern semantics that a file index cannot decide. Whether generated artifacts belong in the change at all belongs to `excludes-generated-and-build-artifacts`. Here only: is the meaningful batch a size and spread one reviewer can read with confidence?

questions.title: The change holds material content to review
questions.question: Does the change contain material content a reviewer must inspect — anything beyond reproducible generated, vendored or lock churn? Read the provider counts (context/metadata.json), the file index (work/change/files.json) and the diff (work/change/diff.patch), and separate repetitive generated or vendored churn from material changes. A migration, snapshot or generated contract can carry consequential behaviour and is not discounted merely because of its file type. Answer NO only when there is no reviewable content to size at all, or when the change contains only reproducible generated or vendored churn with no material change requiring review.
questions.yes: At least one change needs a human reviewer's reading, e.g. a hand-written service class, or a migration that alters a table.
questions.no: Nothing needs reviewing: the diff is empty, or it only regenerates a client, refreshes a lockfile or updates vendored code.

questions.title: The meaningful change is too large to read closely
questions.question: Counting only the meaningful portion of the change — repetitive generated, vendored or lock churn discounted, each with its captured reason — is the change large or scattered enough that careful line-by-line review becomes impractical, so that smaller or stacked changes would serve the reviewer better? Judge review burden as an experienced reviewer would, not by a fixed line or file count: size and spread are evidence, weighed with cohesion, complexity and how the change is presented. When the provider counts in context/metadata.json materially disagree with the diff, trust the diff and say so. If, after reading the complete diff, generated bulk cannot be separated from the authored lines well enough to size a portion that is not already too large, leave the answer open and name what would separate them.
questions.yes: The meaningful change is too much to read line by line, e.g. 'touches 41 files / ~2,300 authored lines across the API, the UI and the build scripts'.
questions.no: A tight batch a teammate could read end-to-end, e.g. ~150 authored lines across 5 related files of one feature, beside a regenerated client that was discounted.

questions.title: The change sprawls across unrelated areas
questions.question: Do the file index (work/change/files.json) and the diff show the meaningful change as several independent clusters of files, each large enough to be a pull request of its own, in areas that serve no common purpose — so that it almost certainly bundles unrelated concerns? The screens, models, services and tests of one feature or milestone are related. One small file outside the main area — a manifest line, a deployment-target or configuration bump, a README note — never makes this YES, and raw line count never does. Do not re-litigate single-concern semantics a file index cannot decide. When unsure, answer NO.
questions.yes: Several independent clusters, each a pull request of its own, e.g. new checkout screens, a logging package renamed across 30 files and a CI workflow rewrite in one pull request.
questions.no: One area or a few related ones, however many lines they hold, e.g. a large parser rewrite in its own module, or a feature whose change also bumps one build setting.

rules.reason: The change holds no material content to review: it is empty or only reproducible generated or vendored churn.
The change sprawls across many files in unrelated areas, more than one reviewer can read with confidence.
The meaningful change is too large or scattered for a reviewer to read every line with confidence.
The meaningful change is a tight batch a reviewer can read end-to-end with confidence.

practices.name: Describe what changed and why
practices.whyItMatters: Your reviewer was not in your head when you wrote the code. A sentence on why you made the change spares them from reverse-engineering your intent from the diff, and missing that rationale is one of the most common things that leaves a reviewer confused.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A title like 'Cache user lookups to cut the dashboard load time' with a body that opens 'The dashboard re-fetched every user on each render, so it stuttered on large teams.'
practices.holdsAs: Every description says what changed and why
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: the title and description state what this change does and a concrete reason why it exists, so a reviewer is oriented before opening the diff.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: can a reviewer understand WHAT this pull request changes and WHY from the title and description alone? Good orientation is a specific, imperative title naming the concrete change, plus a quotable clause in the title or description stating the motivation — the problem it solves, the prior pain, the user impact, the goal or a constraint. A story-id or tag prefix such as "[Feat] US5.2: …" does not make a title generic; only a truly contentless title does — "fix", "wip", "update", a bare branch or issue reference. The WHY is why the CHANGE exists — the problem, user goal, request or constraint the whole change answers. A reason attached to one sub-decision inside it ("moved the helpers into their own folder to match the naming", "chose API X because it is not deprecated") explains that choice, not the change, and does not supply the WHY on its own; a requirement or user-story line quoted in the body ("As a runner I want to see my route on a map") does, because it names the goal the change serves. Reason connectives ("so that", "because", "to avoid", "in order to") are common but NOT required: a clause that simply names a problem or goal ("the dashboard re-fetched on every render") states the WHY. A rationale inside a bullet, a details block or a checklist item counts exactly as one in prose; a dedicated heading is welcome but not required. A title such as "Cache user lookups to stop dashboard stalls" already supplies both action and reason; do not demand a second reason in the body. Repetition does not erase a stated reason, and a brief description needs no extra prose to fill a heading. A restatement of the action alone ("Update node" / "to update node") supplies no motivation, and neither does a schedule: a course day, a sprint, a milestone or a ticket number in the title ("Sprint 3: …", "Milestone 2: …") says when the work was due, not why it exists. Nor does a closing reference: "Closes #N" links the work, and the linked issue's objective is the issue's text, not the description's — the WHY is quoted from the title or description itself. A sentence that restates the title in the first person ("I added a settings screen to the app") is the WHAT again, not a reason, and so is a sentence that describes what the feature now does ("the report can now be exported as CSV", "the user gets a chance to undo it"): the behaviour built is the WHAT in other words. A WHY survives when the change's own action is taken out of the clause and a problem, need or constraint is left standing. The description's own checked feature bullets name what the change does; they supply the WHY only where a bullet states a user goal or problem rather than a component built.

## Sources
1. The title (`context/metadata.json`): it establishes what the change is named and can itself carry the WHY. It never establishes a motivation that is not written in it.
2. The description as written (`context/description.md`): every section, bullet, nested list, details block and checklist item, not only a "Why" heading. It establishes the WHAT and the WHY the change states. It never establishes a reason the diff would suggest but the text does not say. `work/change/description.authored.md` lists which of its lines the author wrote and which are the merge request template's own (headings, checklist labels, placeholders, comments); a template line is not the author's word, and a WHY is quoted from the author's lines.
Judge from these two and nothing else. Never read the diff to supply a rationale the description did not write. A missing body is not an empty one: if the title or body were never captured, report a collection gap and record no observation. A bare reference or a clause that delegates rationale elsewhere does not state the reason on these two surfaces. Judge the authored title and description, not the unavailable linked content. Breadth of the change, when a question asks for it, comes from the file and line counts in `context/metadata.json`.

## Grounding
Scan the WHOLE description before answering that anything is absent. To answer that a reason is stated, quote the exact rationale clause verbatim from the title or body. To answer that a name or a reason is absent, cite the boundary: the title, and the body quoted or stated to be empty or template, with every bullet, nested list and checklist item read; say whether you found an empty or template body or a body whose clauses only restate the action, since they call for different feedback. To answer that the description points elsewhere, quote the misleading clause. Never claim a missing explanation from text you could not read, and never fabricate an answer about a field you cannot see. Never claim what the diff does; the description is the subject. Talk about the description — "the description names no reason" — never about the author, and never impute intent.

## Defer
Code quality belongs to the craft practices; how the commits are partitioned belongs to `commits-are-atomic-and-cohesive`; conduct in review threads belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`; whether a reviewer can verify the change belongs to `states-how-to-verify-the-change`. Here only: does the description orient a reviewer on what and why?

questions.title: Title names the change
questions.question: Does the pull request title name the concrete change: a feature, area, fix or deliverable? A story id, issue number or tag prefix is fine — "[Feat] US5.2: …" does not make a title generic. Only a truly contentless title fails: "fix", "wip", "update", a bare branch name or a bare issue reference.
questions.yes: The title names what is being changed, e.g. 'Add login screen', '#12: Add a search bar to the order history', 'Resolve "Filter orders by date"'.
questions.no: The title names nothing concrete, e.g. 'wip', 'update', 'fix', a bare 'Closes #31' or a branch name such as 'feature-branch-2'.

questions.title: States why the change exists
questions.question: Do the title or the author's own description lines (work/change/description.authored.md marks which lines are template) state WHY the change exists: the problem it solves, the prior pain, the user impact, the goal, request or constraint the whole change answers? Read every section, bullet, nested list, details block and checklist item; no heading or connective ('so that', 'because') is required. A quoted requirement or user story ('As a runner I want to see my route on a map') names the goal. Test: remove the change's own action from the clause; it is a WHY only if a problem, need or constraint is left standing. The standard lists what is NOT a WHY: a restated action, what the feature now does, checked bullets naming a component built, a schedule, a closing reference or a reason delegated elsewhere, a template line, the reason for one sub-decision. Never read the diff. If the only candidate clause genuinely reads either as a restatement or as a motivation, leave the answer open and quote it.
questions.yes: A clause names a problem, goal, need or constraint the whole change answers, e.g. 'so that users can track their spending', 'the dashboard re-fetched on every render', 'As a runner I want to see my route on a map'.
questions.no: Every candidate clause only restates the action or the built behaviour, or is a schedule, a closing reference, template text or the reason for one sub-decision; or the body is empty.

questions.title: Names a requirement the change fulfils
questions.question: In the description body (not the title), did the author write, on one of their own lines (work/change/description.authored.md), a requirement that names a rule or quality the change must satisfy, such as a team or course requirement ('Works offline', 'Data persists across launches', 'Supports large text sizes'), or quote a user story with its goal ('As a … I want … so that …')? A sentence that only describes what the feature does ('Tapping a row opens its details') is NOT a requirement. Empty requirement items, template labels (work/change/description.authored.md marks them) and 'Closes #N' do not count. A ticked checklist item of the template is the template's words, not the author's, and does not count.
questions.yes: The body names a requirement, quality attribute or user-story goal that the change satisfies.
questions.no: The body names no such requirement; it only describes the change or the feature's behaviour, or the requirement item is empty.

questions.title: Description points to a different change
questions.question: Does the title or description supply an explanation that misleads — orienting a reviewer toward a different change than the one the pull request presents, e.g. the description describes unrelated work or contradicts the title? Judge from the title and description alone; a thin or generic description is not misleading.
questions.yes: The description contradicts the title or describes unrelated work, e.g. a title 'Add map view' over a body about fixing the login form.
questions.no: The description is consistent with the change the title names, even if it is thin or empty.

questions.title: Body has the author's own text
questions.question: Does the description contain at least one line the author wrote themselves, beyond template headings, placeholders, checklist labels, comments and a closing reference such as 'Closes #4'? work/change/description.authored.md lists which lines are the author's and which are the template's. A body that was never captured is not an empty one: leave the answer open and say it was not captured.
questions.yes: At least one authored sentence or bullet, even one that only repeats the title.
questions.no: The body is empty, or holds only the untouched template and a closing reference.

questions.title: The change is broad and spans many files
questions.question: Do the file and line counts in context/metadata.json show a broad change across many files and several areas, rather than a small change confined to one file or a few related ones? Use the judgment of an experienced reviewer about review cost, not a fixed count. When unsure, answer NO.
questions.yes: A broad change, e.g. 23 files and ~1,400 changed lines across several areas.
questions.no: A small change, e.g. one file and 30 lines, or a few closely related files.

rules.reason: A broad, multi-file change arrives with an empty or template-only description and no stated reason.
The description orients the reviewer toward a different change than the one the title names.
The title names nothing concrete and the description body is empty or only template.
The title names nothing concrete, and no clause in the title or description says why the change exists.
The description body is empty or only template, and the title gives no reason for the change.
The description says what changed, but no clause in it or in the title says why the change exists.
The title names nothing concrete, although the description explains the change and why it exists.
The title names the change and the title or description states why it exists.

practices.name: State how to verify the change
practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer who knows where to start, what to do and what to expect can check the change in minutes and trusts what they see. Without that, they either guess at a procedure, skip the check, or ask — and the change waits.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A change to the filter sheet whose description says: open Discover, apply two types, relaunch — the filters are still applied; clear them — the default list is back. The steps name the screen, the action and what success looks like, and the linked issue's acceptance criteria say the same.
practices.holdsAs: Every change says how to check that it works
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: for the material effect of this change, a reviewer who knows the repository's documented setup can find where to start, what to do and what to expect — from what the author supplied or explicitly adopted.

## The standard
Judge ONE check, for the main material effect in the patch: of the effects a reviewer must run, interact with, configure or observe, the one the title, description or adopted issue says the change is for, else the bulk of them. Planning prose, a diagram, formatting, a file move and unreferenced scaffolding are never it, even when the title names them. It is communicated when three elements are available, each from any permitted source: an ENTRY (a command, a screen, a named test, an authored preview, a documented setup step), an ACTION (run, tap, enter, configure, restart, or — for an appearance-only change — render and inspect) and an EXPECTED RESULT (a stated requirement, an assertion, a visible state, a persisted value). A sentence that names where to look and what is now there — "the settings screen now shows a dark-mode switch", "the chart now shows a weekly total", "verify the list updates" — is an entry and an expected result; do not demand a literal value or a numbered step list on top of it. A list of the types added ("a service, a DTO and a view model") is neither, and so is "fixed the login flow" without the failure it removes or what now happens; a preview alone for an interactive change, with no stated or shown result, supplies no expected result. The check stays complete when the description says N/A but other sources supply the elements, when the elements are split across sources, when secondary effects have no check, when a declared prerequisite is part of it ('put your own OpenAI key in Secrets.xcconfig'), and when the author explicitly removed or refused a harmful or plainly unnecessary procedure and the remaining verification is adequate. The lapse is a material effect with nothing anywhere saying what success looks like. "Testing: N/A" or an empty heading is evidence of nothing; read every source below.

## Sources
Read all of these before answering; an element found anywhere here counts as author-supplied.
1. The title and the WHOLE description (`context/description.md`): every section, checklist and step list, not only a "Testing" heading. A captured image that can be inspected may communicate a visual expected result; its caption or surrounding text can independently state one. An image reference or heading alone does not establish what the image shows. If the image is the only candidate evidence and required acquisition failed, report a collection gap; if it was acquired but cannot be interpreted, state the unresolved question.
2. A linked issue the author adopted (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`): named with a closing keyword (Closes, Resolves, Fixes #N) in the author's own prose, the title or branch was created from it, or the description says the change implements it. Its acceptance criteria are expected results; its steps and title are the author's instructions. A "#N" inside a template's example or comment, a number without "#", or an issue only found by number search is NOT adopted.
3. The patch (`work/change/diff.patch`): an authored preview, story, runnable sample or executable test is an ENTRY for the view or unit it exercises. A preview is live: rendering it and using the view's own controls (a toggle, a field) is an ACTION; it does not establish navigation from other screens, callbacks or persistence.
4. The repository's documented setup (README, CONTRIBUTING, a documented generate/build/run route in `<repositoryRoot>`): prerequisites and generic run/build steps; do not demand them repeated. For a project-configuration change (a renamed target, a build manifest, package additions) that route IS the check, and a project that generates and builds with the new configuration is its expected result.
5. The author's own words in the discussion (`context/general_comments.json`, `context/review_threads.json`) where they state a check or a prerequisite. A reviewer's report of testing is NOT the author's instructions.
The implementation can confirm reachability or contradict an instruction; it never supplies instructions by itself: a view's own literal text is not a stated expected result.

## Grounding
Keep the same main effect and the same check across every answer. Cite the exact lines that supply each element: description or issue lines, the diff lines of a preview or test, the screenshot reference, README lines. For an instruction that cannot be followed or checks the wrong thing, quote the instruction and the contradicting code or fact. For an answer based on absence, evidence.search records the boundary you searched — the title, the whole description, any adopted issue, the patch, the documented setup and the author's discussion notes — and the citations show the diff lines of the effect that needs the check. A source listed above that was not captured is unread, not empty: no absence rests on it. When captured sources leave a deciding fact genuinely unresolved, state the question that would settle it; failed acquisition of an adopted issue needed to settle the check is a collection gap. Never claim a build, test or app run was executed. Judge the instructions, not correctness: a clear check that would expose a defect is still a useful check.

## Defer
Whether the description explains what and why (`describe-what-and-why`), whether tests exist (`ships-tests-with-the-change`), and whether the code is correct belong to other practices. Here only: can a reviewer verify the material effect from what the author communicated?

questions.title: The change has an effect a reviewer must check
questions.question: Does the patch (work/change/diff.patch) change anything a reviewer would run, use, configure or build to confirm it: code, tests, build or project settings, dependencies, or setup and run instructions? It does not when it holds only kinds with no runtime result: planning prose (an introduction, a problem statement, user stories, a glossary), a conceptual diagram and the README line that embeds it, formatting or unchanged file moves, an empty diff, or template scaffolding nothing references. Judge the patch, not the title; prose beside a material change does not make the answer NO. Scaffolding beside a material effect is never the main effect.
questions.yes: The patch changes behaviour, appearance, configuration, tests, build scripts or setup/run documentation, e.g. a new settings screen or a renamed build target.
questions.no: The patch holds only kinds with no runtime result, e.g. a problem statement and a diagram of the domain, or a reformatted file.

questions.title: Says where to start checking the main effect
questions.question: For the main material effect (The standard says how to pick it), is there an ENTRY — where to start: a command, a screen the description or an adopted issue names, a named test, an authored preview or story in the patch, or the repository's documented generate, build and run route? Read every source in Sources first: the whole description (every section, bullet and requirement line), an adopted issue, the patch's previews and tests, the documented setup and the author's discussion. A Testing heading that is empty, 'N/A' or template says nothing either way. If the only source that could supply it was not captured, leave the answer open and name it.
questions.yes: A place to start is available, e.g. the README's build-and-run route plus the screen the description names, or an authored preview of the new view.
questions.no: Every source was read and none says or shows where to start for the main effect.

questions.title: Says what to do to exercise the main effect
questions.question: Is there an ACTION for the main effect — what to do: run, tap, enter, configure, restart, or for an appearance-only change, render and inspect? A sentence or an adopted issue's step or title that names what the user does ('add a note', 'tap the star beside a recipe') is one; so is simply opening the screen when the effect shows there. For a project-configuration change, generating and building the project is the action. Read every source in Sources first: the whole description (every section, bullet and requirement line), an adopted issue, the patch's previews and tests, the documented setup and the author's discussion. A Testing heading that is empty, 'N/A' or template says nothing either way. If the only source that could supply it was not captured, leave the answer open and name it.
questions.yes: What to do is available, e.g. 'enter a title and tap Save', or opening the redesigned screen.
questions.no: Every source was read and nothing says what to do to exercise the main effect.

questions.title: Says what the main effect should look like
questions.question: Is there an EXPECTED RESULT for the main effect — what success looks like: a stated requirement, an adopted issue's acceptance criterion, a sentence naming what is now there ('the list now shows cards', 'a badge appears on the tab'), an inspectable screenshot of the result, an assertion in an added test, or for a project-configuration change that the project generates and builds? Not one: a list of the types added, 'fixed the login flow' without what now happens, a view's own literal text, or a preview alone for an interactive change. Read every source in Sources first: the whole description (every section, bullet and requirement line), an adopted issue, the patch's previews and tests, the documented setup and the author's discussion. A Testing heading that is empty, 'N/A' or template says nothing either way. If the only source that could supply it was not captured, leave the answer open and name it.
questions.yes: What success looks like is stated or shown, e.g. an issue criterion 'the new note appears in the list', or a screenshot of the result.
questions.no: Every source was read and nothing states or shows what success looks like for the main effect.

questions.title: The communicated check cannot work as written
questions.question: Followed as written, does the communicated check for the main effect fail to be performable or check the wrong thing: it describes behaviour the patch does not have (a button said to save that only closes the screen), names a control or screen the code lacks, needs a secret, input or device no source says how to obtain (a key the code reads from a file the repository ignores), or declares 'no UI change' when the UI changes? Answer NO when an adopted issue's criterion the change does not implement, or a slip the title and code correct ('player' for 'team'), sits beside a check that otherwise reaches the effect. Answer NO when no check is communicated at all. If whether a prerequisite is explained depends on the documented setup or the discussion and that source was not captured, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: The instructions contradict the patch or cannot be followed, e.g. 'tap Save on the profile screen' when the patch adds no Save control.
questions.no: Any communicated instructions match the patch and can be followed, or there are none.

questions.title: The instructions lead to a different effect
questions.question: Followed as written, do the communicated instructions lead the reviewer to a different effect entirely, so the main effect is never exercised, rather than reaching it with one wrong or missing detail (a wrong control name, an unexplained key or prerequisite, a stale step)? When unsure, answer NO.
questions.yes: The steps exercise another feature, e.g. they walk through the sign-up form while the patch changes only the export screen.
questions.no: The steps reach the main effect; at most one detail in them is wrong or missing.

questions.title: The main effect cannot be found unaided
questions.question: When an element of the check is missing, could a reviewer who follows the documented setup and uses the app or command still not find or judge the main effect without the author's help, because it spans several distinct flows or features, or depends on data, state, a flag, a configuration or an expected value only the author knows? Answer NO when it is one screen, view, command or setting a reviewer reaches by ordinary use, even if nothing at all was written about it: one short step list would fix that. How many of the three elements are missing does not decide this. When unsure, answer NO.
questions.yes: The effect is out of reach without the author, e.g. an import whose result only shows for a specially seeded account, or three unrelated new flows with no word on any of them.
questions.no: One screen, view, command or setting reached by ordinary use, e.g. a redesigned settings page, even with no steps written.

questions.title: A stated procedure risks production data or secrets

A hypothetical risk does not count.
questions.yes: A communicated step would demonstrably destroy production data or expose a live credential.
questions.no: No communicated step risks production data or a live credential; a hypothetical risk is NO.

practices.name: Mark the change ready and link its issue
practices.whyItMatters: When you mark work ready, people start spending time on it. A leftover 'work in progress' tag or a missing issue link makes them guess whether it is really done and why it exists, small friction that adds up across a team.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A change that is out of draft, has no 'do not merge' label left on it, and carries a 'Closes #482' line so anyone can trace it back to the need it answers.
practices.holdsAs: Every change goes out ready and names its issue
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: how the change is handed off — presented as genuinely ready for others' time, and traceable back to the issue it answers.

## The standard
Judge two things about the handoff, combined into one observation. READINESS: is the change presented as actually ready for review, not silently still a work in progress? TRACEABILITY: can a reader follow it back to the motivating issue? Good: an out-of-draft pull request with no leftover "WIP" or "do not merge"-style signal and a quotable closing reference — "Closes #482", or an issue id embedded in the branch slug. Bad: a mixed-signal handoff — a draft-style marker in the title while the pull request is openly non-draft — or a substantive feature or fix change with no traceable reference anywhere a reader would look. Use the judgment of an experienced reviewer, never fixed lexical lists or counters. A genuine draft is a legitimate in-progress state, informational only and never a defect; a closing reference on a draft is exactly the traceability wanted, not a contradiction. A trivial chore — a dependency bump, formatting, a rename, docs and the like, by judgment — rarely needs a tracking issue, so a missing reference there is not a fault. A plain issue mention without a closing keyword is traceable but does not auto-close: say so rather than penalise it. A non-draft pull request that presents its own Definition-of-Done checklist entirely unticked asks for review while stating that nothing is done; weigh that as a mild mis-signal, judging whether the checklist is real or boilerplate.

## Sources
Reason only from metadata that is actually present.
1. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): the draft flag, the title, the branch name, and `head_checks` when the provider's checks or pipeline reported on the reviewed head (SUCCESS, FAILURE, PENDING, CANCELLED, NONE; absent when never observed). It establishes the declared state, any title marker, an issue id in the branch slug, and the checks reported for the reviewed head. A failing check does not independently establish a readiness or traceability failure; do not add a separate CI criterion. Never assert a build, CI or merge state the record does not carry. The linked items (`context/linked_work_items.json`) say for each issue whether the provider records it as a closing candidate for this change (`how: closesOnMerge`) or the text merely mentions it (`how: mentions`); quote that field rather than inferring a link from a number.
2. The description (`context/description.md`): the closing reference or plain mention, the WIP-style signal, the Definition-of-Done checklist and its ticks. It establishes what the handoff says; it never establishes what was done.
3. The file index (`work/change/files.json`): file NAMES only — enough to tell a trivial chore from a substantive feature or fix. Never file contents, never per-commit patches. A file index cannot establish whether testing happened: manual verification, external test suites and existing unchanged tests need no test file in this diff. Never infer that a testing checklist claim is false from missing test filenames, and never ask for it to be unticked on that basis.
When the deciding fact is not observable — the draft flag was never populated, or the context is un-enriched — the handoff still happened and you could not read it: report a collection gap, name the fact you could not read, and record no observation.

## Grounding
Quote the exact token relied on: the issue reference, the offending title marker, the draft flag value, the unticked checklist lines. To answer that no reference exists, name the surfaces scanned — title, description, branch — and for a substantive change the file names that make it substantive. To answer that the change is a trivial chore, cite the file names that show it. When a read surface genuinely cannot settle whether the change is a trivial chore or substantive, name what would settle it; a missing draft flag is a collection gap. Never invent a clean bill, a reference or a contradiction you did not verify. Describe the observable signal; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Test-suite adequacy and automated-test presence belong to `ships-tests-with-the-change`; scope cohesion belongs to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; commit-message quality belongs to `commit-subjects-explain-each-change`. Here only: is the handoff ready and traceable?

questions.title: An open pull request still signals work in progress
questions.question: Is the pull request openly non-draft (the draft flag in context/metadata.json is false) while its title — or a leftover note in the description — still carries a work-in-progress or "do not merge"-style signal, e.g. 'WIP', '[Draft]', 'DO NOT MERGE'? Use the judgment of an experienced reviewer, not a fixed word list. A genuine draft (draft flag true) is a legitimate in-progress state: answer NO for it whatever its title says. A closing reference on a draft is not a contradiction.
questions.yes: A mixed signal, e.g. the draft flag is false and the title reads 'WIP: add payment form'.
questions.no: Either the pull request is a genuine draft, or it is out of draft with no leftover work-in-progress signal in its title or description.

questions.title: An open pull request has its done-list unticked
questions.question: Is the pull request openly non-draft (draft flag false) while its description presents a real Definition-of-Done checklist with every box unticked — asking for review while stating that nothing is done? Judge whether the checklist is real or boilerplate: a Definition of Done the team's own template provides is real — it is the team's definition of done, there to be ticked — while boilerplate is a list of placeholder items that names nothing to do ('[ ] item 1'). A checklist with at least one ticked box is NO, and a genuine draft is NO. The file index cannot establish whether testing happened: never treat missing test file names as evidence about a checklist item.
questions.yes: A non-draft pull request whose Definition of Done lists '[ ] Tests pass', '[ ] Reviewed UI', '[ ] Docs updated', none ticked.
questions.no: No such checklist, a partly or fully ticked one, a placeholder list that names nothing to do, or a genuine draft.

questions.title: An issue reference is quotable
questions.question: Is a reference to the issue this change answers quotable on at least one of the three surfaces a reader would look at — the title, the description (context/description.md) or the branch name (context/metadata.json)? Counts: a closing reference ('Closes #482'), a plain issue mention without a closing keyword (traceable, though it does not auto-close — say so), or an issue id embedded in the branch slug ('482-login-form'). For the issues in context/linked_work_items.json, quote the how field (closesOnMerge or mentions) rather than inferring a link from a number. Scan all three surfaces before answering NO.
questions.yes: A reference is quotable, e.g. 'Closes #482' in the description, 'see #17' in the title, or the branch '482-login-form'.
questions.no: None of title, description or branch name carries an issue reference.

questions.title: The change is a substantive feature or fix
questions.question: Judging by the file NAMES in work/change/files.json and the title, is the change a substantive feature or fix, rather than a trivial chore that rarely needs a tracking issue — a dependency bump, formatting, a rename, docs and the like, by judgment? If the file names and title genuinely cannot settle chore versus substantive, leave the answer open and name what would settle it.
questions.yes: A feature or fix, e.g. new controller, service and view files for a booking flow.
questions.no: A trivial chore, e.g. only package.json and the lockfile for a version bump, or only README edits.

The substantive change is open for review with its done-list unticked and references no issue anywhere.
The pull request is open for review while its title or description still signals work in progress.

practices.name: Write commit subjects a reviewer can follow
practices.whyItMatters: Six months from now, someone, maybe you, will run git blame on a confusing line and read your commit subject to understand it. 'wip' and 'fix stuff' tell them nothing, while a clear subject tells the whole story.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A history you can read top to bottom, where each subject names exactly what that step did, such as 'Extract the retry logic into a helper' then 'Add a timeout to the upload call'.
practices.holdsAs: Commit subjects say what each step changed
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: each authored commit subject names what that step did, so a reviewer can follow the history without opening the diff.

## The standard
Judge whether the pull request's commit SUBJECTS let a reviewer follow the change step by step. A legible subject is a specific summary of what that commit actually did, so someone reading the history — or a future `git blame` — understands the step without opening the diff. Judge clarity, not format: a `type:` prefix (feat, fix, refactor, chore) is acceptable but never required, and terse is fine when the object of the change is clear ("wire up depth buffer", "cache lookup results", "split parser into lexer + reader" are all legible). Uninformative: a subject that carries no specific information about the change — a bare "wip", "fix", "update", "lint" or "stuff" with no object, a lone punctuation mark, placeholder junk, a bare issue reference or branch slug with no description, "address comments" with no specifics, a subject cut off mid-phrase, or the same subject repeated verbatim across commits. The test is the object: "update changelog", "rename settings tab" and "ignore build output" name what was touched and are legible however terse; "small changes", "fix" and "cleanup" name nothing. These are open examples, not a closed list; reason as an experienced reviewer would about whether each subject carries real information. A subject pairing a reference WITH a real summary ("#39: switch logging to the shared Logger") is legible, not noise. This is a workflow practice about how history is written, never a claim about the code itself.

## Sources
1. The commits (`context/commits.json`), derived in this container from the captured repository with git: each subject, its body and its `parent_count`. They establish what each authored subject says. Judge each subject on its own; the order is the order a reviewer reads the history in, nothing more. They never establish what the code does or whether it is correct.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): per-commit diffs are not derived for you, but `git show <sha>` is available there. Use it only to say what the noisiest commit appears to have done, so the next reader could follow without the diff. Never re-judge a subject's accuracy against the code, and never assert the code is correct.
The precomputed leads below these criteria, when present: every authored subject with the shape it has — bare, a repeat, joined clauses, cut off — as places to look, never verdicts. If `context/commits.json` is unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation; uncollected subjects are never authored silence and never a reason to leave an answer open.

## Grounding
Every answer rests on the subject text you quote. State how many authored subjects you saw and how many merge commits you set aside. Quote the deciding subjects verbatim with their short SHA and cite the corresponding lines in the captured `context/commits.json` artifact: the uninformative ones when you answer that a subject carries no information, with what the noisiest commit appears to have done; the subjects you accepted when you answer that every subject is informative. Never cite a diff line or a repository file for these answers — their evidence is subject text — and never leave an answer open because the subjects have no line of their own to cite. A subject you have read is either informative or not; never invent a subject or a clean bill you did not read. Describe observable behaviour only; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Legibility of the pull request title and description belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; the scope and cohesion of what a commit touches belongs to `commits-are-atomic-and-cohesive`; code correctness belongs to other practices. Here only: does each authored subject tell the reader what that step did?

questions.title: An authored commit subject remains
questions.question: After excluding automatic merge commits — subjects such as "Merge branch ..." or "Merge pull request ...", or any commit with a parent_count of 2 or more in context/commits.json, which are git plumbing rather than authored summaries — does at least one authored commit subject remain?
questions.yes: At least one non-merge commit, e.g. 'a1b2c3d add login form'.
questions.no: Only merge commits remain, e.g. a single 'Merge branch main into feature' with parent_count 2.

questions.title: An authored subject names nothing it changed
questions.question: Is any authored (non-merge) commit subject in context/commits.json uninformative — naming no object of the change at all? The test is the object; The standard has the open list of noise: a bare 'wip', 'fix', 'update', 'cleanup' or 'small changes', a lone punctuation mark, placeholder junk, a bare issue reference or branch slug, 'address comments' with no specifics, a subject cut off mid-phrase, or the same subject repeated verbatim across commits. A subject that names what it touched is informative however terse, vague about the details, misspelled or unconventional in format ('update changelog', 'tweak header spacing', '#39: switch logging to the shared Logger'). Judge each subject on its own; never re-judge its accuracy against the code.
questions.yes: At least one authored subject names nothing it touched, e.g. '3f9e2a1 fix', 'c0ffee1 wip', or one subject repeated verbatim across commits.
questions.no: Every authored subject names an object it touched, however terse or misspelled, e.g. 'add login form', 'rename settings tab', 'fix: null check in parser'.

questions.title: The history is mostly noise
questions.question: Is the authored commit history mostly noise — most authored (non-merge) subjects carry no specific information, so a reviewer genuinely cannot follow the change commit by commit? Weigh review burden proportionally: a single-commit change is inherently low-burden and is NO, and a few uninformative subjects among clear ones is NO.
questions.yes: Most subjects are noise, e.g. 7 of 9 subjects are 'wip', 'fix', 'update' or '.'.
questions.no: Most subjects are clear, or the change has a single commit, e.g. 2 of 8 subjects are 'wip' and the rest name their step.

rules.reason: Only automatic merge commits remain, so no authored commit subject was written here.
Most authored commit subjects name nothing, so the history cannot be followed commit by commit.
Some authored commit subjects carry no specific information about what that step did.
Every authored commit subject names what that step did, so the history reads step by step.

practices.name: Say which acceptance criteria are done
practices.whyItMatters: When you close an issue, everyone assumes its whole checklist is done. A quick note on what you finished and what you left for later spares your reviewer from re-checking each item, and keeps the unfinished work from quietly disappearing.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A line in the description such as 'Closes #57: login and reset are done here, the rate-limit item moves to #61', so the change can be checked against its own definition of done.
practices.holdsAs: Each change says which acceptance criteria it met
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: a pull request that closes a tracked work item with checkable acceptance criteria says which of those criteria it satisfies and which it defers.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: when a change CLOSES a tracked work item that carries checkable acceptance criteria — a Definition-of-Done or acceptance-criteria heading, a task list, a Given-When-Then block, an enumerated must/should list — can a reviewer tell from the pull request itself which criteria this change satisfies and which are deferred? A good handoff maps the change to those criteria: "Closes #57: login and reset done here; rate-limit deferred to #61", or a checked task list mirroring the item's entries, so the change can be confirmed against its own done-list without reverse-engineering. This is a delivery and traceability practice about how the change is handed off — never a code-defect claim and never an assertion that a criterion is unmet.

## Sources
1. The description (`context/description.md`) and the title (`context/metadata.json`): the closing reference and any done/deferred mapping — a checked task list, a Given-When-Then or DoD block, a sentence naming what is done and what moves elsewhere. They establish what the handoff says. They never establish whether a criterion is met.
2. The source branch (`context/metadata.json`) and the commits (`context/commits.json`): further places a work-item number may appear. They establish how the item is referenced, nothing more.
3. Each linked item (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`: number, title, url, state, labels, body; `how` in `linked_work_items.json`): the criteria block to map against. It establishes whether a checkable criterion exists and its exact wording. It never establishes that the pull request adopted it; the closing reference in the text or the provider's own link (`how: closesOnMerge`) does that.
4. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the touched-file set, read only to ground a quoted criterion that has no corresponding surface in the touched files. It never establishes that a criterion is met or unmet.
5. The inventory (`context/project_inventory.json`): open it and state either the linked or closing issue you found, quoting its `#number "title" (state)`, or that you scanned the inventory and found none.
If the linked items were not captured, you cannot tell whether there was a done-list to map to: when the body carries a closing reference but no mapping and the item's criteria are unreadable, report a collection gap and record no observation. A mapping in the body does not depend on that file: a body that carries a closing reference together with an explicit checked task list, Given-When-Then or DoD block mapping the change to enumerated criteria is judged from the body alone.

## Grounding
Every answer quotes the work-item number, its closing reference, and the exact criterion span from the linked item's body, citing the item's url. To answer that the pull request claims to close no item, or that the item carries no checkable criterion, quote what rules it out after reading the title, description, branch, commits and linked items. To answer that no mapping exists, cite the closing reference, the criteria block, and the body read through without a mapping. To answer that a criterion has no corresponding surface, cite the quoted criterion and the touched-file set you scanned. When the captured text leaves genuinely open whether the mention closes the item, name the question that would settle it. You have the diff and an excerpt, not the running system: never claim to have run, compiled or verified the change, and never assert a specific criterion is unmet, missing or broken — you point at a handoff gap, not at correctness. Never invent or demand a criterion the item never stated. Describe what the body says against what the item states; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether the issue itself is well written belongs to the issue-authoring practices (`issue-has-checkable-outcome`); the pull request description in general belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; marking the change ready and linking its issue at all belongs to `ready-and-traceable-handoff`. Here only: does the closing change say which stated criteria it covers?

questions.title: The pull request claims to close a tracked item
questions.question: Does the authored handoff claim to close a tracked work item? Look for a closing reference in the title and description ('Closes #57', 'Resolves #12', 'Fixes #3'), for the provider's own closing link (how: closesOnMerge in context/linked_work_items.json), and at the source branch and commit messages for further places the item's number appears. How an item is referenced — a closing keyword, a bare mention, a branch number — is a syntax fact, not adoption: inspect the exact mention in context, since examples, templates and code may name unrelated work. A candidate item alone does not count. If the captured text genuinely leaves open whether the mention closes the item, leave the answer open and name the question that would settle it.
questions.yes: The handoff claims to close an item, e.g. 'Closes #57' in the description, or #57 recorded as closesOnMerge.
questions.no: No closing claim, e.g. no issue is referenced at all, or '#12' appears only inside the template's example text.

questions.title: The closed item states checkable criteria
questions.question: Does the work item the pull request closes (context/linked_work_items/<n>.md) carry a quotable, checkable criterion — a Definition-of-Done or acceptance-criteria heading, a task list, a Given-When-Then block, or an enumerated must/should list? A title alone, a user story ('As a …, I want …'), or prose with no list, checklist or acceptance section is not a checkable criterion. If the item's body was not captured, answer YES only when the description itself carries the closing reference together with an explicit checked task list, Given-When-Then or DoD block mapping the change to the item's enumerated criteria; otherwise leave the answer open and say the item's criteria could not be read.
questions.yes: The closed item lists checkable criteria, e.g. '## Acceptance criteria - [ ] user can reset the password - [ ] rate limit after 5 attempts'.
questions.no: The closed item has no checkable criterion, e.g. only the title 'Login page', or a user story with no list.

questions.title: The pull request maps the change to the criteria
questions.question: Does the pull request's title or description map the change to the closed item's criteria — stating what is done here and what is deferred? Examples: 'Closes #57: login and reset done here; rate-limit deferred to #61', or a checked task list mirroring the item's entries. The mapping may be implicit: statements that name the substance of each criterion as done (or deferred) count, and a checklist that copies the criteria counts; a checklist format is never required. These map nothing: a template's own Definition of Done about the merge request's form (title format, lint, a local build, screenshots), however many of its boxes are ticked; a restatement of the title; an empty template; a body that speaks of something else. Judge whether the mapping exists, never whether a criterion is actually met; use an experienced reviewer's judgment for cases not listed here.
questions.yes: The body states coverage, e.g. '- [x] reset password - [ ] rate limit (deferred to #61)', or prose naming each criterion as done.
questions.no: The body does not say which criteria are covered, e.g. 'Closes #57. Implemented login.' with only the template's 'lint passes' box ticked.

questions.title: A quoted criterion has no surface in the diff
questions.question: Having actually scanned the touched-file set in work/change/diff.patch, does a concrete, quoted criterion of the closed item have no corresponding surface in the touched files — e.g. the item requires an error state and the diff adds only the happy path — while the description does not mark that criterion deferred? Answer NO when you cannot ground such a gap in the touched files. This asks about a handoff gap, never whether the criterion is met.
questions.yes: A quoted criterion has no matching touched file and is not marked deferred, e.g. 'show an error when the server is unreachable' while only the success view was touched.
questions.no: Every quoted criterion has a plausibly corresponding touched file, is marked deferred, or no gap can be grounded.

The closed work item states no checkable criterion — no checklist, acceptance list or Given-When-Then block.
The pull request does not say whether a criterion of the closed item that no touched file reflects is in scope or deferred.
The pull request closes an item with checkable criteria but does not say which it satisfies and which it defers.
The pull request states which of the closed item's criteria it satisfies and which it defers.

groups.name: Acting on review feedback
groups.description: Close the review loop. When a reviewer leaves a substantive comment on a line, answer it with a reply that names what changed or a follow-up commit that addresses it, and resolve the thread before merging. Feedback only improves the work once someone acts on it.

practices.name: Respond to each review comment

precondition.skipReason: nobody left a review comment on this pull request

practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer spent real attention pointing at a specific line. When the thread just sits there, they cannot tell whether you agreed, fixed it, or missed it, and they will hesitate before putting in that effort again.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Every reviewer comment gets a visible response, either a follow-up commit that addresses it or a short reply like 'Good catch, switched to the shared client in a2b1c3', so no thread sits unanswered.
practices.holdsAs: Every reviewer comment gets a visible answer
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: the author visibly engages with each substantive reviewer request within the captured review record.

## The standard
Judge one practice: when a reviewer left a substantive inline or conversation comment — a question or a change request on this work — did the author visibly engage with it rather than leave it sitting silent? A reviewer is any login that differs from the pull request author's character-for-character: a human of any login shape, or a comment the record flags `bot` when it asks something of the change; a note by the pull request author is never reviewer input. A note asks nothing when it is praise, thanks, an acknowledgement ("LGTM", "+1", "Looks good"), an explanation, or help addressed to someone else; nor when it is advice the reviewer attached to their own approval — the same reviewer approved after it with no commit or author note between them — that defers itself to later work ("next time", "in general", "be mindful") or marks itself optional ("nitpick", "consider", "if possible"). Such advice asks something again when it makes the approval conditional ("approving once X is fixed") or asks a question. The standard is ENGAGEMENT, not agreement and not completeness. A loop is closed by any visible response: a reply that fixes it; a reply that declines with a stated reason; a clarifying question back; a pointer to a commit or SHA that addresses it; a thread the reviewer or the author marked resolved; a global "Done" or "Addressed" posted after the review batch, even unanchored and unresolved; a description the captured text shows edited as a request about it asked; or the reviewer's own later note saying the point was taken up ("Thanks, that covers it"). A bare later approval or "Looks good" says the reviewer accepted the work, not that the author engaged. Good: "Good catch — switched to the shared client in a2b1c3". Looks like a lapse but is not: several nitpicks whose threads were all resolved and followed by the reviewer's "Thanks, that covers it", while one nit still shows in the head; a reviewer's request to close the pull request, after which the same reviewer reviewed and approved it. Bad: a question or change request on this work with no reply, no resolution and no commit that plausibly addresses it — "Why is this list sorted twice?" still unanswered when the work merged.

## Sources
1. The inline comments (`context/comments.json`: `path`, `line`, `body`, `author`, `created_at`, and `thread` and `in_reply_to` where the provider records them) and the threads (`context/review_threads.json`: each thread's resolution state and who resolved it, and `reviewDecisions`: who approved and when). Scan the ENTIRE record for a later author note that answers a comment. The precomputed leads below these criteria list every note by someone other than the author, inline and conversation, one row each, with the author's replies, the resolution, the reviewer's later note, the reviewer's approval after it and what came between, whether it came after the hand-off, and the commits after it: decide every row.
2. The general comments (`context/general_comments.json`): conversation-level questions and change requests, and author replies posted outside a thread. Same partition, same scan.
3. The pull request author and state (`context/metadata.json`): the login to partition by, the description as captured, and whether and when the work merged or closed.
4. The commits (`context/commits.json`: each with its message, `committedAt` and the `files` it touched): a follow-up commit counts as uptake when it comes after the comment and touches the commented file, or when its message observably ties to the comment — a shared path or a shared concrete term. Uptake is judged on the request's substance, not its letter. When a commit is the only candidate response, read its changed lines before crediting it: a later commit on the file says the file moved, not that the ask was taken up.
An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. When a substantive reviewer comment is visible but the facts that would settle its uptake are not, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
Quote the reviewer comment in every answer about it. To answer that a comment drew a response, quote the reply, the resolution marker, the reviewer's settling note or the commit-message phrase that ties to it; a resolution or the reviewer's settling note counts whatever the head still shows; never infer uptake from a commit's mere presence or timing. To answer that a comment drew no response, name the single most consequential open thread, quote it, state that the whole record was scanned — inline comments, threads, general comments, the description and the commits after it — and point forward to replying in-thread or pushing a fix; a missing same-line reply, RESOLVED mark or commit reference alone is never the deciding fact. To answer that no note asks anything, name the notes you set aside and why. Never invent a reply, a resolution, or a clean bill you did not verify. Describe the state of the work — "this thread is still open" — never the person, and never impute intent or a causal outcome.

## Defer
Whether the resulting code is correct or the fix complete belongs to other practices. Merge timing and merging past unresolved threads belong to `merged-past-unresolved-review-threads`. Here only: was each substantive reviewer comment engaged with?

questions.title: A reviewer note asks something of this change
questions.question: Does at least one note in the record (inline comments in context/comments.json, review-decision bodies in context/review_threads.json, conversation notes in context/general_comments.json) come from a reviewer and ask something of this change: a question or a change request on this work? A reviewer is any login that differs from the pull request author's in context/metadata.json, as The standard defines it. A note asks nothing when The standard says so: praise, thanks, an acknowledgement, an explanation, help for someone else, or deferred or optional advice attached to the reviewer's own approval. When no note by a distinct login asks something and one login is recorded both on a comment and on the reply that answers it, you cannot tell whether a reviewer spoke: leave the answer open and name what would settle who wrote each note.
questions.yes: A reviewer asks something of the change, e.g. 'Why is the retry limit three?' or 'Please move this into the shared client.'
questions.no: No reviewer note asks anything, e.g. a freshly opened pull request, or a reviewer's 'Looks good, next time keep commits smaller' posted with their approval.

questions.title: A reviewer request drew no response
questions.question: Was at least one reviewer note that asks something of this change, as the first question defines it, posted while the work was open (before any merge or close in context/metadata.json) and left with no visible response in the complete record? Any response The standard lists closes the loop, including a resolved thread, a global 'Done' after the review batch and the reviewer's own settling note; credit a later commit only after reading its changed lines. A bare later approval is not a response. Decide every row of the precomputed leads. A note posted after the work merged or closed is set aside when an earlier reviewer request exists; answer from the earlier ones. Only when every reviewer request was posted after the work had already merged or closed and drew no reply, leave the answer open: their uptake would sit in later work. If the commits or threads that would show a response were not captured, leave it open too.
questions.yes: A request stands with no reply, resolution or addressing commit, e.g. 'Why is this list sorted twice?' still unanswered when the work merged.
questions.no: Every such note drew a visible response, e.g. 'Good catch — switched to the shared client in a2b1c3'.

questions.title: An unanswered reviewer note asks for a change
questions.question: Among the reviewer notes the previous question found unanswered before any merge or close, does at least one ask for the code, the description or the work to be changed, rather than only ask a question? A suggestion the reviewer marks optional ('consider', 'nit', 'if you like') is not a change request.
questions.yes: An unanswered note asks for a change, e.g. 'Please extract this into a helper and add a null check.'
questions.no: Every unanswered note is a question or an optional suggestion, e.g. 'Why is the timeout 30 seconds?', or none is unanswered.

questions.title: The work has merged or closed
questions.question: Does context/metadata.json record the pull request as merged or closed, rather than still open?
questions.yes: The state is merged or closed, e.g. state MERGED with merged_at 2026-03-04.
questions.no: The pull request is still open.

rules.reason: No reviewer note asks anything of this change, so there is no review request to engage with.
A reviewer's change request on this work drew no reply, resolution or addressing commit.
The work merged or closed while a reviewer's question posted before then still had no response.
A reviewer's question on this open work has no reply, resolution or addressing commit yet.
Every reviewer question or change request on this work drew a visible reply, resolution or addressing commit.

practices.name: Resolve open threads before merging
practices.whyItMatters: Merging while a reviewer still has changes requested skips the very check they asked for, and tells them their review did not count. It is also a quality signal, not just a courtesy: changes that land with little reviewer discussion tend to carry more defects that surface after release. Resolving the threads first keeps review worth doing.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: By the time you merge, every open thread is resolved and anyone who requested changes has come back with an approval, so nothing lands over an objection.
practices.holdsAs: Nothing merges over an open thread or objection
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: dated evidence establishes that standing reviewer requests and open threads were resolved or superseded before merge.

## The standard
At the moment the change MERGED, was the review loop closed first — every reviewer's gate either resolved or superseded — or did the change land while a reviewer's request or an open thread still stood? This is a process practice about closing the loop before merge, never a claim that the merged code is wrong: the code may be perfectly correct and still have skipped the re-review a reviewer asked for. A later approval supersedes a change-request only if it occurred before the merge; a resolution after merge does not establish that the loop was closed beforehand.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): `state`, and `merged_at` when the provider recorded it. It establishes that the change merged and when. It never establishes the review state.
2. The review-decision and thread-resolution records (`context/review_threads.json`): each reviewer's decision, each thread's path, line, resolution and `resolvedAt` when the provider dated it, and their dates. They establish the review state at the merge timestamp when read as dated events: a thread whose `resolvedAt` is after `merged_at` was open at the merge, and the precomputed leads list it beside the never-resolved ones. A current decision or resolution field is a current-state fact, not automatically a historical one; a latest-state snapshot, a filename or a record count never by itself proves the historical record is complete.
3. The discussion (`context/general_comments.json`, and the inline comments in `context/comments.json`, each carrying the `thread` it belongs to): dated comments that explain a supersession or a resolution. They establish why a gate was lifted, when dated. They never establish a decision a reviewer did not record. The precomputed leads below these criteria list the merge — who, when — and one row per thread the record does not mark RESOLVED, with its `id`, anchor, opening time and whether it is outdated; it says whether the threads file was captured at all.
The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) establishes nothing here: never use the code to infer a reviewer's decision. If the change merged but `context/review_threads.json` is absent or truncated, the loop had some state at merge and you could not read it: report a collection gap and record no observation. Never treat a missing file as an empty loop.

## Grounding
To answer that a gate stood at merge, quote the deciding review evidence — the reviewer and their decision, or the thread's path:line — and the dated facts that show it still stood at the merge timestamp. To answer that nothing stood, cite the complete bounded review record — the merge timestamp, every decision and every thread's resolution with dates — that shows none remained. To answer that the change did not merge, quote the state. When the qualified sources were inspected but cannot establish the state at merge — a change-request with no date that could precede or follow the merge, a current resolution or approval with unknown timing — name the unresolved historical question instead of answering. Describe only the observable state: "merged with N request-changes still standing; thread at <path:line> unresolved at merge". Never "you ignored the reviewer" or "you merged broken code"; never a claim about the code's correctness; never a current open or resolved state offered as proof of the state at merge.

## Defer
Whether threads on an OPEN pull request are being taken up belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`. Here only: was the loop closed at the moment of merge? Do not double-flag.

questions.title: The change merged
questions.question: Does context/metadata.json record the change as merged (state merged, with merged_at when the provider recorded it)? A pull request that is still open, or closed without merging, is NO.
questions.yes: The change merged, e.g. state MERGED, merged_at 2026-05-12T09:14Z.
questions.no: The change did not merge: it is open, or closed unmerged.

questions.title: A change-request still stood at merge
questions.question: At the merge timestamp, did any reviewer's change-request decision (context/review_threads.json) still stand? Read decisions as dated events against merged_at: a change-request submitted after the merge did not stand at it. A change-request is superseded only by that reviewer's later approval, or a dated reviewer comment lifting it, before merged_at; an approval or comment after the merge does not supersede it, and a current decision field is not proof of the state at merge. If a deciding change-request or approval carries no date, so that it could precede or follow the merge, leave the answer open and name what would settle it. If context/review_threads.json was not captured or is truncated, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: A request stood at merge, e.g. reviewer 'mkim' requested changes on 05-10 and the change merged on 05-12 with no later approval from mkim.
questions.no: No change-request stood at merge, e.g. 'mkim' requested changes on 05-10 and approved on 05-11, before the 05-12 merge; or no reviewer requested changes.

questions.title: A review thread was unresolved at merge
questions.question: At the merge timestamp, was any review thread in context/review_threads.json still open: opened before merged_at by someone other than the pull request author, and neither resolved before merged_at nor withdrawn before it by a dated note from the reviewer who opened it? A thread opened after the merge did not exist at it; a resolution after the merge does not close it beforehand, and an outdated anchor closes nothing. Read each candidate's comments in context/comments.json by its id. If a deciding opening or resolution carries no date, so that it could precede or follow the merge, leave the answer open and name what would settle it. If context/review_threads.json was not captured or is truncated, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: A thread was open at merge, e.g. the thread at src/api/client.ts:42, opened before the merge, has no resolution, or was resolved an hour after merged_at.
questions.no: Every thread opened before the merge was resolved or withdrawn before merged_at, or no review thread existed at the merge.

rules.reason: The change has not merged, so there is no merge-time review loop to assess.
The change merged while a reviewer's request for changes still stood.
The change merged while a review thread was still unresolved.
Every reviewer change-request and review thread was resolved or superseded before the change merged.

groups.name: Writing issues a maintainer can act on
groups.description: Write issues someone can pick up without coming back to ask what you meant. State the problem clearly, what you saw versus expected plus steps to reproduce for a bug, or the who and why for a request, keep each issue to one concern, say how to tell when it is done, and link the design or decision the work depends on.

practices.name: State a problem a maintainer can act on
practices.whyItMatters: A maintainer cannot fix what they cannot picture. An issue that leaves out what you saw versus what you expected, or the who and why behind a request, comes straight back with 'can you clarify?' and you both lose a day.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A bug report that reads 'uploading a 0-byte file returns 500, I expected a clear validation error' and lists the exact steps to reproduce, so a maintainer can start straight away. Or a request that names one concrete capability with who it helps and why, such as 'reviewers lose track of which files changed in large diffs, so add a per-file changed-lines summary to the review view'.
practices.holdsAs: Issues state a problem a maintainer can act on
