practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: the issue, read on its own, gives a maintainer enough to start work without a clarification round-trip.

## The standard
Judge whether this issue lets a maintainer picture what is wrong or what is wanted, and begin. The bar is the one a senior triager applies. A reader must be able to identify the kind of work and find the concrete substance it needs. For a defect report: the actual or observed behaviour, the expected behaviour, and how to reproduce it — a concrete reproduction path (numbered steps, or a stack trace, an exact error or a failing test) is the single most valuable and most-often-missing element, so weight it accordingly. For a capability request: a concrete capability stated clearly, ideally with who benefits and why. A specific title that locates the work — not a bare slug, an empty template or "it's broken" — is part of being act-on-able. Use judgment for forms not enumerated here: an issue that ships a quotable acceptance-criteria, Definition-of-Done or Given-When-Then block is act-on-able on that block alone; do not then demand a beneficiary or a "so that" clause. An epic, umbrella or requirement card carrying substantive prose is act-on-able at the requirement level; its detail lives in child stories, so judge it as a requirement, never as a thin story. An untyped issue that nonetheless asserts a malfunction IS a defect report; judge it as one.

## Sources
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`context/description.md`): every section, template field, step list and criteria block. It establishes the kind of work and the substance stated inline. An image: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
2. The title and labels (`context/metadata.json`): a deliverable-type label names the kind of work. It never establishes substance by itself; an empty template echoing the title under such a label is still empty.
3. The comments (`context/comments.json`): part of the observable artifact; substance stated there counts. They never establish substance you cannot quote from them.
4. Linked design, decision or spec documents (`context/docs/`): when the issue delegates its substance to a document materialized here, read it. A concrete capability or interface the document actually specifies is substance an implementer can start from; count it as observed rather than demanding the issue restate it inline. A generic document or a placeholder marker that does not concretely pin THIS work supplies nothing.
When the issue delegates its substance to a specific named document that was NOT materialized, you cannot tell whether that substance exists: report a collection gap and record no observation, never a claim against prose you were never shown. If the issue text was not captured completely, the same.

## Grounding
To answer YES that an element is present, quote it from the body, a comment, or the materialized document with its `context/docs/...` path; an element you cannot quote is absent. A NO that rests on absence must first search the whole body, the labels, the comments, and the `context/docs/` documents or their absence, and name that boundary. To answer that the issue is not work, quote the question or discussion it poses. Never invent content and never grant a clean bill you did not verify. Describe the observable gap — "the body names a symptom but no reproduction path" — never the reporter's intent or character.

## Defer
Whether the issue has a checkable or measurable outcome belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Whether it duplicates another filed issue, beyond noting an evident restatement, belongs to `issue-scoped-to-single-concern`. Here only: can a maintainer picture the work and start?

questions.title: Asks for engineering work
questions.question: Does the issue assert a defect or request a capability or task, meaning work a maintainer could start on? A title that names a task or a capability is engineering work even when the body is empty. An untyped issue that asserts a malfunction is a defect report. Only a pure question or an open discussion that asserts no defect and requests no capability is not work.
questions.yes: The issue asserts a defect or requests a capability or task, e.g. 'uploading a 0-byte file returns 500', or a bare title such as 'Add a dark mode toggle'.
questions.no: The issue is a pure question or an open discussion, e.g. 'Which charting library should we use?'.

questions.title: Gives a concrete starting point
questions.question: Does the issue give a concrete starting point, quotable from the title, the body, a comment, or a materialized document under `context/docs/` that it delegates to? For a defect, that is a concrete symptom (the observed behaviour, an exact error, a stack trace, a failing test), which the title alone may state, or reproduction steps. For a capability or task, it is the concrete capability; a bare title naming it is not enough. An acceptance-criteria, Definition-of-Done or Given-When-Then block counts on its own, and so does an epic or requirement card with substantive prose. These do not count: an empty body; an untouched template that echoes the title, even under a 'bug' or 'feature' label; 'it's broken'; a generic or placeholder document. If the issue delegates its substance to a specific document or link that was not captured, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: A concrete symptom, reproduction steps or capability is quotable, e.g. 'uploading a 0-byte file returns 500' or 'add a per-file changed-lines summary to the review view'.
questions.no: No concrete symptom anywhere, title included; or, for a capability, nothing past a bare title: an empty body, an untouched template, or 'it's broken'.

questions.title: Reports a defect
questions.question: Is the issue a defect report, asserting that something behaves wrongly (a crash, an error, a wrong result), whatever its label or type? A capability request, a task or an epic is not.
questions.yes: The issue asserts a malfunction, e.g. 'the export button does nothing in Safari'.
questions.no: The issue requests a capability or a task, or is an epic, e.g. 'add CSV export to the reports page'.

questions.title: States observed, expected and how to reproduce
questions.question: Does the defect report state the observed behaviour, the expected behaviour and a concrete reproduction path (numbered steps, a stack trace, an exact error or a failing test)? The reproduction path is the element most often missing, so look for it first. The symptom can make the expected behaviour plain: a crash, an exception or an error message is expected not to happen, and needs no sentence saying so. An acceptance-criteria, Definition-of-Done or Given-When-Then block is enough on its own. Elements stated in a comment or in a materialized document the issue delegates to count. If the issue delegates to a document that was not captured, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: Every element is quotable, e.g. 'returns 500', 'I expected a validation error' and numbered steps, or 'the app crashes on launch' with its stack trace.
questions.no: An element is missing, e.g. a symptom with no steps, trace or exact error, or a wrong result with no statement of the right one.

questions.title: Title locates the work
questions.question: Does the title locate the work specifically, naming the behaviour, component or capability concerned? A bare slug, an empty template's default title or 'it's broken' does not.
questions.yes: The title names what is wrong or wanted, e.g. 'Upload of 0-byte file returns 500' or 'Add a dark mode toggle'.
questions.no: The title locates nothing, e.g. 'bug', 'issue-3', 'it's broken' or a template's default title.

rules.reason: The issue is a question or discussion that asserts no defect and requests no capability.
The issue names no concrete symptom, reproduction path or capability a maintainer could start from.
The defect report names the problem but leaves out its expected behaviour or a concrete reproduction path.
The issue body states the work, but the title does not say what is wrong or wanted.
The issue states what is wrong or wanted with the substance a maintainer needs to start.

practices.name: Keep the issue to one concern
practices.whyItMatters: An issue that quietly bundles three unrelated asks cannot be assigned, estimated, or closed cleanly. One part lands, the rest linger, and the whole thing stays open forever, tracking nothing.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: One issue, one deliverable, such as 'add CSV export to the reports page', rather than 'add CSV export, fix the date picker, and bump the chart library' crammed into one ticket.
practices.holdsAs: Each issue asks for one deliverable, not a bundle
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: how the issue is scoped — one cohesive deliverable at the issue's intended level, rather than unrelated asks stapled into one ticket.

## The standard
A good issue tracks ONE cohesive deliverable: something that can be picked up, worked and closed as a single unit. Judge cohesion as an experienced reviewer would: is there a single thread of intent, or have unrelated asks been stapled together so that part can land while the rest lingers? The test is whether a maintainer would naturally assign, estimate and close it as one thing, or would be fighting to. One feature, one bug, one question is one concern. Internal decomposition is still ONE concern: implementation sub-steps, a checklist that builds up one capability, a sub-issue rollup that breaks one feature into trackable children. An epic that bundles several RELATED facets of the same feature area (create, rename, delete plus search for one entity) is ONE concern at its altitude; that breadth is what makes it an epic. The tell of bundling is separable threads of intent targeting different concerns, never the mere presence of "and" or a long checklist.

## Sources
Judge only from the issue body, its labels and its sub-issue rollup as captured.
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`context/description.md`): every section, checklist and step list, and the sub-issue rollup when the capture carries it. It establishes the deliverable(s) named and how they relate. It never establishes what the author meant beyond the written spans.
2. The labels and title (`context/metadata.json`): the issue's intended level — epic, feature, bug, task. They establish the altitude at which to judge cohesion. They never establish cohesion by themselves.
3. The workspace inventory (`context/project_inventory.json`): sibling issues. Open it and state either the overlapping or duplicate issue you found — quote its `#number "title" (state)` — or that you scanned the inventory and found none. A bundled concern that clearly warrants its own existing or separate sibling is evidence of multiple concerns; confirm against actual titles and bodies, never from sibling count alone.
An image in the body: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. If the issue was only partly captured, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
To answer that the issue names a deliverable, quote the span that names it; to answer that it names none, quote the question, discussion or template text, or say the body is empty. To answer YES on bundling, quote the spans that name each separable concern; to answer NO, quote the span that names the one deliverable or its related facets. State the inventory result with every bundling answer: the overlapping or duplicate sibling as `#number "title" (state)`, or that you scanned the inventory and found none. Describe the observable bundling — "the body names three deliverables with no shared thread" — never carelessness or intent. Never invent a deliverable, a clean bill, or a bundling you did not read.

## Defer
Whether an epic should itself be split into tracked child stories belongs to `breaks-large-work-into-trackable-subtasks`; do not double-count it. Here only: is this issue one concern at its level?

questions.title: Names a concrete deliverable
questions.question: Does the issue name at least one concrete deliverable to scope: a feature, a bug, a task? It does not when it is a pure question, a support request, an open discussion, an empty or title-only body, or an untouched template.
questions.yes: The body names something to build or fix, e.g. 'add CSV export to the reports page'.
questions.no: There is no concrete deliverable to scope: a question, a support request, a discussion, an empty or title-only body, or an untouched template.

questions.title: Fuses unrelated deliverables into one ticket
questions.question: Does the issue fuse unrelated deliverables into one ticket: separable threads of intent aimed at different concerns, which a maintainer would not assign, estimate and close as one thing? Judge at the issue's intended level, which its labels and title give (epic, feature, bug, task). These are one concern: implementation sub-steps, a checklist that builds one capability, a sub-issue rollup that splits one feature, an epic of related facets of one feature area. 'And' or a long checklist is never the tell by itself. Check `context/project_inventory.json`. An ask that plainly duplicates an existing sibling's title and body is evidence of a separate concern; the number of siblings is not. If the complete text leaves one journey versus separate deliverables unresolved, leave the answer open and say what would settle it.
questions.yes: Separable threads of intent are stapled together, e.g. 'add CSV export, fix the date picker, and bump the chart library'.
questions.no: One cohesive deliverable at its level, e.g. an epic to create, rename, delete and search projects.

questions.title: The bundled asks share nothing
questions.question: Do the bundled asks share no feature, component or goal at all, as with a UI feature, a dependency upgrade and an unrelated bug fix, so that each would land on its own and the ticket would stay open after the first one lands? Asks within one feature area, or separable asks a maintainer could still split without either part left open on its own, are not this. When unsure, answer no.
questions.yes: The asks have nothing in common, e.g. a new report view, a library upgrade and an unrelated login bug.
questions.no: The asks share a feature, component or goal, or the issue holds one concern.

rules.reason: The issue names no concrete deliverable to scope: it is a question, a discussion or an empty template.
The issue bundles deliverables that share no feature or goal, so part can land while the rest stays open.
The issue bundles separable asks that would track more cleanly as linked issues.
The issue tracks one cohesive deliverable at its level.

practices.name: Define a checkable outcome
practices.whyItMatters: Without a clear line for 'done', nobody can tell when the work is finished, including the person doing it. A checkable outcome turns 'improve performance' from an open-ended wish into a task someone can actually complete.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A short acceptance checklist a maintainer can tick off when the work is truly finished, such as 'export downloads a valid CSV' and 'an empty result shows a friendly message', rather than a vague hope of improvement.
practices.holdsAs: Every issue says what done looks like
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: a quotable finish line — an outcome a maintainer could later verify as DONE from the issue alone.

## The standard
Judge one thing: does this issue define an outcome a maintainer could later verify as done? A good issue draws a clear finish line: a reader can tell, from the issue alone, what state of the world means the work is complete. The line can take many shapes — an acceptance checklist, a Given-When-Then block, a story's who/what/why phrased so the result is testable, or, for a bug, a stated expected behaviour a fix must restore. The form does not matter; the testability does. Use judgment as an experienced reviewer would; do not hunt for a keyword or label. Good: "export downloads a valid CSV; an empty result shows a friendly message". Bad: "improve performance" with nothing that could ever read as done, or a body that only echoes its title. For an umbrella, epic or requirement card, the right checkable outcome is a definition of done that decomposes into child work, not an inline checklist: bundling many capabilities is expected of it.

## Sources
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`context/description.md`): every section, checklist, criteria block and expected-behaviour statement. It establishes a finish line you can quote. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
2. The labels and title (`context/metadata.json`): the kind of issue, including whether it is an umbrella, epic or requirement card. They never establish a finish line by themselves.
3. The comments (`context/comments.json`): a finish line stated there counts. They never establish one you cannot quote.
4. A linked design or spec document the issue delegates to, materialised as a `.md` file under `context/docs/`: when it states a concrete, testable contract THIS work must satisfy — specific behaviours, status codes, API or state conditions — that contract IS a quotable finish line. Read and quote it before concluding none exists. A generic guideline, or a placeholder document that does not pin this deliverable's done-state, supplies nothing. A document never materialised is not evidence in either direction: when the issue delegates its finish line to a specific document you were not shown, report a collection gap and record no observation, never a claim against prose you were not shown.
5. Child work: sub-issues or a task list referenced in the body or comments, or child entries in `context/project_inventory.json` when captured. For an umbrella, they establish the decomposition that makes its outcome checkable.

## Grounding
To answer YES, quote the span you relied on: the checklist, criteria block, expected behaviour, the document sentence with its `context/docs/...` file path, or the child references. A NO that rests on absence must first search the whole body, the labels, the comments, and the `context/docs/` documents or their absence, and name that boundary. To answer that the issue is not work, quote the question, discussion or placeholder text. Never invent a checklist, a clean bill or an exoneration you did not read. Never assert technical feasibility, design correctness or the author's competence. Describe the observable gap in the issue, never the author's character or motive.

## Defer
Whether the problem itself is well stated — observed versus expected, who/what/why as a narrative — belongs to `issue-states-an-actionable-problem`; do not write that relationship into the feedback. Here only: is there a verifiable finish line?

questions.title: Asks for engineering work
questions.question: Does this issue ask for engineering work: a capability to build, a task to do or a bug to fix? A title naming a task or a capability counts even when the body is empty. These are NOT work: a question, a support request, an open discussion, a bare board or ceremony placeholder with no asserted problem and no requested capability.
questions.yes: The issue names a deliverable: a capability, a task or a bug fix.
questions.no: The issue is a question, a discussion, a support request or an empty placeholder.

questions.title: Says what done looks like
questions.question: Can a reader tell, from the body, the comments or a materialized document under `context/docs/` that the issue delegates to, what state of the world means the work is done? Any of these is a finish line: an acceptance checklist; a Given-When-Then block; a story whose 'I want …' names an observable capability; for a defect, the expected behaviour a fix must restore (for a crash or an error report that is plain: the crash or error stops); or a delegated document's concrete contract for this work. These are not: a body that only echoes the title, a vague aim such as 'improve performance', a generic guideline or placeholder document, a label. If the issue delegates its finish line to a specific document or link that was not captured, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: A finish line is quotable, e.g. 'As a reader, I want to export a report as CSV', or 'export downloads a valid CSV; an empty result shows a friendly message'.
questions.no: Nothing past the title says what done looks like, e.g. an empty body, or only 'improve performance'.

questions.title: Umbrella with child work
questions.question: Is this an umbrella, epic or requirement card whose done is carried by child work: child issues or a task list referenced in the body or comments, a non-zero `sub_issues_total`, or child entries in `context/project_inventory.json` when captured? An issue that is not an umbrella is a no. For an umbrella whose text names no child work while `sub_issues_total` is null, the provider's rollup was not captured: leave the answer open.
questions.yes: The issue is an umbrella and its child work is quotable, e.g. 'sub_issues_total: 3' or '- [ ] #41 sign-in'.
questions.no: The issue is not an umbrella, or it is one with a captured rollup of zero and no child work named.

questions.title: Umbrella that describes its requirement
questions.question: Is this an umbrella, epic or requirement card (by its labels, title or body) that carries substantive prose describing the requirement it covers? Bundling many capabilities is expected of such an issue. A bare epic title over an empty body does not count.
questions.yes: The issue is an umbrella, epic or requirement card with substantive prose, e.g. an 'Epic: Accounts' body describing sign-up, sign-in and password reset.
questions.no: The issue is not an umbrella, or it is one with no substantive prose.

rules.reason: The issue is a question, a discussion or an empty placeholder, not a deliverable.
The issue asks for a deliverable but states no outcome and no child work that would show when it is done.
The umbrella issue describes its requirement but maps its done to no child issues or task list.
The issue states a finish line a maintainer could check, or maps its done to child work.

practices.name: Point the issue to the context it depends on
practices.whyItMatters: An issue that silently depends on decisions made elsewhere forces every implementer to re-discover the context — or, worse, to guess it and build the wrong thing.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: When work depends on an existing design or decision, the issue links the document that holds it, so whoever picks it up starts with the rationale already in hand.
practices.holdsAs: Issues link the design or decision they rest on
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: an issue that depends on a design, decision, spec, runbook or data model recorded elsewhere points the implementer to the document that holds it.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when an issue clearly depends on prior context an implementer would need to act on it correctly — an existing design, a decision record, a spec, a runbook, a data model — does the issue point them to that context with a link to the relevant wiki document, instead of assuming the reader already carries it? The signal is judged from the issue's own text: it leans on decisions or designs made elsewhere — "per our architecture", "following the agreed rollout plan", "as decided for the billing redesign", "must match the data model" — such that someone picking it up cold could not proceed correctly without locating that source. A link count is never the signal, and a link to an unrelated document is not credit. Do not infer a hidden dependency the text does not express.

## Sources
1. The title and the whole body (`context/description.md`, `context/metadata.json`): every phrase that appeals to context made elsewhere, and every link. It establishes whether the issue leans on external context and whether it points anywhere. It never establishes that a linked document is relevant; a bare link is not evidence on its own. An image: read its caption and the sentence around it. A link outside the wiki is never materialized: it is a document you were not shown, below.
2. The linked wiki documents materialized under `context/docs/`: read each to judge whether it is actually the context the issue leans on. A document establishes relevance when a passage in it carries the design, decision or spec the issue depends on. It never establishes relevance by its title alone.
When the issue links a specific document that was NOT materialized for you, you cannot tell whether it carries the context: report a collection gap and record no observation — neither credit nor criticism.

## Grounding
To answer that the issue leans on outside context, quote the exact phrase that appeals to it ("as decided…", "per the design", "must match…"); to answer that it does not, say the issue reads as self-contained. To answer that it points to the context, cite the materialized document's `context/docs/` file path and quote or closely paraphrase the passage that carries it. A NO that rests on absence must first read the whole title and body and every materialized document, and state what context an implementer would need but is not pointed to. Never invent a document, a decision or a dependency; talk about the issue's text, never the reporter's intent or character.

## Defer
Whether the issue is actionable on its own terms belongs to `issue-states-an-actionable-problem`; the two are disjoint. Here only: does an issue that depends on external design or decision context actually point to it?

questions.title: Issue depends on context recorded elsewhere
questions.question: Does the issue's own text lean on an existing design, decision record, spec, runbook or data model made elsewhere ('per our architecture', 'following the agreed rollout plan', 'as decided for the billing redesign', 'must match the data model'), such that someone picking it up cold could not proceed correctly without locating that source? Most issues are self-contained: a clear bug report, a small well-described change, a question. When the issue reads as self-contained, the answer is no. A link count is never the signal, and do not infer a hidden dependency the text does not express.
questions.yes: The text appeals to context made elsewhere, e.g. 'as decided for the billing redesign, use the new invoice states'.
questions.no: The issue reads as self-contained, e.g. a bug report with steps, or a small change described in full.

questions.title: Links the document that holds the context
questions.question: Does the issue point to the document that holds the context it leans on? Yes when a document the issue links, materialized under `context/docs/`, carries that design, decision or spec in a passage, not just in its title. No when the issue links nothing, links only material plainly unrelated to that context, or links a materialized document that does not carry it. When the issue links a specific document that was not materialized (any link outside the wiki, such as a repository file or a shared document), you cannot read it: leave the answer open.
questions.yes: A linked document under `context/docs/` carries the context, e.g. 'billing-redesign.md' states the invoice states the issue refers to.
questions.no: The issue links nothing, or only material that does not carry the context it leans on.

questions.title: Missing context would likely lead to the wrong build
questions.question: Is the outside context the issue leans on load-bearing enough that an implementer would likely build the wrong thing without it, because the text defers a concrete design choice, contract or data shape to that source? A mild lean that a link would merely make convenient is not. When unsure, the lean is mild.
questions.yes: Without the source an implementer would likely build the wrong thing, e.g. 'must match the data model' with fields and rules decided only there.
questions.no: The lean is mild: the issue is workable, and a link to the source would be a convenience.

rules.reason: The issue is self-contained and leans on no design or decision recorded elsewhere.
The issue defers a load-bearing design or decision to a source it does not link.
The issue leans on a design or decision made elsewhere without linking the document that holds it.
The issue links the document that holds the design or decision it depends on.

groups.name: Reviewing a teammate's work constructively
groups.description: Review a teammate's change well. Leave specific, actionable comments, raise concerns as questions rather than commands, and read the change before approving it rather than waving it through.

practices.name: Leave specific, actionable review comments
practices.subject: REVIEWER
practices.whyItMatters: 'This looks off' leaves the author guessing what to change and why. A comment that points at the exact line and names the concern gets fixed, while a vague one just slows the change down.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A note anchored to the line that says 'this throws when items is empty, so guard the loop or return early on a null list', so the author knows exactly what to do next.
practices.holdsAs: Review comments name the line and the fix
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: the substantive comments a reviewer wrote on this pull request each point at something concrete and tell the author what to do about it.

## The standard
Judge the craft of the comments a reviewer wrote — never whether the reviewer's claim about the code is correct, and never the author's code. A useful comment names a specific construct or anchors to a real line AND states an actionable substance: what is wrong, what to change, a concrete alternative, or a pointed question a maintainer can actually answer. A vague comment is a content-free gesture that leaves the author guessing: "this is messy", "fix this", "cleanup", a bare "?". Inline (diff-anchored) notes and conversation-tab notes meet the same standard. A blunt but specific comment is useful here; a polite but vague one is not. A reviewer comment is one whose author differs from the pull request author in the metadata.

## Sources
1. The inline review comments (`context/comments.json`): each comment's author, body and path:line anchor. They establish the diff-anchored comments and their positions. The review decisions (`context/review_threads.json`, when captured) add the body a reviewer wrote with an approval or a request for changes; such a body is a review note without a position.
2. The conversation notes (`context/general_comments.json`): each note's author and body. A conversation note has no position; it establishes only author and body.
3. The pull request metadata (`context/metadata.json`): the pull request author, which separates reviewer comments from author notes.
4. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the hunk a comment anchors to. Read it to confirm the comment points at something real. It never establishes whether the comment's claim is correct; assess the comment, not the code.
If the artifact shows a review happened but the comment bodies were not materialized for you, reviewer craft exists that you could not read: report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
Quote verbatim every comment you answer is vague — with its path:line for an inline comment; by author and body for a conversation note, which has no position, so never invent a file:line for it. Quote at least one useful comment when one exists. To answer that no substantive reviewer comment survives, say which notes you listed and why each was set aside. Never call a comment vague without quoting it; never fabricate a comment to avoid looking idle. A comment you can read is judged; one you cannot read is a collection gap. Talk about the comments; never grade the reviewer as a person or impute intent.

## Defer
Whether the author took the comments up or left threads open belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`; tone and politeness belong to `reviews-respectfully-asks-rather-than-demands`. Here only: could the author act on what the reviewer wrote?

questions.title: A substantive reviewer comment survives
questions.question: List every review note in your context: inline comments (context/comments.json), review-decision bodies (context/review_threads.json, when captured), conversation notes (context/general_comments.json) and any discussion rendered in the artifact text. Set aside the pull request author's own notes (by the login in context/metadata.json); comments flagged bot; bare approvals, acknowledgements, thanks or praise that ask for nothing ('LGTM', '+1', 'Nice!'); status replies that report what was done; off-topic chatter unconnected to this diff. Does at least one substantive reviewer comment remain? Never set a real reviewer comment aside because a field or flag is missing. If a review is recorded but its comment bodies were not captured, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: A person other than the author left a substantive note, e.g. 'parser.ts:88 — this loop re-reads the file on every token; read it once above.'
questions.no: Nothing survives the filter, e.g. a freshly opened pull request, or only a bot's coverage report and a reviewer's 'LGTM'.

questions.title: A reviewer comment is vague
questions.question: Among the substantive reviewer comments the first question kept, is at least one vague: a content-free gesture that leaves the author guessing what to change, such as 'this is messy', 'fix this', 'cleanup' or a bare '?'? A useful comment names a specific construct or anchors to a real line (confirm the hunk in work/change/diff.patch) AND states what is wrong, what to change, a concrete alternative or a pointed question; a short note whose line makes the ask plain ('unused import') is useful. Inline and conversation notes meet the same standard. A blunt but specific comment is useful; a polite but vague one is not. Judge the comment's craft, never whether its claim is correct.
questions.yes: At least one comment leaves the author guessing, e.g. 'this is messy' on a 40-line hunk, or a bare '?'.
questions.no: Every substantive comment says what to change, e.g. 'Use Optional.ofNullable here; get() throws when the user has no email.'

questions.title: The review is mostly empty gestures
questions.question: Are most of the substantive reviewer comments the first question kept content-free gestures, like 'fix this', 'cleanup' or a bare '?', so that the author cannot act on the review? A stray vague comment among useful ones is NO, and a lone vague comment is a light cost, never this case.
questions.yes: Most comments are empty gestures, e.g. 'fix this', 'cleanup', '?' and one specific comment.
questions.no: Most comments are actionable, or a single vague comment stands alone or among useful ones.

rules.reason: No substantive reviewer comment survives on this pull request, so there is no review craft to assess.
Most of the review comments are content-free gestures that leave the author unable to act.
A review comment is too vague for the author to tell what to change.
Every substantive review comment points at something concrete and says what to do about it.

practices.name: Comment on the code, not the person
practices.subject: REVIEWER
practices.whyItMatters: The same point can be made as a question or as a put-down, and people remember which one you chose. A curious question gets acted on, while sarcasm and bare orders breed defensiveness and make the next review harder.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: 'What happens if this runs twice, could we hit a race here?' rather than 'this is obviously broken, did you even test it?', so disagreement lands on the code and never on the author.
practices.holdsAs: Comments land on the code, never on the author
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: how the REVIEWER's substantive comments are voiced — as questions, suggestions and reasoned disagreement aimed at the code, or as orders, sarcasm or contempt aimed at the person.

## The standard
Judge whether the reviewer's comments stay civil and collaborative: concerns raised as questions or suggestions, disagreement carrying a reason ("I'd prefer X because Y"), rather than bare orders, belittling, sarcasm, contempt, name-calling or hostility aimed at the author. This is about HOW feedback is voiced, never whether the technical point is correct. Directness, brevity and strong technical disagreement are not incivility: "This will NPE when items is empty" is blunt and civil. A command paired with a reason is fine. Do not flag a word like "just" or "obviously" when it reads neutrally; judge the whole phrasing in context as an experienced reviewer would. The subject is the reviewer, never the changed code: "a big pull request got little review" is not an observation.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): the author, to apply the filter, and the state. It establishes who is a reviewer. It never establishes tone.
2. Inline review comments (`context/comments.json`): each carries path, line, body and author. They establish what a reviewer said at a position in the code. The review decisions (`context/review_threads.json`, when captured) carry the body a reviewer wrote with an approval or a request for changes, which is reviewer speech too.
3. Conversation-tab comments (`context/general_comments.json`): author and body, no path or line. They establish what a reviewer said about the change as a whole.
Judge tone across every comment source. An image in a comment: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. If the record shows a review happened but the comment bodies are not in your context, there was reviewer speech you could not read: report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
Quote every incivility marker you count verbatim, with its author; never fabricate a comment, a clean bill or an exoneration. Cite an inline comment only by the path and line it actually carries; cite a conversation-tab comment by author and quoted text and leave the location empty. To answer that every comment is civil, cite the surviving comments you read. To answer that no reviewer comment survives, name what the filter set aside. When the complete captured context leaves the tone of a quoted comment genuinely ambiguous, name what would settle it instead of answering. Frame everything about the COMMENT — "this phrasing reads as a demand" — never about the reviewer as a person; no hunches, no psychoanalysing, no intent inferred beyond the words.

## Defer
Whether a comment is specific, actionable or technically right belongs to `leaves-useful-specific-review-comments` and `reviews-substantively-with-understanding`; a vague-but-civil comment is still civil here. Here only: does the phrasing land on the code and not on the author?

questions.title: A substantive reviewer comment survives
questions.question: Does at least one substantive comment by a reviewer survive, across inline comments (context/comments.json), review-decision bodies (context/review_threads.json, when captured) and conversation comments (context/general_comments.json)? A reviewer is anyone whose login differs from the pull request author's in context/metadata.json; never count the author's own words. Skip comments the record flags bot and bare approvals ('LGTM', '+1'). The flag is the provider's classification: a numeric or token-like login without it is a human reviewer. An unreviewed pull request has none. If a review is recorded but its comment bodies were not captured, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: A human reviewer wrote at least one substantive comment, e.g. 'Why not reuse the existing DateFormatter here?'
questions.no: No substantive human reviewer comment survives, e.g. no review yet, or only a bot's lint report and 'LGTM'.

questions.title: A reviewer comment carries an incivility marker
questions.question: Does at least one surviving reviewer comment carry a quotable incivility marker: a bare order with no reason stated or evident from the line it sits on ('Change this.'), belittling that implies the author should not have needed telling, sarcasm or contempt, name-calling, or hostility aimed at the person? Judge how the point is voiced, never whether it is correct. Directness, brevity and strong technical disagreement are not incivility: 'This will NPE when items is empty' is blunt and civil, a command paired with a reason is fine, and a short specific instruction whose line makes the reason plain ('Remove this debug print.') is direct, not a bare order. Judge a word like 'just' or 'obviously' by the whole phrasing. If a comment's tone stays genuinely ambiguous, leave the answer open and say what would settle it.
questions.yes: A comment reads as an order, sarcasm or contempt, e.g. 'Change this.', 'Did you even run this?', 'Obviously this is wrong, as anyone would know.'
questions.no: Every comment raises its point as a question, suggestion or reasoned disagreement, e.g. 'I'd prefer a map here because lookups are O(1).'

questions.title: Incivility forms a pattern or targets the person
questions.question: Do the surviving reviewer comments (not the author's, not bot-flagged, not bare approvals) show incivility as a pattern across several comments, or contain contempt, name-calling or hostility aimed at the author as a person? A single sharp-but-impersonal edge, such as one bare 'Change this.', is NO.
questions.yes: Several comments are bare orders or sarcasm, or one attacks the person, e.g. 'Are you even a developer?'
questions.no: At most a single sharp but impersonal comment, or none.

rules.reason: No substantive human reviewer comment survives on this pull request, so there is no reviewer phrasing to judge.
Several review comments read as demands or sarcasm, or one aims contempt or hostility at the author rather than the code.
A review comment reads as a bare order, sarcasm or belittling rather than a point about the code.
Every review comment raises its point about the code as a question, suggestion or reasoned disagreement.

practices.name: Explain consequential review judgments
practices.subject: REVIEWER
practices.whyItMatters: A short explanation makes the basis of an important approval or concern available to the author and other reviewers. A bare approval alone does not show what was checked; it also does not prove that the reviewer failed to read the change.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: For a consequential authorization change, a reviewer names the permission check they considered and explains why it addresses the concern, or asks a specific unresolved question. A routine change with no material concern may need only a brief approval.
practices.holdsAs: Reviews that call for reasoning get it in writing
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: a review whose captured context called for written reasoning carries a substantive comment grounded in the change.

## The standard
Judge the written explanation accompanying a review, not whether the reviewer read or understood the change. A substantive comment makes the reviewer's reasoning inspectable: it names or quotes a concrete diff element — a path, a symbol or a term that actually appears in the diff or summary you can see — or asks a real clarifying question about the change. One such comment is enough; polish, tone and specificity are not graded here. A bare approval or acknowledgement ("LGTM", "+1", a lone thumbs-up) supplies no written reasoning, but it does not establish that the review was careless or superficial. Written reasoning is owed only when the captured context establishes an occasion for it: a request to explain a consequential trade-off, or a documented review requirement. Change size or risk alone does not make commentary mandatory. A reviewer is anyone whose login differs from the pull request author. Discount machine noise and empty ceremony: a comment or decision the record flags `bot` is not human review, and a content-free approval is not engagement. The flag is the provider's classification of the account; a login's shape decides nothing.

## Sources
1. The inline comments (`context/comments.json`) and the review threads (`context/review_threads.json`): the inline diff comments with their authors, and the review decisions with the body a reviewer wrote with each. They establish who reviewed, what was approved, and any inline reasoning. An empty inline record never establishes missing reasoning across the other sources, nor an unperformed review.
2. The general comments (`context/general_comments.json`): the conversation and discussion notes. The substance of a review may live here rather than inline; read whatever review notes are materialized, under whatever heading, before concluding nothing substantive exists. They also establish a request for an explanation, when one was made.
3. The description and metadata (`context/description.md`, `context/metadata.json`): the author's login for the reviewer filter, and any documented review requirement or trade-off the change raises. They never establish that reasoning was written.
4. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) and the checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether a comment's named path, symbol or term actually appears in the change, and the real size of the change once obviously generated or vendored bulk (lockfiles, generated clients, migrations, snapshots) is discounted — a "big" diff that is mostly generated is smaller than its line count. They never make commentary mandatory on their own.
Judge from the review notes and the change-size signals present in your context; do not claim per-comment or per-line facts you cannot see. Missing or incomplete required sources are a collection gap with no observation; never read a missing count as zero.

## Grounding
Inspect every declared source of review comments before answering. Cite the written comment that makes reasoning inspectable, and the diff element it names when it names one. To answer that written reasoning was required or requested, cite the context that establishes it — the request, or the documented review requirement. To answer that no substantive comment exists, cite the approval that supplied none and the boundary: every declared review-comment source inspected. When the captured requirement or explanation stays genuinely ambiguous after every source is inspected, name the unresolved question instead of answering. Never invent a comment, a file, a size or a clean bill you did not verify. Neither a not-yet-reviewed change nor an approval without commentary establishes a superficial review; describe what was written, never how the reviewer read.

## Defer
Whether the comments were specific and well-worded belongs to `leaves-useful-specific-review-comments`; whether the author acted on them belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`. Do not double-flag them here. Here only: does the written explanation meet its demonstrated purpose?

questions.title: A reviewer comment carries inspectable reasoning
questions.question: Does at least one comment by a human reviewer (a login that differs from the pull request author's in context/metadata.json, on a comment or decision the record does not flag bot) make the reviewer's reasoning inspectable: it names or quotes a concrete element that actually appears in the diff or summary (a path, a symbol, a term), or asks a real clarifying question about the change? Read the inline comments (context/comments.json), the review-decision bodies (context/review_threads.json) and the conversation notes (context/general_comments.json), under whatever heading; one empty source does not mean the others are. One such comment is enough; polish, tone and specificity are not graded. A bare approval or acknowledgement ('LGTM', '+1') is not reasoning. If a source of review notes was not captured, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: A reviewer comment engages the change, e.g. 'Why does RetryPolicy back off linearly here?' or 'The migration drops user.legacy_id — is anything still reading it?'
questions.no: The human review notes hold only bare approvals or acknowledgements, e.g. a lone 'LGTM' with an approval, or there are no review notes.

questions.title: The context calls for written review reasoning
questions.question: Does the captured context establish an occasion for written review reasoning — a request to explain a consequential trade-off (e.g. the description or a comment asks reviewers to weigh in on a choice), or a documented review requirement (e.g. in the description or a contributing guide in the checkout)? Read the description, metadata, general comments and review threads. Change size or risk alone never makes commentary mandatory; a 'big' diff that is mostly generated or vendored bulk (lockfiles, generated clients, migrations, snapshots) is smaller than its line count.
questions.yes: The context asks for reasoning, e.g. the description says 'Reviewers: please confirm whether dropping the cache is acceptable' or the repository requires reviewers to justify approvals.
questions.no: Nothing in the context requests or requires written reasoning, e.g. a routine change with no question for reviewers.

questions.title: A human reviewer approved the change
questions.question: Did a human reviewer (a login that differs from the pull request author's in context/metadata.json, on a decision the record does not flag bot) record an approval decision in context/review_threads.json?
questions.yes: A human reviewer approved, e.g. 'mkim APPROVED 2026-04-02'.
questions.no: No human approval is recorded: no review yet, only comments or change requests, or only a bot's approval.

questions.title: The unexplained decision is consequential
questions.question: Is the decision the reviewers were asked to weigh, or the sign-off the requirement covers, consequential and hard to revisit, so that without a written basis the author and other reviewers cannot later tell why it was accepted: for example dropping compatibility, changing stored data or a public contract, or a security trade-off? A routine choice that one follow-up question would settle at little cost is NO, and so is a blanket requirement to justify every approval when the change itself is routine. Judge the decision's consequence, never how carefully the reviewer read. When it is a close call, answer NO.
questions.yes: A consequential, hard-to-revisit choice stands unexplained, e.g. the author asked whether dropping backward compatibility is acceptable and the approval says only 'LGTM'.
questions.no: The missing explanation costs little to recover, e.g. the author asked which of two names reviewers prefer, or a quick follow-up question would settle it.

rules.reason: No review reasoning was written, and nothing in the captured context requests or requires it.
No human reviewer has approved the change or written a substantive comment, so no review explanation has come due.
The change was approved without written reasoning, leaving a consequential decision with no inspectable basis.
The change was approved with only bare acknowledgements although the context asked for written reasoning.
A reviewer comment names a concrete element of the change or asks a real question about it.

groups.name: Testing your changes
groups.description: When a change adds or fixes behaviour, it comes with the tests that exercise it. And it never quietly deletes, skips, or weakens a test just to make the build pass.

practices.name: Include tests with the change
practices.whyItMatters: Code without a test is a promise nobody can check, and it is one careless refactor away from quietly breaking. Adding the test alongside the logic locks in the behaviour you just built, which matters most when you are fixing a bug.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: New logic arrives with a test beside it, and a bug fix comes with a test that fails on the old code and passes on the new, proving the behaviour is what you say it is.
practices.holdsAs: New logic and fixes arrive with a test beside them
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: a test for the changed production behaviour arriving in the same change.

## The standard
Judge one workflow practice: when the change introduces non-trivial production behaviour, does a test for THAT behaviour arrive in the same diff? You are not hunting for missing edge cases, doing a lint sweep or re-judging the change's size; you are asking whether the new logic ships locked in by a test that could observe it. Production behaviour: a new function or endpoint, a new branch or computation, a changed validation or state transition. A covering test plausibly exercises that behaviour: it touches the same symbol, endpoint or path, or asserts the corrected result. A bug fix is strongest when it ships a test that would fail on the old code and pass on the new. Judge the PRESENCE and plausible linkage of a covering test, never its naming, readability or assertion style.

## Sources
This is decided from the diff alone.
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with the file list (`work/change/files.json`): classify each changed file as production or test by its path and name, using judgment about test conventions across languages. The production hunks establish the behaviour added or changed; the test hunks establish whether a test names the same symbol, endpoint or path, or asserts the corrected result. Neither establishes that any test ran.
2. The commits (`context/commits.json`): subjects that say what the change does, such as naming a fix. They establish the shape of the change; they never establish a per-commit mapping, since per-commit patches are not in your context.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): existing tests near the changed code, for context on where a covering test would live. The absence of a repository-wide test inventory is never a reason to abstain: load-bearing, testable logic shipped into a repository with no test target at all is the lesson, and is judged, not abstained from.
If a required part of the production or test diff is truncated or unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
Quote the exact added span each answer relies on. For YES on the behaviour question, quote the `[L<n>]` production line embodying the behaviour; for a NO there, name what the production changes are (layout, docs, config, a rename). For YES on the test question, quote the `[L<n>]` test span naming the shared symbol, endpoint or path, or asserting the corrected result. A NO on the test question rests on absence: quote the untested production line AND state the scan of every test file in the diff that found none covering it — that scan is the boundary. For the defect-fix question, quote the commit subject, title or production line that shows the correction. Never invent a test, a file or a clean bill you did not read. Never claim a test ran or passed, and never claim a per-commit mapping you did not observe. Describe the observable delivery; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Change size belongs to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; weakening an EXISTING suite belongs to `keeps-the-test-suite-honest`. Here only: did a test for the new behaviour ship with it?

questions.title: Adds testable production behaviour
questions.question: Does the diff add or change non-trivial production behaviour a test could observe: a new function or endpoint, a new branch or computation, a changed validation or state transition? Classify each changed file as production or test by its path and name, and first set aside generated, vendored, lock and migration files. These do not count: an empty diff; a test-only, docs-only or config-only change; a pure rename, format or type-only change; layout, meaning a view, control or style change with no branch, computation or state transition, such as a title, a colour, a spacing or a button whose action is empty. A view that gains a condition or changes state does add behaviour.
questions.yes: An added production line introduces logic a test could observe, e.g. a new function body, an if/switch branch, a computation, a validation, a state transition, a persistence or network call.
questions.no: The diff is empty, changes only tests, or its production changes are layout, styling, docs, config, renames, formatting or type-only, e.g. a new title and colour on a button whose action is empty.

questions.title: A test in the diff exercises the main new behaviour
questions.question: Does a test file added or changed in this same diff plausibly exercise the most consequential production behaviour the diff adds or changes, the logic the change exists for rather than an incidental helper? It does when it calls or names the same type, function, endpoint or path, or asserts the corrected result. Scan every test file in the diff first. Judge presence and plausible linkage, never naming, readability, assertion style or whether it ran. Tests in the checkout that this diff does not touch do not count, and a repository with no test target at all is still a NO. If the diff is truncated where test files could be, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: A test in the diff names the same symbol, endpoint or path as the main new behaviour, e.g. a new `parseDate` branch and a changed `ParseDateTest` that calls `parseDate` with that input.
questions.no: No test file in the diff touches the main new behaviour: the diff has no test changes, or its test changes concern something else.

questions.title: The untested behaviour fixes a defect
questions.question: Is the untested behaviour a fix for a defect, i.e. behaviour that was wrong before this pull request, which the title or a commit subject names as a bug or a changed production line visibly corrects? A new feature is not a defect fix, and neither is a commit that repairs this pull request's own earlier commit, the build or the layout. Answer about the behaviour the test question found untested.
questions.yes: The untested change corrects behaviour that was wrong before, e.g. a commit 'Fix off-by-one in pagination' and a changed loop bound with no test.
questions.no: The untested behaviour is new, or its only fixes repair this pull request's own work, build or layout, e.g. 'fix crash in settings screen' where that screen arrives here.

questions.title: The untested behaviour is substantial logic
questions.question: Is the untested behaviour, the most consequential one the test question found untested, itself substantial multi-path logic that one focused test would not pin, such as a state machine with several transitions or a save that deletes and replaces stored records? Judge that one behaviour by its consequence, never by line count or by adding up several pieces: a handful of small units that one test each would pin is NO, and so is a single if/else, guard, filter or switch mapping. When it is a close call, answer NO.
questions.yes: The main untested behaviour needs several tests to pin, e.g. a loader with idle, loading, loaded and failed states and a retry, or a save that replaces a record's children.
questions.no: The main untested behaviour is a small, focused piece one test would pin, e.g. a date helper, a sort-and-filter, or a switch mapping codes to labels.

rules.reason: The diff adds no production behaviour a test could observe: only tests, docs, config, layout or renames.
The change fixes a defect with no test in the diff to lock the corrected behaviour in.
The change adds substantial multi-path logic with no test in the diff that exercises it.
The change adds production behaviour without a test in the same diff that exercises it.
A test in the same diff exercises the production behaviour the change adds.

practices.name: Keep the test suite honest
practices.whyItMatters: Deleting or skipping a failing test to get a passing build hides the breakage instead of fixing it, and removes the alarm that would have caught it next time. The suite only protects you while it tells the truth.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Existing checks retain their regression coverage. A check that no longer applies is removed with a reason tied to the changed behavior; a still-relevant failing check is fixed at the cause rather than disabled.
practices.holdsAs: Existing checks stay effective or their removal is justified
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: changed existing checks retain their regression coverage, or their removal is justified by the captured change.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: does the change preserve the existing checks, or does it weaken them without a justified reason? An honest suite keeps telling the truth: when a test starts failing, the fix addresses the underlying cause, and when a test genuinely must go, it goes with a stated, quotable reason. Unjustified weakening deletes, disables, skips, comments out or hollows out a test or its assertions without explaining why the check is gone. Do not infer the author's motive or whether the build passed. The test is one of judgment, not keywords: can the check still fail on the regression it guarded? A faithful migration that preserves assertion strength — a rename, a move, an API upgrade, splitting one test into several, or deleting a test whose subject under test is itself removed in this same diff — is not a suppression. This is a craft practice about how the change treats its safety net, not a line-by-line lint sweep and never a merge gate.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, read exhaustively, with `work/change/files.json` to find the test files): every test hunk — an added skip or disable, a removed assertion or test block, commented-out executable test code, an assertion made trivially true, and any adjacent comment naming a tracker or a `reason=` / `@Disabled("…")` argument. It establishes what happened to each check and any reason written beside it. It never establishes that the suite ran.
2. The commits (`context/commits.json`) and the description (`context/description.md`): a line explaining a removal or skip. They establish a quotable reason tied to the change; they never establish a reason they do not state.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the unchanged surroundings of a touched test, to tell a hollowed assertion from a faithful move or split, and whether a deleted test's subject is gone. It never supplies a justification nobody wrote.
When the change touches a test surface but the patch is truncated so those hunks cannot be read, report a collection gap and record no observation; unread required evidence is not a judgment.

## Grounding
Quote the deciding test line(s) from the diff for every answer: the added skip or weakened assertion, or the removed line for a deletion. For YES on the existing-check question, cite the test hunk and file that changes an existing check. For a NO on the weakening question, cite the test hunks inspected, name the test file(s), and quote any reason relied on — the comment, `reason=` or `@Disabled("…")` argument, description line or commit subject. A YES on the weakening question rests on the absence of a reason: state that the diff, the description and the commit subjects were read and none explains the weakened check. Never claim to have run, compiled or executed the suite; you see only the patch. Never assert a suppression, or a justification, you cannot point to in the captured files — if you cannot quote it, it does not exist. Describe the observable behaviour of the diff; never impute intent or character, and never grade the author.

## Defer
Whether NEW tests were added for new logic belongs to `ships-tests-with-the-change`. Here only: does the change WEAKEN the existing safety net without saying why?

questions.title: Changes an existing hand-written check
questions.question: Does the diff change, move, skip, disable, comment out or delete an existing hand-written test or assertion, one that existed before this change? Use work/change/files.json to find the test files and inspect every changed check, however much generated output surrounds it. Generated or vendored test code does not count, and neither does a project template's placeholder test that asserts nothing. New tests alone are not existing checks, and a feature with no test changes does not count. A changed existing check counts whether it is preserved or weakened.
questions.yes: A test hunk modifies or removes lines of an existing test, e.g. an edited assertion, an added `@Disabled`, a deleted test method, or a test renamed, moved or split.
questions.no: The patch is empty, touches no test file, only adds new tests, or only changes generated, vendored or empty template placeholder tests.

questions.title: Weakens a check without a quotable reason
questions.question: Does the diff weaken an existing check with no quotable reason tied to it? Weakening: a real assertion becomes trivially true, a test block is dropped, executable test code is commented out, or a test is skipped or disabled. Ask whether the check can still fail on the regression it guarded, not whether a keyword appears. Not weakening: a faithful rename, move, API upgrade or split that keeps assertion strength, or deleting a test whose subject is itself removed in this diff. A reason counts only when it is written beside the check, in the description or in a commit, and the change supports it. If the hunk and the checkout cannot show whether a check can still fail, leave the answer open and name what would settle it.
questions.yes: An existing check is weakened and nothing in the diff, description or commits explains it, e.g. `@Disabled` added with no argument, or `assertEquals(expected, actual)` replaced by `assertTrue(true)`.
questions.no: Every changed check is as strong as before, or each removal or skip carries a supported reason, e.g. `@Disabled("flaky on CI, tracked in #412")`, or a test deleted with the class it tested.

questions.title: Unexplained weakening deletes, hollows or recurs
questions.question: Among the existing checks this diff weakens without a quotable reason, is any a deleted test or a hollowed assertion (made trivially true, or removed while its test stays), or are there several unexplained suppressions, rather than a single unexplained skip, disable or commented-out test?
questions.yes: e.g. a test method removed while the code it tested stays, `assertEquals(3, total)` turned into `assertNotNull(total)`, or three tests marked `@Ignore` with no reason.
questions.no: The only unexplained suppression is a single skipped, disabled or commented-out test, or there is none.

rules.reason: The diff changes no existing hand-written test or assertion, so no check could be weakened.
The change deletes or hollows existing tests, or suppresses several, without a stated reason.
The change skips, disables or comments out an existing test without a stated reason.
Every existing check the change touches stays as strong, or its removal or skip has a stated reason.

groups.name: Writing maintainable code
groups.description: Keep the changed code easy for the next person to read and change. Factor out duplication, keep units small and single-purpose, and leave no clutter behind, such as dead code, debug leftovers, or comments that just restate the line.

practices.name: Factor out duplication instead of copy-pasting
practices.whyItMatters: Copy-pasted logic means every future fix has to land in every copy, and the copy you forget keeps the old behaviour, which is exactly the bug. Pull the shared part into one place and you fix it once.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: By the time the same validation logic shows up a third time, you stop copying it and lift the shared concept into one named helper every caller uses, leaving a single source of truth instead of copies that drift apart. You hold off when blocks only look alike by coincidence, since forcing a shared abstraction on them is worse than the duplication.
practices.holdsAs: Repeated logic gets lifted into one named helper
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: added hand-written code expresses each maintained rule in one appropriate place, without unjustified copy-paste.

## The standard
Judge one closed corpus: the lines this pull request adds. A senior reviewer flags copy-paste: two or more added blocks near-identical in shape that differ only in a few literals, identifiers or types — the kind of repetition an Extract Function, a shared constant, a loop or a small lookup table would collapse into one source of truth (Fowler; Hunt & Thomas, DRY; Martin). The harm is drift: a fix has to land in every copy, and the copy that is forgotten becomes the bug. Judge the repeated unit of knowledge — the same computation or rule expressed twice — not text that merely looks alike. A coherent multi-line computation, validation, mapping or transform, or constant or config block can be a flaggable copy. A one-liner, a guard clause, a field assignment or a forced-similar idiom (equals/hashCode, builder chains, switch arms, DI or route registrations) is not — an idiom is a few lines the platform dictates; a repeated multi-line block can carry duplicated knowledge, including a view body or a fetch-decode-assign sequence. Length alone never establishes that two blocks express the same rule. Legitimately parallel repetition is not a defect: test cases, fixtures and table-driven or parametrized bodies are meant to look alike. Duplication can live within one function: sibling `if`, `case` or branch bodies that each repeat the same multi-line computation differing only in a constant are as flaggable as cross-function copies. Use judgment on whether two blocks are a genuine copy-paste or a coincidental shared idiom.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the `[L<n>]` new-side spans of the added hunks. It establishes every candidate pair — a flaggable pair must sit inside these lines. It never establishes duplication against unchanged repository code, which is out of scope either way; pre-existing duplication you cannot see being introduced here is not judged.
2. The file spread (`work/change/files.json`): which paths are generated or vendored (`*.gen.*`, lockfiles, OpenAPI specs, route trees, migrations and the like) or test fixtures. It establishes the hand-authored remainder you assess. It never establishes a pair.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the surrounding lines of a hunk cut off mid-block. It establishes the full shape of an added block. It never establishes a pair against code the change did not add.
The precomputed leads below these criteria list every pair of added blocks whose lines share a shape once names and literals are set aside, with both spans, the run length and the names that differ: decide every pair, and quote both spans. If the diff was not captured completely, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
For YES on the copy-paste question, quote both occurrences by path and `[L<n>]` span and name the delta between them; a duplication claim you cannot ground in two quoted added spans is not made. For the spread question, quote every further occurrence or distinct pair. A NO on the copy-paste question rests on a closed corpus: record `evidence.search` over the diff, cite the repeated-looking blocks you actually checked, including every pair in the precomputed leads, and state in the boundary that duplication against code outside the diff is out of scope either way. For a NO on the surface question, name what the added lines are (docs, generated, vendored, fixtures). Describe only the observable copy-paste practice: never assert the code is buggy, will diverge or will break, and never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether one block is too long or does too many things belongs to `keeps-functions-small-and-single-purpose`; never flag a single block here. Here only: repetition across added blocks.

questions.title: Adds hand-written code or configuration
questions.question: After setting aside generated or vendored files (`*.gen.*`, lockfiles, OpenAPI specs, route trees, migrations and the like) and test fixtures, does the diff add any hand-written code or configuration lines? A documentation, diagram or image diff does not count. Hand-written configuration that could repeat a maintained rule does count. Answer YES whenever such added lines exist, even when you read them and find no repetition.
questions.yes: The diff adds hand-written source or configuration lines, e.g. a new service class, a view, or an edited YAML config block.
questions.no: The added lines are only documentation, diagrams, images, generated or vendored output, or test fixtures.

questions.title: Two added blocks are near-identical copies
questions.question: Among the lines this diff adds, are two or more hand-written blocks near-identical in shape, differing only in a few literals, identifiers, bindings or types, that express the same computation or rule, so an Extract Function, a shared constant, a loop or a lookup table would collapse them into one source of truth? Both blocks must sit inside the added lines; duplication against unchanged code is out of scope. Decide every pair in the precomputed leads and every sibling `if`, `case` or branch body. A delta of only such literals or names is what makes two blocks copies, never what separates them. Can be a copy: a multi-line computation, validation, mapping, transform, constant or config block, view body, or fetch-decode-assign sequence. NOT a copy: a one-liner, a guard clause, a field assignment, an idiom of a few lines the platform dictates (equals/hashCode, one view's modifier chain, switch arms, DI or route registrations); parallel tests, fixtures, preview sample data, table-driven bodies; a single long block. Length alone never makes a copy.
questions.yes: Two quoted added spans repeat one rule with a small delta, e.g. two `case` bodies that each parse, validate and format a date and differ only in the format string.
questions.no: Every added hand-written block was read and none is a near-identical copy of another added block; the look-alikes are short idioms, tests, fixtures or coincidental shapes.

questions.title: The same copied logic sits in three or more places
questions.question: Does one copied unit of logic — a computation, validation, mapping, transform or fetch-decode-assign sequence that produces or checks data — appear in three or more added places? Two separate pairs are not three places. A view, markup or styling block that lays out or chooses what to show is not logic here, however often it is copied. Quote every occurrence. Answer NO when there is no copy.
questions.yes: e.g. the same input-validation block pasted into three form handlers, each occurrence quoted by path and `[L<n>]` span.
questions.no: Each copied unit appears twice, the copies are view, markup or styling blocks, or there is no copy.

rules.reason: The change adds no hand-written code or configuration: only docs, generated, vendored or fixture files.
The change pastes the same logic into three or more places instead of sharing it.
The change adds near-identical blocks that repeat one rule instead of sharing it.
The added code expresses each rule once, with no near-identical copies among the added blocks.

practices.name: Keep functions small and single-purpose
practices.whyItMatters: A function that does five things is hard to name, hard to test, and hard to change without breaking a part you forgot it touched. Small, focused functions are the ones you can actually hold in your head.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Instead of one long method that parses, validates, saves, and notifies, you have a few short functions, each doing one clearly named step you can read and test on its own.
practices.holdsAs: Functions stay short and do one named step each
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: added or substantially rewritten functions keep a coherent, scannable purpose without tangled concerns or obscuring nesting.

## The standard
Ask of the largest function the change introduces or substantially rewrites what a senior reviewer asks: can I hold its purpose in my head, name it in a phrase, and follow it at a glance? A focused function does one nameable job. The defect is a single body that visibly interleaves several SUBSTANTIAL, separable concerns — each a real multi-step block, genuinely interwoven, not a short serialize/encode/respond tail on a coherent pipeline — OR nests control flow so deep the core action is lost in indentation, OR runs so long its purpose stops being scannable. Not a defect: a linear pipeline of single-purpose stages (guard → build → encode → return; validate → operate → respond) is ONE purpose even when it ends by serializing a result; a thin body that delegates each step to a named helper in one call each (parse → fetch → render) is ONE orchestration, because the responsibilities live in the helpers — counting one-line delegated calls as separate concerns is the false positive to avoid. A defect: one body that parses input AND performs I/O AND applies business rules AND formats output, each written out and tangled together; a handler whose real action sits four conditionals deep. Reason like an expert about THIS code's shape. Apply no line count and no fixed concern count, and never quote a threshold to the developer. Use your judgment for cases these examples do not cover.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and rewritten bodies with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers — a closed set you can enumerate. It establishes each body's length, nesting and the concerns written out in it. It never establishes that a function is correct, or how it is factored against collaborators you cannot see.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the pinned source of a body the diff truncates. Read it to finish reading that body. It never adds an unchanged caller, or a function merely renamed or called but not shown, to what you judge.
If a required body cannot be captured from either, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
For YES on the shape questions, quote the specific `[L<n>]` added span and name the responsibilities to split out or the nesting to flatten; a sprawl you cannot anchor to a quoted hunk is not claimed. A NO on the shape question rests on the full read: record `evidence.search` over the diff, cite the largest body you read, and say in the boundary that you judged shape, not whether the functions are correct or well factored against collaborators you cannot see. For a NO on the function-body question, name what the diff holds instead (docs, config, a rename, a deletion, generated code). Judge only function bodies visible in the diff or its pinned source; never reason about an unchanged caller, a function merely renamed or called but not shown, or code you did not read. Never claim to compile or run anything. Describe the observable shape; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Repeated or near-identical blocks belong to `removes-duplication-instead-of-copy-pasting`; dead, commented-out or leftover scaffolding belongs to `leaves-the-code-clean-with-intent-revealing-comments`. Do not repeat another practice's complaint. Duplication or dead code alone does not establish tangled responsibilities, but neither removes the function-body occasion: assess the shape on its own evidence, answering that every body is focused only after the full read. Here only: does each introduced body hold one nameable job a reader can follow?

questions.title: Adds or rewrites a function body
questions.question: Does the diff add or substantially rewrite at least one hand-written function, method or closure body?
