These do NOT count: a documentation, diagram, image or configuration-only diff; a pure deletion or rename; a diff dominated by generated or vendored files with essentially no hand-written body; an unchanged caller, or a function merely renamed or called but not shown. Answer YES whenever such a body exists, even when every body is focused.
questions.yes: e.g. a new `handleUpload` method, or an existing handler whose body is largely replaced.
questions.no: e.g. only Markdown and YAML changed, a file was deleted, or a function was renamed with its body untouched.

questions.title: An added body tangles concerns, nests or sprawls
questions.question: Read every added or substantially rewritten body through. Does any one carry one of these defects: (a) it interleaves several substantial, separable concerns, each a real multi-step block written out inline — e.g. one body that parses input AND performs I/O AND applies business rules AND formats output, tangled together; (b) it nests control flow so deep its core action is lost in indentation — e.g. the real action four conditionals deep; (c) it runs so long its purpose stops being scannable? NOT a defect: a linear pipeline of single-purpose stages (guard → build → encode → return; validate → operate → respond), even when it ends by serializing a result; a thin body that calls one named helper per step — one-line delegated calls are not separate concerns; many small focused functions. Apply no line count and no fixed concern count. Duplication or dead code alone is not a defect here. If the only body that could carry a defect is cut off and its pinned source was not captured, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: Quote the `[L<n>]` span and name the tangled responsibilities or the nesting, e.g. a `submitOrder` that parses JSON, queries the database, applies discount rules and builds the response inline.
questions.no: Every added body does one nameable job a reader can follow, e.g. a validate → save → respond handler, or a thin orchestrator calling named helpers.

questions.title: A body does it all or buries its action
questions.question: Is there an added or substantially rewritten body that clearly does it all — several substantial concerns written out in one body with no single nameable job — or whose core action is genuinely obscured by nesting, rather than a body a reader can still follow where a single extraction would help? Grade the single most consequential function; never sum across files, and never count how many separate small functions exist. Answer NO when every added body is focused.
questions.yes: e.g. one controller method that reads the request, runs queries, applies pricing rules, sends mail and renders HTML, or an action buried under nested conditionals and loops.
questions.no: The weakest body is still readable and one extracted helper would fix it, or every body is focused.

rules.reason: The change adds or rewrites no hand-written function body: only docs, config, renames, deletions or generated code.
An added function body does it all, or buries its core action under deep nesting.
An added function body mixes separable concerns, nests deeply or sprawls where one extraction would help.
Every function body the change adds holds one nameable job a reader can follow.

practices.name: Leave the code clean and comment the why
practices.whyItMatters: Stray debug output, blocks of commented-out code, and comments that just echo the line all add noise the next reader has to wade through. Clean code with a comment that explains the why reads like someone meant it.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: No leftover print statements or commented-out branches, and where a line looks surprising, a short comment gives the reason, such as 'retry once: the upstream API drops the first call after an idle period', rather than restating what the line does.
practices.holdsAs: Code lands clean, with comments that explain why
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: added hand-written code has no established writing residue, and comments explain intent or constraints rather than restating code.

## The standard
Judge the added lines, every one, for code that ships clean and comments that earn their place. A senior reviewer scanning them should find no residue: no commented-out code, no leftover debug or trace output, no throwaway scaffolding shipped as if final. Any comment that IS present should explain the WHY — intent, a non-obvious constraint, a unit, a caveat, a reference — rather than restate the WHAT the next line already says. Blemishes, open and illustrative: an added line that is itself plausible source behind a comment marker (a commented-out assignment, call or control statement); a bare trace print or breakpoint; a "TEMP" or "remove before merge" stub; "// increment i" above `i++`; a comment that narrates the editing session rather than the code ("// changed this to use X", "// moved from Foo"); a comment with no code under it, left where code was meant to follow; a scratch or empty file added to the tree (a `notes.txt` holding a pasted snippet); a template placeholder left in a manifest the change edited (`# TODO: Adjust …`). A bare `print`, `NSLog`, `console.log`, `dump` or `debugPrint` can be a debug leftover when its surrounding purpose establishes that it is temporary tracing. The spelling alone does not establish that purpose. Clean, open and illustrative: a comment that gives a reason ("retry once: upstream drops the first call after idle"); output that is the file's deliberate purpose (a CLI's own stdout, a test's expected output); a logger call through a real logging facility; a sanctioned TODO referencing a tracked issue. Code-shaped text inside a comment is not sufficient evidence of debris: documentation examples, API usage, commands and explanations may legitimately quote executable syntax. Assess the surrounding purpose, and flag an inactive implementation only when the captured context establishes it is leftover rather than an intentional example.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): only the lines marked ADDED (`[L<n>] +` in the annotated diff). Residue is visible in the line itself. Removed and unchanged lines are not graded; code the author commented out and DELETED is a cleanup, never a blemish.
2. The file list (`work/change/files.json`): which files are generated or vendored and so excluded.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the surrounding purpose of a file — whether its output is deliberate, whether a quoted snippet is an example. It never turns an unquotable line into a blemish.
An image or an external link: nothing.

## Grounding
Quote the exact `[L<n>]` span and file path for every blemish; a blemish you cannot quote is not counted. For an inactive implementation, also quote the context that shows it is leftover. Never infer that a line is dead or debug-only unless its quoted text shows it. A NO on the blemish question rests on reading every added hand-written line: cite the search over the diff and state the boundary you did not cover — unchanged lines, files this diff does not touch, generated and vendored surface. For a NO on the source-line question, name what the diff adds instead. Never claim a build or test ran. Describe what was left in the code; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Naming, function and file size belong to `keeps-functions-small-and-single-purpose`; scope to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; duplication to `removes-duplication-instead-of-copy-pasting`; swallowed errors to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; a print-style call in application code to `logs-through-the-platform-logger`, which asks whether it should be a logger call. Dead branches in live code and runtime defects belong to other practices. Here only: residue on added lines, and WHAT-versus-WHY comments.

questions.title: Adds hand-written source-code lines
questions.question: After excluding generated or vendored files (lockfiles, `*.gen.*`, specs, build output, migrations) using `work/change/files.json`, does the diff add at least one hand-written source-code line? An empty diff does not count, and a change that adds no source-code line — a documentation, diagram, image or configuration-only diff — does not count. Answer YES whenever such added lines exist, even when they are clean.
questions.yes: The diff adds hand-written source lines, e.g. a new Swift view, a changed TypeScript handler, a Python script.
questions.no: The diff is empty, or adds only documentation, diagrams, images, configuration, or generated or vendored files.

questions.title: An added line carries residue or a WHAT comment
questions.question: Does any added hand-written line (`[L<n>] +`) carry a blemish? Code commented out and DELETED is a cleanup, never a blemish. Blemishes, open and illustrative (the list in The standard): plausible source behind a comment marker (a commented-out assignment, call or control statement); a breakpoint or a trace leftover the surrounding purpose shows to be temporary; a "TEMP" or "remove before merge" stub; a comment that restates the next line ("// increment i" above `i++`); a comment narrating the editing session ("// changed this to use X"); a comment with no code under it where code was meant to follow; a scratch or empty file added to the tree; a template placeholder left in a manifest the change edited (`# TODO: Adjust …`). NOT blemishes: a comment giving the WHY — intent, a constraint, a unit, a caveat, a reference; output that is the file's purpose; a sanctioned TODO with a tracked issue; code-shaped text that is a documentation example, API usage or a command. A print-style call in application code is judged by `logs-through-the-platform-logger`, not here. One blemish is enough.
questions.yes: Quote the line, e.g. `+ // let total = items.count` above live code, `// increment i` above `i++`, or a comment narrating an edit.
questions.no: Every added hand-written line was read and none carries residue; each comment explains intent, a constraint, a unit, a caveat or a reference.

questions.title: Residue misstates what the live code does
questions.question: Does a quoted blemish state something false about the live code — a restating or narrating comment that describes a behaviour, unit or value the code beside it does not have, or a TEMP stub that returns placeholder data where the change presents a finished feature? Commented-out code never counts, however much it hints at an abandoned path: its marker shows it is inactive. Count and length never count. Do not borrow error-handling or security consequences from other practices. Answer NO when no added line carries a blemish.
questions.yes: e.g. `// timeout in seconds` above a value the call reads as milliseconds, or a TEMP stub returning a hard-coded list the screen shows as loaded data.
questions.no: The residue is commented-out code, a stray comment, marker or file a reader can see past, or there is none.

rules.reason: The change adds no hand-written source-code line: only docs, config, or generated or vendored files.
Residue left on the added lines states something false about how the maintained code works.
The added code ships leftover residue or a comment that restates the code instead of explaining why.
The added code ships without residue, and its comments explain intent rather than restate the code.

practices.name: Log through the platform logger, not print
practices.whyItMatters: A `print` is a debugging note that ships: it has no level, no category and no subsystem, cannot be filtered or turned off, and on a device it goes nowhere anyone reads. The platform logger — `Logger` on Apple platforms, `Log`/Timber on Android, SLF4J on the JVM, `logging` in Python, a logger module in Node — gives every message a level and a place, so the app can be diagnosed where it runs.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Application code reports through the platform's logger with a level and a category; `print`, `console.log`, `println` and `System.out` are left to command-line output and scripts, and a debugging print is removed before the change lands.
practices.holdsAs: Application code logs through the logger, never print
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: diagnostic messages the change adds go through the platform's logger with a level and a category, not through print-style output, in application code.

## The standard
Judge one thing about the application code this change adds: when it reports a diagnostic — a state, an error, a step reached — does it use the platform's logger or print-style output? Print-style output is the closed list `print(`, `debugPrint(`, `dump(`, `NSLog(` (Swift and Objective-C), `println(`/`print(` and `Log.d/v` with an ad-hoc tag (Kotlin and Java on Android), `System.out.println`/`System.err.println`/`printStackTrace()` (JVM), `console.log/debug/info/warn/error` (TypeScript and JavaScript in application code), `print(` (Python). A logger is `Logger(subsystem:category:)` / `os_log`, Android `Log` behind a shared tag or Timber, SLF4J/Log4j/`java.util.logging`, a `winston`/`pino`/framework logger, Python `logging`. Print-style output is not a lapse where it is the program's output: a command-line tool, a script, a build step, a test, a playground, a `#Preview`, or a `DEBUG`-only block (`#if DEBUG`) that removes itself from release. Judge added lines only; an existing print the change did not touch is not this change's.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers and the file list (`work/change/files.json`): each added print-style or logger call, the file it lands in, and whether a `#if DEBUG` or a test target encloses it. It establishes what was added where. It never establishes what an unchanged file does.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether the project already has a logger (`Logger(` definitions, a logging dependency in the manifest) and whether the file is an application target or a tool. Read it to classify the file and to say whether the print was written beside an existing logger.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the print-style and logger calls it found per file, and whether the checkout defines a logger, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where the calls are added, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` call and its file for every answer that rests on a call. For YES on the print question, say why the file is application code (its target, its `import SwiftUI`/`UIKit`, its path); for a NO, name the fact that makes each added print the program's output or test, preview or `DEBUG`-only code. For a NO on the logger question, quote a representative logger call with its level and category. For the error-or-sensitive question, quote the print and the error path or the data it emits. A NO that rests on absence states that every added line of the diff was enumerated. Never claim a print is debugging output without the line; never claim a file is a tool without the fact that makes it one.

## Defer
An error swallowed rather than reported belongs to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; a secret in a message to `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions`; a leftover debugging line of another kind to `leaves-the-code-clean-with-intent-revealing-comments`. Here only: does the diagnostic go through the logger?

questions.title: Adds a diagnostic line in application code
questions.question: Does the diff add at least one diagnostic line — a print-style call or a logger call that reports a state, an error or a step reached — in application code? Print-style calls and loggers are the closed lists in The standard. Do NOT count prints that are the program's own output: a command-line tool, a script, a build step, a test, a playground, a `#Preview`. A print inside a `#if DEBUG` block in application code, or an added logger call, does count. Only added lines count.
questions.yes: e.g. `+ logger.error("Sync failed: \(error)")` or `+ print("Loaded items")` in an app's view model.
questions.no: The change adds no print-style or logger call, or its only prints are a CLI's or script's own output or sit in tests or previews.

questions.title: A print reports a diagnostic in shipping code
questions.question: Does an added print-style call (the closed list in The standard: `print(`, `NSLog(`, `println(`, `System.out.println`, `printStackTrace()`, `console.log`, and the rest) report a diagnostic in application code that ships — outside a command-line tool, script, build step, test, playground, `#Preview` or `#if DEBUG` block? Classify the file from its target, its imports (`import SwiftUI`/`UIKit`), its path, or the checkout. If neither the diff nor a captured checkout shows whether the file is application code, leave the answer open and name the file.
questions.yes: e.g. `+ print("Loaded \(items.count) items")` in `Sources/App/ItemStore.swift`, an app target file importing SwiftUI.
questions.no: Every added print-style call is the program's output or sits in a test, preview or `DEBUG`-only block, or the change adds none.

questions.title: Logger calls lack a fitting level or any category
questions.question: Does an added logger call lack a level or a category where the platform has them — a failure or error logged at a debug, info or default level, errors and ordinary steps all logged at the same default level, or a logger created with no category at all (a bare `Logger()`)? A shared logger with a named category has a category. Quote the call. Answer NO when the change adds no logger call.
questions.yes: e.g. `+ logger.info("Upload failed: \(error)")` for an error, or every message through a bare `Logger()` with no subsystem or category.
questions.no: The added logger calls use a level fitting each message and a named category, or the change adds none.

questions.title: A print carries an error path or personal data
questions.question: Does an added print-style call in shipping application code (outside a command-line tool, script, build step, test, playground, `#Preview` or `#if DEBUG` block) report an error path that nothing else logs, or emit personal data such as an email address, a name or a location? A credential or token in the message belongs to `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions` and does not count here. Answer NO when no added print sits in shipping application code.
questions.yes: e.g. `+ catch { print("Save failed: \(error)") }` with no logger call, or a print of the signed-in person's email address.
questions.no: Every added print in shipping code reports an ordinary state or step, or there is none.

rules.reason: The change adds no diagnostic line in application code; any added print is a tool's or script's own output.
Application code reports an error, or personal data, only through a print-style call.
Application code reports diagnostics through a print-style call instead of the platform logger.
The added logger calls log a failure below error level, use one level for everything, or have no category.
Every diagnostic the change adds goes through the platform logger with a level and a category.

groups.name: Handling failure well
groups.description: Fail safely when things go wrong. Handle errors instead of swallowing them, check inputs and edge cases where data enters, and do not crash on a problem the code could recover from.

practices.name: Handle errors instead of swallowing them
practices.whyItMatters: An empty catch block turns a failure into a silent one: the code carries on as if nothing went wrong, and you find out only when something downstream breaks with no clue why. Surfacing the error saves the 2am debugging session.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A failed call either surfaces the error to a caller who can react or recovers safely, for example by rolling back the partial work and failing closed, instead of logging and then continuing (or silently continuing) with bad or missing data.
practices.holdsAs: Failures surface or recover, never get swallowed
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: added failure paths propagate or meaningfully record failures, or deliberately absorb them with an evidenced safe reason.

## The standard
When this change introduces a failure path — a call that can throw, reject or return an error — the failure should stay visible: surfaced to a caller who can react, or recorded with enough context that someone can diagnose it later. Handled: the error propagates (rethrown, wrapped with context, returned or forwarded), is recorded meaningfully (logged at a level a human would notice, a failure metric, an error state the UI reads), or is deliberately absorbed with an in-diff comment naming WHY that is safe. Swallowed: the failure is discarded — an empty or no-op catch, a caught error variable that is never used, an ignored error return, a dropped async rejection, a result discarded with a `try?`-style shortcut, and a failed lookup or parse answered by a bare early return or an `if let` with no else branch: nothing logs it, no state carries it and no comment says why silence is safe. A handler that logs the failure at a level a human would notice and leaves the caller an empty value the interface renders as an empty state has recorded it — that is handled, not swallowed; it is a swallow only when nothing records the failure and nothing can react to it. A failable call on data the author ships — a literal URL, a constant, an interpolated integer — cannot fail on any runtime value, so a bare guard around it drops no failure; and a failure already recorded where it was caught is not swallowed again by a later check on the empty value the handler returned. These are illustrations, not a closed list; recognise the same shape in any language or idiom as an experienced reviewer would. Judge this as a craft practice in how the ADDED code handles errors, not a line-by-line lint sweep.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified lines with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers and the visible in-diff context. It establishes every failure path the change adds — a closed set you can enumerate from the added lines — and where each error goes. It never establishes that the handling is CORRECT, that the recovery works, or that paths outside the diff behave.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it when where a caught error goes, or what downstream does with the missing value, sits just outside the hunk. It never establishes that anything was run, compiled or tested.
Per-commit patches are not in your context; reason from what the diff shows. If the change adds a failure path but the relevant diff is truncated or unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation: unread required evidence establishes neither absence nor uncertainty in the work.

## Grounding
Judge only constructs this diff adds or modifies (new-side `[L<n>]` markers); never grade pre-existing context or assume code you cannot see. For YES on the failure-path question, quote the added constructs you enumerated. For YES on the swallow question, cite the added hunk with the discard; if you cannot point to the dropped error in a quoted added line, the answer is not YES. A NO on the swallow question rests on the walk: cite every construct you enumerated and where each error goes, record `evidence.search` over the diff, and state the boundary — not that the handling is correct, not that recovery works, not that code outside the diff behaves. For the consequence question, quote the line that shows what the swallowing path persists, communicates, authenticates or parses. Never claim to run, compile or test. Never invent a construct, an exoneration, or a clean bill you did not verify. Describe the observable behaviour; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether inputs and edge cases are validated belongs to `validates-inputs-and-edge-cases-at-the-boundary`; a deliberate fail-fast crash on an unrecoverable state belongs to `avoids-unsafe-panics-and-chosen-crashes`. Whether a recorded failure goes through the platform logger or a print-style call belongs to `logs-through-the-platform-logger`: a printed failure is recorded here. Here only: does an added failure stay visible, or is it dropped?

questions.title: Adds a failure path
questions.question: Does the hand-written change add or modify source code with a failure path — a call that can throw, reject or return an error — or an error-handling construct such as `catch`, `try?` or `try!`, `guard … else`, `if let`, an early `return` or `throw`, `Result` or `.failure`, a `??` fallback on a failable call? Enumerate the added constructs, quoting each added line, before answering. A change that adds no source-code line — a documentation, diagram, image or configuration-only diff — does not count. Answer YES whenever such a path exists, even when every one is handled well.
questions.yes: e.g. an added `try await client.fetch()` inside `do/catch`, or `+ guard let user = try? decoder.decode(User.self, from: data) else { return }`.
questions.no: The added lines contain no call that can fail and no error-handling construct, e.g. a layout-only view change or a docs-only diff.

questions.title: An added failure is swallowed
questions.question: Walk every added failure path. Does any one discard a failure that can actually occur, so that nothing records it, no state carries it, no caller can react, and no in-diff comment says why silence is safe? Swallowed, e.g.: an empty or no-op catch; a caught error never used; an ignored error return; a dropped async rejection; a `try?`-style discard; a failed runtime lookup or parse answered by a bare early return or an `if let` with no else. NOT swallowed: the error propagates (rethrown, wrapped, returned, forwarded); it is logged at a level a human would notice, printed (the channel is `logs-through-the-platform-logger`'s), counted or put in an error state; an in-diff comment says why absorbing it is safe. What is recorded must be the failure itself — the caught error, its message or a failure state; a `try?` that discards the error records nothing, however the values that did load are logged. A failure already recorded where it was caught is not swallowed again by a later `if let` or guard on the empty value. A failable call on data the author ships (a literal URL, a constant) cannot fail, so its bare guard drops nothing. If where an error goes lies outside the hunk and the pinned source was not captured, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: Quote the discard, e.g. `+ } catch { }`, `+ try? context.save()`, or `+ guard let data else { return }` on a fetched value with nothing recording the failure.
questions.no: Every added failure path propagates, is recorded where a human would notice, is absorbed with an in-diff reason, or cannot fail on runtime data.

questions.title: A swallow hides a fault on the main operation
questions.question: Does a swallowed failure hide a real fault in what the change exists to do — a save or delete the user made, a request or message sent to another system, a sign-in, or the fetch or decode the feature's data comes from — so the user or caller carries on as if it succeeded? Answer NO for a swallow on a secondary path: one image or link skipped, an optional detail, cleanup, teardown, telemetry, or a failure logged a touch too quietly. Several secondary swallows are still secondary. Answer NO when nothing is swallowed.
questions.yes: e.g. `+ try? context.save()` after the user edits a record, an empty catch around the login request, or `try?` on the fetch a detail screen is built from.
questions.no: The only swallows are on secondary paths — a skipped image or link, cleanup, teardown, telemetry, a too-quiet log — or there is none.

rules.reason: The change adds no failure path: no call that can fail and no error-handling construct in hand-written source.
The change swallows a failure in what it exists to do, so the fault never surfaces to the user or caller.
The change swallows a failure on a secondary path, with nothing recording it or saying why silence is safe.
Every failure path the change adds propagates, is recorded, or is absorbed with a stated reason.

practices.name: Validate inputs and edge cases at the boundary
practices.whyItMatters: Data from a user, a file, or another service will not always arrive in the shape you expected: it can be empty, null, negative, or huge. Checking it where it enters means a clear rejection instead of a confusing crash three layers deep.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Code that reads an external value first asks what happens if it is missing or out of range and handles that on purpose, so an empty list or a malformed payload meets a clean guard instead of a null-pointer surprise.
practices.holdsAs: External values meet a guard before they are used
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: added consuming sites handle the obvious bad case of values they do not control.

## The standard
Judge whether added or modified code that consumes a value it does not control handles the obvious failure case on purpose, instead of assuming a happy path. A boundary value enters from outside the local logic: a request param, body or header; text a user typed, once it is parsed or used as a number; a decoded network or file payload, including a bundled data file; a collection filled at runtime, such as a response array or a stored list the user populates; an env, config or defaults read; the result of a third-party or RPC call. Not a boundary value: a parameter of the app's own function or view, a framework callback's arguments, view state the code owns, an author literal or constant, and a value a control already bounds (a Slider or Stepper range, a Picker over an enum). A site is in scope only when the same change also USES that value — indexes or slices it, divides by it, converts it to an integer, aggregates it, or passes it into logic that assumes a shape. A value merely forwarded, stored or displayed as the type it already has is not a consuming site: an empty string saved or shown breaks nothing.
A guard is anything on the value's path that rules out the case the site itself needs, in the hunk or in code you can trace to: a count, bounds or empty check (`isEmpty` guards `[0]`, not `[1]` or a wider slice); a zero check before integer division or before a ratio that is shown or converted to an integer; a clamp; do/catch, `try?`, or a `try` that propagates out of a throwing function; a default for an absent value; an early return; a button disabled on the bad case. An operation already total on the bad case needs no guard: a Swift optional the type forces the author to unwrap (`Int(text)`, `.first`, `dict[key]`, `URL(string:)`, `as?`) handled with `if let`, `guard let`, `?.` or `??`; `reduce`, `map`, `filter`, `prefix` or `ForEach` over an empty collection; `items[i]` inside `ForEach(items.indices)`. A default counts unless it is an extreme sentinel (`Int.max`, `.infinity`) that reaches output unchanged. Judge the PRACTICE — is the obvious failure handled at all — not an exhaustive lint: a finite check on a decoded Double, or a zero check on a field the source never sends as zero, is not the obvious case.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified lines with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers and the visible in-diff context. It establishes every consuming site the change introduces — a closed set you can enumerate from the added lines — and whether each meets a guard you can see. It never establishes that the guards are sufficient for every input or that callers beyond the diff are safe.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it when the guard that would decide a site could sit outside the hunk — above a truncated hunk, or in the caller or view that builds the value. It establishes whether such a guard exists. It never establishes that anything was run, compiled or tested.
Per-commit patches are not in your context. If the context a deciding site needs remains unavailable after reading the pinned source, report a collection gap and record no observation, rather than asserting absence or inapplicability.

## Grounding
Judge only the added and modified lines and their visible in-diff context, plus pinned source you actually read; a site in unchanged code is never charged, even when a changed line feeds it. For YES on the consuming-site question, quote the `[L<n>]` line that uses the boundary value and name where the value comes from. For YES on the unguarded question, cite the `[L<n>]` span of each unguarded site, name the realistic input that breaks it and the missing guard ("count >= 2 before [0..<2]"). A NO on the unguarded question rests on the walk: quote the guard or total operation for each consuming site, record `evidence.search` over the diff, and state in the boundary what you did NOT establish — that the guards are sufficient, that they cover every case, that callers beyond the diff are safe. Never assert a missing guard you cannot point to; never claim to run, compile or test anything; never invent a clean bill of health. Describe the observable code behaviour, never intent or character.

## Defer
A value interpolated raw into a URL, query, command or markup belongs to `validates-and-escapes-untrusted-input`. A crash operator the author wrote — `x!`, `try!`, `as!`, `fatalError`, `unwrap()` — belongs to `avoids-unsafe-panics-and-chosen-crashes`: it is neither a guard nor a consuming site here. An implicit trap stays here: an unchecked subscript or slice, an integer division, a conversion to an integer of a value that can be NaN or infinite. The quality of error handling once input is guarded belongs to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; a catch that merely prevents the crash satisfies the guard here regardless of its body. Do not repeat another practice's complaint, and do not let another kind of defect stand in for this one.

questions.title: Uses a value the code does not control
questions.question: Does the added or modified source code USE a boundary value — index or slice it, divide by it, convert it to an integer, aggregate it, or pass it into logic that assumes a shape? A boundary value enters from outside the local logic: a request param, body or header; text a user typed, once it is parsed or used as a number; a decoded network or file payload, including a bundled data file; a collection filled at runtime, such as a response array or a stored list the user populates; an env, config or defaults read; the result of a third-party or RPC call. NOT a boundary value: a parameter of the app's own function or view, a framework callback's arguments, view state the code owns, an author literal or constant, a value a control already bounds (a Slider or Stepper range, a Picker over an enum). A value merely forwarded, stored or displayed as the type it already has is not used: an empty string saved or shown breaks nothing. An empty diff, docs, diagrams, images, configuration, generated or vendored files, and a view drawing a typed array it was handed do not count.
questions.yes: e.g. `+ let first = response.items[0]` on a decoded array, or `+ let avg = total / scores.count` on a list the user fills.
questions.no: The added code only forwards, stores or displays outside values, or works on typed in-app data, view state, constants and bounded controls.

questions.title: A consuming site lacks a guard for its bad case
questions.question: Walk every added site that uses a boundary value and trace it to its guard. Is any one used with nothing on its path ruling out its obvious bad case, so a realistic input — an empty or short array, an absent field, text that is not a number, a zero count — traps an unchecked subscript, slice, integer division or conversion, or shows a wrong value? A guard must rule out the case the site itself needs (`isEmpty` guards `[0]`, not `[1]`), in the hunk or in code you can trace to; the guards in The standard count. Already total: a Swift optional handled with `if let`, `guard let`, `?.` or `??`; `reduce`, `map`, `filter`, `prefix` or `ForEach` over an empty collection; a `try` that propagates out of a throwing function. Only the obvious bad case counts. A crash operator the author wrote (`x!`, `try!`, `as!`, `fatalError`) is neither a guard nor a site here. If the deciding guard could sit outside the hunk and the pinned source was not captured, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: Quote the site, the breaking input and the missing guard, e.g. `+ let first = response.items[0]` on a decoded array with no count or empty check.
questions.no: Every consuming site meets a guard or a total operation that rules out its obvious bad case.

questions.title: An ordinary input crashes or corrupts a site
questions.question: Does an unguarded site break on an input its source ordinarily produces — an empty list before the user has added anything, an empty result for an ordinary query, a field the user leaves blank — with a crash or a wrong value that is saved, sent or decided on? Answer NO when the breaking input is possible but unusual for that source (a record with fewer entries than nearly all do), when the effect is an odd value shown in a label, or when every site is guarded.
questions.yes: e.g. `+ let first = results[0]` on a search response that is empty whenever nothing matches, or an average divided by a list the user has not filled yet before it is saved.
questions.no: The breaking input is possible but unusual, the effect is a value shown oddly, or every site is guarded.

rules.reason: The change uses no value it does not control; it only handles typed in-app data, constants or bounded controls.
A site the change adds crashes or corrupts data on an input its source ordinarily produces.
The change uses an outside value without guarding its obvious bad case, such as an empty or short list.
Every outside value the change uses meets a guard for its obvious bad case.

practices.name: Avoid crashing on recoverable problems
practices.whyItMatters: Reaching for a force-unwrap or a panic on a condition that can actually happen turns an ordinary hiccup into a hard crash for your users. A problem the code can recover from deserves a graceful path, not a deliberate stop.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Where a value might legitimately be absent, the code unwraps it safely and falls back to a default or a clear error, instead of force-unwrapping and bringing the whole thing down.
practices.holdsAs: Missing values fall back instead of crashing
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: added crash-shaped operators are safe under their captured provenance or contract, rather than aborting on recoverable runtime failure.

## The standard
Code degrades gracefully on ordinary, recoverable runtime failure rather than deliberately aborting. A chosen crash is an ADDED crash operator the author wrote — force-unwrapping or force-casting a value that can legitimately be absent, `try!` on a call that can throw, or a deliberate abort, panic, exit or fatal error — when its value rides an ordinary runtime path: user input, network, database, disk, a decoded payload, a fallible API's result. Judge two things: can a real input reach the operator and make it fail, and did the change crash on it anyway. Bad, for example: `try! decoder.decode(T.self, from: data)` on a server response; `Int(ageText)!` on text a user typed; `results.first!` on a fetched array; `fatalError` in the catch of a network call. Not a chosen crash, though each looks like one: a genuine programmer invariant that cannot fail unless surrounding code is already broken (an unreachable enum default, a force unwrap of a value just proven non-nil); a fail-fast at a CLI or startup entry point where aborting IS the contract; data the author ships — a literal, a constant, an Info.plist key the change commits, a resource bundled with the app, `URL(string: "https://api.example.com")!`; an operation total by language or platform contract (`String.data(using: .utf8)!`). Code that runs only in an Xcode `#Preview`, a preview-only sample or in tests is not an ordinary runtime path: `try! ModelContainer(…)` or `fatalError` in a preview is scaffolding. A `!` alone is not the defect; whether the operation can ACTUALLY return nil or throw on some real input is. Reason about provenance across languages as an experienced reviewer would, not from the spelling of a construct or a precompute label.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified lines with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers. It establishes the closed set of crash operators the change adds and, where the hunk shows it, where each crashed-on value came from. It never establishes anything about removed lines, unchanged code or code outside the diff, and it never establishes that anything compiled or ran.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it only to trace the origin of a value the hunk crashes on but does not source, or where the operator runs. It never adds an operator to judge — only operators the diff adds are judged — and it never establishes that unchanged code cannot crash.
If the diff is truncated or unavailable for a change that adds a crash operator, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
Cite the exact added-line span of each operator and the value's origin from observable diff evidence. Judge only added or modified lines with new-side `[L<n>]` markers; never reason about removed lines or code outside the diff, and never claim to compile or run it. For YES on the runtime-input question, quote the deciding added line, name the value's runtime source and the real input that makes it return nil or throw; a crash you cannot tie to a runtime-sourced value and a real input is not a YES. A NO on that question cites every operator you enumerated with the reason each is safe — guarded, invariant, total, author-shipped data, preview or test code, entry-point contract — records `evidence.search` over the diff, and states that you judged the operators the diff adds, not whether unchanged code can still crash. When the trace runs out of evidence, say which operator and which fact would settle it. Never invent a file, a line, a value source or a clean bill you did not verify. Describe the observable behaviour of the code; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Empty or swallowed catches and logged-and-continued errors belong to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; missing input validation and implicit traps — an unchecked subscript or slice, an integer division, a trapping conversion — belong to `validates-inputs-and-edge-cases-at-the-boundary`. Here only: does an added crash operator deliberately crash on a recoverable runtime condition?

questions.title: Adds a crash operator
questions.question: Do the added source lines contain a crash operator the author wrote, from this closed list: a force unwrap (`x!`, `.first!`, `dict[key]!`), `try!`, a force cast (`as!`), `fatalError`, `precondition`/`preconditionFailure`, `assert`/`assertionFailure`, `exit`/`abort` — or their equivalent in another language (`panic`, `unwrap()`, `expect()`, `!!`, `process.exit`, a non-null assertion, `Optional.get()`)? An implicit trap — a subscript, a slice, an integer division, a trapping numeric conversion — is not on the list. An operator guarded on the same path, or in preview or test code, still counts. The precomputed list marks places to read, not answers: scan the added lines themselves. A docs-, config- or data-only diff, or a generated- or vendored-only diff, has none.
questions.yes: e.g. `+ let user = users.first!`, `+ let model = try! JSONDecoder().decode(Model.self, from: data)`, `+ fatalError("unexpected")`.
questions.no: No added line contains an operator from the list, e.g. the code uses only `if let`, `guard let`, `??` and subscripts.

questions.title: An operator crashes on a recoverable runtime input
questions.question: Does an added crash operator sit on an ordinary runtime path and crash on a value with a named runtime source — user input, network, database, disk, a decoded payload, a fallible API's result — that a real input you can name (a missing field, a failed request, text a user typed) makes nil or throwing? Trace where each value comes from and where the code runs. Bad, e.g.: `try!` decoding a server response; `Int(ageText)!` on typed text; `results.first!` on a fetched array; `fatalError` in a network call's catch. NOT this: an operator guarded on its path; a programmer invariant (an unreachable enum default, a value just proven non-nil); a fail-fast at a CLI or startup entry point where aborting is the contract; data the author ships — a literal, a constant, a bundled resource, an Info.plist key or build setting the project ships (a misconfigured build is a setup fault, not a runtime input); an operation total by contract (`String.data(using: .utf8)!`); code that runs only in a `#Preview`, a preview sample or tests. If a value's origin lies outside the hunk and the pinned source was not captured, leave the answer open and name the fact that would settle it.
questions.yes: Quote the line, the value's source and the input, e.g. `+ let age = Int(ageField.text)!`, which fails when the user types letters.
questions.no: Every added operator is guarded, an invariant, a total operation, author-shipped data, preview or test code, or an entry-point contract.

questions.title: Crashes outright on decoded or fetched input
questions.question: Does an added crash operator turn a clearly recoverable failure on a clearly ordinary runtime source — decoded or fetched input — into an outright crash? Answer NO when the input that makes the operation fail is possible but unusual, when recoverability is genuinely uncertain, or when no added operator crashes on runtime input.
questions.yes: e.g. `+ try! decoder.decode(Feed.self, from: data)` on every server response, or `results.first!` on a fetched array that is empty for a new user.
questions.no: The input that makes the operator fail is possible but unusual, recoverability is genuinely uncertain, or no added operator crashes on runtime input.

rules.reason: The added source lines contain no crash operator such as a force unwrap, `try!`, a force cast or `fatalError`.
An added crash operator aborts on decoded or fetched input that can ordinarily fail.
An added crash operator aborts on a runtime value that a real input can make fail.
Every crash operator the change adds is guarded, or safe by its provenance or contract.

groups.name: Making changes secure by default
groups.description: Make each change secure by default. Validate and escape untrusted input before it reaches a dangerous sink, avoid insecure defaults and over-broad permissions, and change dependencies deliberately.

practices.name: Neutralize untrusted input before a dangerous sink
practices.whyItMatters: Gluing raw user input straight into a query, a shell command, or a page is how injection bugs are born, the kind that leak a database or run an attacker's code. Parameterizing or escaping it first is what keeps that door shut.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: User-supplied values reach the database through bound parameters and the page through proper escaping, never concatenated into a SQL string or dropped into HTML as-is.
practices.holdsAs: Untrusted input is bound or escaped before a sink
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: untrusted input is neutralized for the exact dangerous sink it reaches in added code.

## The standard
When code added in this diff carries a value from outside the trust boundary into an operation where that value can change the operation's meaning, the value must be neutralized first — parameterized, escaped for the exact sink context, or validated against an allow-list or strict type — rather than concatenated or interpolated raw. Reason as an experienced security reviewer. A source is any externally-controlled value: a request param, header or body, an uploaded filename, a CLI arg, a remote service's response. A dangerous sink is any place where raw text changes execution: a built query string, a shell command, an HTML or template render, a filesystem path, a redirect target, a deserializer or eval, or a constructed URL whose path or query interpolates the value — `"/auth/\(token)"` then `URL(string: base + path)`, where the fix is percent-encoding via the platform URL builder, not raw interpolation. These lists are illustrative; recognize the shape in any language or stack, including sinks not named here. Neutralized looks like: bound as a parameter, run through a context-correct encoder, passed as an args array to exec, confined under a canonicalized base path, rendered through auto-escaping left on. Not neutralized looks like: string-concatenated or interpolated straight into the sink with nothing in the quoted hunk neutralizing it. For the constructed URL, the most common sink in an app, the rules are these: a remote or typed String interpolated into a path or query segment is a flow, and it is neutralized only by an encoder correct for the segment — `.urlQueryAllowed` is not a safe encoder for an individual query value or path segment: reserved delimiters can remain and change structure. Use a component builder or an encoder appropriate to the exact component; a value whose type renders as digits (an integer, a coordinate) cannot change the URL's meaning and is no flow; a whole remote URL string handed to the platform parser (`URL(string: remoteUrl)`) and then to a loader is parsed, not interpolated, and is no sink here; an author constant is no source.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified `[L<n>]` lines and their immediate in-diff context. It establishes the closed set of source-to-sink flows this change introduces and whether each is neutralized in those same lines. It never establishes that code outside the diff sanitizes — or fails to sanitize — the value; never assume either.
2. The file spread (`work/change/files.json`) and the checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): which paths are generated or vendored. They establish the hand-written remainder you assess. They never establish neutralization for a flow the added lines do not show.
Trace only what you can see. If the diff was not captured completely, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
For YES on the flow question, quote the added `[L<n>]` line where the source enters and the line where it reaches the sink, and name both ends. A NO on the flow question rests on the scan of every added line: when the diff contains a sink-shaped line — raw input concatenated into a query, command, path or markup — name the single most suspicious line by file:line and state why it is safe. For YES on the unneutralized question, quote the exact added hunk where the source reaches the sink raw; if you cannot point to both ends on quoted added lines, the answer is not YES. A NO there quotes the neutralizing call for each flow, records `evidence.search` over the diff, and states in the boundary what you did NOT establish: that the escaping is correct for every input, that sinks reached from unchanged code are safe, that the application has no other exposure. Never claim the code runs, compiles, is exploitable, or that a payload triggers; assert only the visible practice. Never invent a file, a line or a clean bill. Describe the observable behaviour — raw input flowing into a sink — never intent or character.

## Defer
A generic missing bounds, null or format check with no dangerous sink belongs to `validates-inputs-and-edge-cases-at-the-boundary`; a committed secret belongs to `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions`. Defer to the sibling rather than double-flag. Here only: a taint-to-sink injection flow.

questions.title: Untrusted input reaches a dangerous sink
questions.question: In the added hand-written lines, does a value from outside the trust boundary reach a dangerous sink, whether or not it is neutralized on the way? Sources and sinks are those The standard describes, in any language or stack: a request param, header or body, an uploaded filename, a CLI arg, a remote service's response or text a user typed, reaching a built query, a shell command, an HTML or template render, a filesystem path, a redirect target, a deserializer or eval, or a URL whose path or query interpolates it. Still YES when a prepared statement, a component-built URL or auto-escaping handles the flow. Not a flow: a value only shown by a text control that does not interpret markup; a value whose type renders as digits; a whole remote URL string handed to the platform parser; an author constant. Scan every added line before answering NO.
questions.yes: e.g. `+ let url = URL(string: base + "/users/\(name)")` with `name` from a text field, or `+ db.query("SELECT … WHERE id = ?", req.params.id)`.
questions.no: No external value reaches a query, command, render, path, redirect, deserializer or URL in the added lines; any sink-shaped line is named with why it is safe.

questions.title: A flow reaches its sink unneutralized
questions.question: Does an untrusted value reach a dangerous sink in the added lines raw — concatenated or interpolated, with nothing in the quoted hunk neutralizing it for that exact sink? Neutralized: bound as a parameter, run through a context-correct encoder, passed as an args array to exec, confined under a canonicalized base path, rendered with auto-escaping left on, or validated against an allow-list or strict type. In a URL, a String in a path or query segment is neutralized only by an encoder correct for that segment, such as a component builder; `.urlQueryAllowed` is not one, since reserved delimiters survive it. Never assume that code outside the diff sanitizes, or fails to sanitize, the value.
questions.yes: Name source and sink end to end, e.g. `token` from a response interpolated into `"/auth/\(token)"` and passed to `URL(string: base + path)` with no encoding.
questions.no: Every flow is bound, encoded for its exact context, validated, or rendered with auto-escaping, e.g. `URLComponents` with `queryItems`, or a prepared statement.

questions.title: Raw input can change code or data execution
questions.question: Does an unneutralized flow in the added lines let raw input change code or data execution — an injection, traversal or code-execution shape: a built query, a shell command, a filesystem path, a deserializer or eval? Answer NO when every unneutralized flow is a constructed URL, a render, a redirect or a header, or a value partly constrained but missing its context-correct escape, and when no flow is unneutralized.
questions.yes: e.g. `+ db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'")`, or `+ exec("convert " + req.query.file)`.
questions.no: The unneutralized flow is a constructed URL, a render, a redirect, a header or a partly constrained value, or there is none.

rules.reason: No untrusted value reaches a query, command, path, URL or markup sink in the added lines.
Raw untrusted input reaches a query, command, path or eval sink in the change without neutralization.
Untrusted input reaches a sink in the change without the escape its exact context needs.
Every untrusted value the change carries to a dangerous sink is bound, escaped or validated first.

practices.name: Avoid insecure defaults and over-broad permissions
practices.whyItMatters: A default or permission that ships wider than it needs sits quietly until someone exploits it, and this kind of misconfiguration is among the most common security gaps there is. Starting locked down means you only open what you can justify.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A new endpoint or credential grants exactly the access it needs and no more, with scoped permissions and a specific allowed origin from an allowlist, not an origin reflected back from the request or a blanket wildcard, instead of a permissive default dropped in to make things work.
practices.holdsAs: New access grants exactly what it needs and no more
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: added access and exposure settings stay appropriately constrained under the captured boundaries and safeguards.

## The standard
Code should start locked down and open only what it can justify. Hunt the added lines for a change that ships an insecure default or widens an access or exposure boundary without an adequate, evidenced justification. Judge the SETTING the change adopts, not the data flowing through it, and never as a blanket vulnerability scan. A sink-hunt, not a posture rating: do not read the top-level intent, conclude "looks secure" and stop. Walk these sink classes over the added lines; they are classes to think in, not a closed value list, so recognise the same shape on any stack:
1. transport, certificate or host verification toggled off;
2. cross-origin, CORS or permission scope widened — a credentialed response that reflects the request Origin back without an allowlist, or a bare wildcard on an authenticated route;
3. a file, resource or object mode made world-readable or world-writable, or otherwise over-broad;
4. an existing auth or authz guard removed or loosened;
5. secret or credential exposure — trace dataflow here, do not pattern-match names: inspect EVERY logging, string-interpolation, persistence and URL-building call in the added lines and ask what the interpolated value can hold at runtime. A value that can carry credential material at runtime is a leak when logged, printed, persisted in clear or put in a URL, even when the variable is not named "token": a hardcoded secret, the key itself, an Authorization or cookie header, or the request or response body of an auth, login, token or credential exchange (a login response that carries the issued token, for example). A value that cannot carry credential material — the data or error body of an ordinary API call, a status code, the name of a missing key — exposes none;
6. a debug, verbose-error or permissive default shipped to a non-test surface.
Spotting one tightened setting (an ATS flag removed, say) does not discharge the hunt; finish every class. A candidate sink class establishes what to inspect, not an automatic defect. Clean: a setting correctly scoped, least-privilege or tightened; a widening whose quoted purpose and captured constraints establish an appropriate exception. A reason, or a test, sample or local filename, does not by itself make exposure safe: verify the actual boundary, the permitted audience and the applicable safeguards from the captured evidence. The absence of an insecure setting is a clean baseline, not a hardening act.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added lines with their `[L<n>]` markers, and any removed or weakened guard line. It establishes every candidate sink the change introduces — a closed corpus you can walk — and any in-diff comment or profile guard that justifies a widening. It never establishes that the existing configuration is sound, that unchanged settings are safe, or that the system has no other exposure.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it when the boundary, audience or safeguard that would decide a candidate line sits outside the hunk (a dev profile, a network policy, the route's auth wrapper). It establishes the constraints an exception rests on. It never establishes that anything was run, compiled or tested.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria, when present: leads to inspect, never evidence. An absent or empty candidate list is never grounds for answering that no setting is touched while a candidate line is visible.
Never infer a setting from a filename or a count you cannot quote.

## Grounding
Every answer that rests on a line quotes the exact added `[L<n>]` line, or the removed or weakened guard line, and names the file. A claim that a setting was added, removed, hardened or mitigated must quote the changed line that does it. An appropriate exception must quote both the justification and the constraints that support it, and it does not turn a touched setting into an untouched one. Always state what you found for the credential-exposure class (5). A NO on the setting question rests on a full pass: when the diff contains a config-shaped line (a keychain, permission, CORS or allow-all setting, a token in a URL or path), name the single most suspicious one by file and `[L<n>]` and state why it is safe. A NO on the insecure-setting question is a covered search: record `evidence.search` over the diff, name the sink classes you walked in `lookedFor`, and state in the boundary what you did NOT establish — a report on a search, never a security clearance. Never claim to run, compile or test; never invent a file, a line or a clean bill of health. Point forward to the safer default: verification on; the exact origin named instead of `*`; the toggle behind a dev profile; the least-privilege mode; the guard restored or its reason recorded. Talk about the configuration, never the contributor.

## Defer
Whether untrusted input is escaped or validated belongs to `validates-and-escapes-untrusted-input`; a debug print that carries no credential material belongs to `logs-through-the-platform-logger`. This practice is the terminal owner of exposed credential material — a hardcoded secret, token, API key or password on a non-test path, or in a URL or log: report it here as consequential exposure, never defer it, and never answer that the change touches no setting while it is visible.

questions.title: Touches a security-relevant setting
questions.question: Do the added lines, or a removed or weakened guard line, touch a setting of any sink class in The standard: (1) transport, certificate or host verification; (2) cross-origin, CORS or permission scope; (3) a file, resource or object mode; (4) an auth or authz guard; (5) secret or credential exposure — a hardcoded secret, or any logging, print, string-interpolation, persistence or URL-building call that interpolates a runtime value; (6) a debug, verbose-error or permissive default? Such a logging, print or persistence call always counts, as class 5. Answer NO only for a change with none of these, such as a pure layout, documentation, model or test change. Assess only the hand-written remainder, and never answer NO because the precomputed candidate list is empty while a candidate line is visible.
questions.yes: e.g. `+ print("login response: \(body)")`, `+ NSAllowsArbitraryLoads = true`, `+ cors.allowedOrigins("*")`, a keychain accessibility value, or an `@PreAuthorize` line removed.
questions.no: The added lines touch no setting of any class, e.g. a SwiftUI layout change with no logging, persistence or configuration; any config-shaped line is named with why it is safe.

questions.title: A setting ships unsafely open
questions.question: Walking every sink class over the added lines, not just the first: does a concrete added setting, or a removed or weakened guard, ship an insecure default or widen access or exposure beyond what the captured evidence justifies? Examples are the shapes The standard lists: verification turned off, a credentialed response reflecting the request Origin, a bare wildcard on an authenticated route, an over-broad mode, a loosened auth guard, a debug default on a non-test surface. For class 5, ask what each logged, printed, persisted or URL-built value can hold at runtime, and count it only when that value can carry credential material: a hardcoded secret, the key itself, an Authorization or cookie header, an auth or login exchange's body. An ordinary API response or error body, a status code or a missing key's name carries none. Not this: a setting that is scoped, least-privilege or tightened, or a widening whose quoted purpose and captured constraints establish an exception. A reason, or a test or sample filename, does not by itself make exposure safe. If the boundary, audience or safeguard that decides a candidate line lies outside the captured diff and checkout, leave the answer open and name the line and what would settle it.
questions.yes: Quote the line and file, e.g. `+ print(String(data: data, encoding: .utf8) ?? "")` on a login response, or `+ .anyRequest().permitAll()` replacing an authenticated rule.
questions.no: Every touched setting is scoped, tightened or an evidenced exception, and no added call carries a value that can hold credential material, e.g. a print of a weather API's error body.

questions.title: The exposure widens the blast radius
questions.question: Does the insecure setting meaningfully widen the blast radius: verification disabled on a shipped path, credentialed origin reflection or a wildcard on an authenticated route, a removed or loosened auth or authz guard, or exposed credential material (a hardcoded secret, token, API key or password on a non-test path, or a credential in a URL or log)? A merely asserted internal or dev rationale does not reduce this. Answer YES only when the captured boundaries establish that consequential exposure. Answer NO for a lower-blast-radius misconfiguration, or when no setting is insecure. When unsure, answer NO.
questions.yes: e.g. a trust-all certificate delegate shipped to production, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` echoing the request origin with credentials, or `let apiKey = "sk_live_…"` in app code.
questions.no: The insecure setting has a lower blast radius, e.g. an over-broad mode on a non-sensitive cache file, or no setting is insecure.

rules.reason: The added lines touch no transport, origin, permission, file-mode, auth, credential, logging or debug setting.
The change disables verification, opens origins, loosens an auth guard or exposes credential material.
The change ships a setting more permissive than its captured purpose and constraints justify.
Every security-relevant setting the change touches stays scoped, tightened or an evidenced exception.

practices.name: Change dependencies deliberately
practices.whyItMatters: Every dependency you add is code you now trust and have to keep patched, and many malicious packages slip in disguised as a real name a letter or two off. A one-line note on why a package is there, plus a lockfile that moves with the manifest, lets a reviewer sanity-check the addition and keeps the build reproducible.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A new package arrives with a sentence on what it is for. The manifest and resolution stay consistent with the ecosystem and the repository policy, updating a lockfile when needed rather than requiring one for every edit.
practices.holdsAs: Dependency changes stay coherent and notable choices have a reason
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: a dependency edit whose manifest and lockfile stay coherent under the ecosystem's resolution rules, with a recorded reason for a notable addition or bump.

## The standard
Judge whether this pull request edits its dependencies deliberately. Two things hold together: the manifest and any lockfile remain consistent with the ecosystem's resolution rules and the repository's documented policy, and a notable new dependency or version bump carries a one-line reason a reviewer can read — in the manifest context, the title or body, or a commit subject. The reason says what the package is for in this change or why it moves; a subject or sentence that only names the package or the edit ("add X dependency", "bump Y to 3.0") is a label, not a reason, even when the package's name describes what it does. This is a supply-chain workflow practice about how a dependency edit is justified and kept coherent. It is never a claim about the dependency's own correctness, its CVEs, or whether the chosen version is the "right" one. The principle — coherence plus a traceable reason for notable changes — decides, not a fixed file list: reason as an experienced reviewer about manifests, lockfiles and ecosystems not named here. A patch or minor bump and a transitive-only delta need no prose. A large generated lockfile delta is normal evidence of coherence, not a problem. A supported version range is not itself a defect: libraries may deliberately declare compatible ranges, and a manifest edit need not change an already compatible locked resolution.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) and the file spread (`work/change/files.json`): the manifest hunks and the matching or missing lockfile spans. They establish what changed on the dependency surface and whether manifest and lockfile move together. They never establish the dependency's quality or the correctness of the chosen version.
2. The title (`context/metadata.json`) and the whole description (`context/description.md`): where an explaining sentence for a notable add or bump may live. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
3. The commit subjects and bodies (`context/commits.json`): a subject can carry the reason. Per-commit patches are not in your context; judge from subjects, the file spread and the quoted hunks.
4. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the repository's documented policy — a stated reproducibility requirement, a lockfile rule, a pinning convention. It establishes the policy a constraint removal is measured against. It never establishes a defect on its own.
Before calling a notable change unexplained you must have read the diff, the title, the body and the commit subjects. If one of those surfaces was not materialized for you, your search is incomplete: report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
Quote the manifest line, the matching or missing lockfile span, and the explaining sentence or commit subject verbatim. For YES on the incoherence questions, quote the deciding entries on both sides and, for a constraint removal, the documented policy it conflicts with. For a NO there, quote the manifest change and the lockfile span that matches it, or the ecosystem rule that makes no lockfile change necessary. A YES on the unexplained-change question rests on absence: name the notable add or bump and state that the diff, the title, the body and the commit subjects were read and none says why. For a NO there, quote the reason. Never invent a file, a reason, a CVE, or a clean bill you did not verify. Never claim a build resolved or ran. Describe the observable edit; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Artifact hygiene about generated churn belongs to `excludes-generated-and-build-artifacts`; review size belongs to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; whether a decision the dependency serves — a persistence, contract or cross-cutting choice — records its rationale belongs to `records-significant-decisions-with-rationale`, which leaves the reason for adding or bumping the dependency itself to this practice. Here only: is the dependency edit coherent, and is a notable change explained?

questions.title: Touches a dependency manifest or lockfile
questions.question: Does the change touch a dependency manifest or lockfile, in any ecosystem — package, build, module, container or workflow pin? Reason about manifests and lockfiles not named here as an experienced reviewer would.
questions.yes: e.g. an edited `package.json` or `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `build.gradle`, `go.mod`, `Package.resolved`, a `FROM` image tag, or a pinned workflow action.
questions.no: No changed file declares or resolves a dependency; the change touches only source, docs or ordinary configuration.

questions.title: Dependency edit is incoherent
questions.question: Is the dependency edit incoherent: the captured manifest and lockfile contradict one another under the ecosystem's resolution rules, with the deciding entries quotable; or a resolution constraint is removed in conflict with an evidenced repository reproducibility requirement (a stated lockfile rule or pinning convention in the checkout)? Establish the ecosystem's semantics and the captured policy before answering YES. NOT incoherent: an unchanged or absent lockfile alone, which proves neither coherence nor a defect; a manifest edit that does not change an already compatible locked resolution; a supported version range a library deliberately declares; a large generated lockfile delta; a routine transitive resolution refresh that is internally consistent.
questions.yes: Quote both sides, e.g. `package.json` now requires `"zod": "^4.0.0"` while the committed lockfile still resolves `zod@3.23.8`.
questions.no: The manifest and lockfile agree under the ecosystem's rules, any required resolution update is present, and no constraint removal conflicts with a documented policy.

questions.title: The contradiction is on a shipped dependency
questions.question: Is a dependency on which the captured manifest and lockfile contradict each other one that ships with the product, rather than one used only in development, tests or tooling? Answer NO when the edit is coherent, when only a non-shipping dependency is out of step, or when the only incoherence is a removed constraint. When unsure, answer NO.
questions.yes: e.g. a runtime dependency bumped to `^4.0.0` in the manifest while the committed lockfile still resolves 3.x.
questions.no: Only a development, test or tooling dependency is out of step, or the edit is coherent.

questions.title: A notable add or bump lands without a reason
questions.question: Does a notable dependency change — a new direct dependency, or a version bump beyond patch or minor — land with no quotable clause saying what the package is for in this change or why it moves, in the manifest context, the title, the description, or any commit subject or body? A subject or sentence that only names the package or the edit ("add X dependency", "bump Y to 3.0") is a label, not a reason, even when the package's name describes what it does. A patch or minor bump and a transitive-only delta need no reason. Read all four surfaces before answering YES; if one of them was not captured, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: e.g. `+ "chartkit": "^2.0.0"` added, and the only mention anywhere is the commit subject 'add chartkit dependency'.
questions.no: Each notable add or bump says what it is for, e.g. 'add date-fns for locale-aware dates on invoices', or the edit is only patch, minor or transitive.

rules.reason: The change touches no dependency manifest or lockfile.
The manifest and lockfile contradict each other on a dependency that ships with the product.
The dependency edit leaves manifest and lockfile inconsistent, or drops a constraint the repository requires.
A notable dependency addition or version bump lands without a stated reason anywhere in the change.
The dependency edit is coherent, and any notable addition or bump says why.

groups.name: Recording decisions and documenting changes
groups.description: Capture the why. Record the evidenceRationale behind significant design decisions, and document changes to public APIs and shared behaviour, so the people who maintain or build on the code later can understand it.

practices.name: Record significant decisions and the rationale
practices.whyItMatters: When you pick one design over another, the rationale is the first thing to fade. A maintainer who cannot find why you chose it will either undo a good decision or be too afraid to touch it, and both cost the team later.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A meaningful design choice arrives with its rationale written down, in the description or a short architecture decision record (ADR), such as 'chose an event queue over direct calls so a slow consumer cannot block checkout', not just the code that does it.
practices.holdsAs: Significant decisions land with their reasoning
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: a written rationale for the architecturally significant decision this change makes, recorded where a future maintainer can find it.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when this pull request makes an architecturally SIGNIFICANT decision, is the WHY recorded — a constraint, a trade-off, or an alternative rejected — rather than left to be reverse-engineered from the code? A recorded WHY may be one clause, but it must say something the code does not already show: the need the decision serves ("so a customer can save a draft and return to it", "a stored type because attachments must survive a restart") or the constraint that forced it ("the provider only accepts signed requests") records it; the lapse is silence about the decision, not brevity, and a clause quoted for the description's WHY may be the same clause. A sentence that names the model or the mechanism and the effect it produces ("added the AuditLog interceptor; every request is now logged") restates WHAT the diff shows and is not a rationale, and a commit subject that names the addition is a label, not a why. Never demand the alternatives considered or the reason this approach over another: the need served is the rationale a maintainer needs. Significance is a closed list, so two readers find the same subject: a change to a PERSISTED model or schema (a stored type, a migration, a field that is saved); a public-contract or wire-API change (an endpoint, a message format, an exported library API); a new cross-cutting mechanism the rest of the app plugs into (a shared aspect, interceptor or event bus, a base class many types extend); an auth or security mechanism; the removal of a feature and its stored data. Not on the list, and never significant on their own: a new or bumped dependency in a manifest, whose reason `changes-dependencies-deliberately` judges; a call to an external web service (an HTTP API consumed at runtime is a mechanism used, not a decision on the list); a build or project setting; a view or view model and how screens navigate; an in-memory draft, cache or value type; adopting the stack the project already uses (its persistence framework, UI framework or map kit); a helper, extension or calculation; a rename. When the only candidate is one of these, stage 1 finds no significant decision. Work in two stages, in order. (1) Decide whether the hand-written diff contains a significant decision. (2) Only if it does, check whether its rationale is recorded in the title, the description, a commit subject or body, or an ADR or design document the change links, adds or edits. A reason given in a review comment or the conversation is not recorded where a maintainer finds it and does not count; the discussion is where a rationale was asked for, not where it lives. A rationale clause counts in prose or inside a bullet or checklist item — "chose X because Y", "an event queue so a slow consumer can't block checkout", "to avoid Z" — so scan the whole body. Restating WHAT changed, an empty or template body, or a bare "added dependency X" does not record a why.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, with `work/change/files.json`): the added lines that establish significance, and any ADR or design document the same change adds or edits. Its code lines establish what was decided and never supply the why; an ADR or design document the change adds or edits is a place the why can be recorded, so read it.
2. The title (`context/metadata.json`) and the WHOLE description (`context/description.md`): every paragraph, bullet and checklist item. They establish a recorded rationale you can quote. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
3. The commit subjects and bodies (`context/commits.json`): a rationale stated there counts. Per-commit patches are not in your context; never claim a per-commit file mapping.
4. A linked ADR or design document materialised as a `.md` file under `context/docs/`: read it before concluding the why is absent.
