Cite its file path together with the quoted or closely paraphrased rationale sentence; a bare URL is not evidence the why was recorded. When the change names a specific document that was not materialised, the rationale may be there: report a collection gap and record no observation, never a claim against prose you were not shown.
5. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): what a changed symbol or mechanism means, and an in-repository ADR the change points to. It never supplies a rationale the change did not write.

## Grounding
Quote the exact added `[L<n>]` line(s) that establish significance in every answer about a significant decision, and for a routine change the hunks that show it decides nothing on the list. For a recorded why, also quote the verbatim rationale sentence, commit subject or document reference and where it lives. A NO about the why rests on absence: the citations show the search — the title, the whole description, the commit subjects and bodies, and the referenced rationale sources or their absence. When the diff is unreadable, the change still made whatever decisions it made and you could not read them: report a collection gap and record no observation, never an answer that the change is routine or significant. Never invent a rationale, never infer the why from the code itself, and never assert that the dependency, schema or endpoint is wrong — answer only whether the why is recorded. Never claim a build or test ran. Describe the observable record; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
The overall adequacy of the description — a clear title and a why for the change as a whole — belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; here judge only whether THAT significant decision's rationale is recorded, so the two never double-flag. Whether a public-surface change is documented for its consumers belongs to `documents-public-api-and-behaviour-changes`; whether a linked wiki document now contradicts the code belongs to `change-keeps-linked-docs-consistent`; whether a new or bumped dependency states its reason belongs to `changes-dependencies-deliberately`.

questions.title: The diff makes a decision on the significance list
questions.question: Do the hand-written hunks make a decision on the closed significance list in The standard: a change to a PERSISTED model or schema (a stored type, a migration, a field that is saved); a public-contract or wire-API change (an endpoint, a message format, an exported library API); a new cross-cutting mechanism the rest of the app plugs into (a shared interceptor or event bus, a base class many types extend); an auth or security mechanism; the removal of a feature and its stored data? Nothing else counts on its own: not a new or bumped dependency (another practice judges it), a web-service call, a build setting, views or navigation, in-memory types, the stack the project already uses, helpers, renames, constants, tests or docs.
questions.yes: e.g. a new stored type or migration, a field newly saved to disk, a new or changed endpoint, or a new auth interceptor.
questions.no: The change is routine: views, navigation, helpers, renames, a dependency, a build setting, a web-service call, an in-memory type, tests or docs.

questions.title: Each significant decision's why is recorded
questions.question: For each listed decision, is its WHY recorded in the title, the description, a commit subject or body, or an ADR or design document the change links (under `context/docs/`), adds or edits? One clause in prose or a bullet is enough if it says something the code does not show: the need served ('so a customer can save a draft and return to it'), a trade-off ('an event queue so a slow consumer can't block checkout') or the constraint that forced it. Never demand alternatives. Not a WHY: naming the model or mechanism and the effect it produces; a commit subject naming the addition; an empty or template body; a bare URL; a reason given only in review discussion. If the change names a document that was not materialised, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: A quoted clause gives the need, constraint or trade-off behind each decision, e.g. 'Drafts are saved to disk so they survive a restart'.
questions.no: A listed decision has only a restatement of what was added, e.g. 'Added the AuditLog interceptor', or nothing at all.

questions.title: An unexplained decision is consequential
questions.question: Is a listed decision whose why is not recorded genuinely consequential: an auth or security mechanism, a persistence change beyond one isolated stored field (a new stored type, a migration, a changed or removed saved field), a public-API or wire-contract change, or a cross-cutting mechanism other code builds on? A contained decision is NO: one isolated stored field, one app-internal type. When unsure, answer NO.
questions.yes: e.g. a new token-refresh interceptor, or a changed endpoint response, ships with no why anywhere.
questions.no: Each unexplained decision is contained, e.g. one added stored field, or every decision's why is recorded.

rules.reason: The change is routine: it makes no persisted-schema, contract, cross-cutting, auth or removal decision.
A consequential decision, such as an auth mechanism or a contract change, ships with no recorded reason.
A significant decision, such as a schema or contract change, ships with no recorded reason a maintainer could find.
The significant decision ships with its why recorded where a maintainer will find it.

practices.name: Document public API and behaviour changes
practices.whyItMatters: People outside your code depend on what you export. Change a public function or endpoint without a note and they find out at runtime, in their own project, with no warning, and they trust your library a little less each time.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A renamed parameter or a changed response shape lands with its reference docs and a changelog line updated in the same change, so the people building on your API hear about it from you, not from a broken build.
practices.holdsAs: API and behaviour changes ship with their docs
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: consumer-facing documentation of the changed public surface — a downstream caller hears what moved from the change itself.

## The standard
Judge one practice: when the change alters a PUBLIC or SHARED surface — something a SEPARATE consumer depends on and compiles or integrates against — does the change carry, in the same diff or in the description, documentation that tells consumers what moved? Public surfaces: a library's or framework's exported symbols, a published package's API, a documented HTTP or RPC contract, a persisted or wire schema, an error or response shape callers branch on, a config default a consumer sets. Good: the renamed parameter, new endpoint, changed response field or breaking removal lands with its doc-comment, a changelog line, or a description sentence naming the consumer-facing effect. Bad: a real exported-surface change ships with nothing a consumer could read to adapt. A generated API specification or reference documents a contract when its authoritative source and meaning are captured: judge the contract and the information a consumer receives, not whether the text was handwritten. Irrelevant generated output is not documentation, and generated churn alone never establishes an authored contract decision.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, with `work/change/files.json`): the surface change itself, and any documentation shipped beside it — a doc-comment on or above the surface, a changelog or docs addition, an updated reference. It establishes what changed and what documentation arrived with it. It never establishes a consumer by itself.
2. The description (`context/description.md`): a sentence naming the consumer-facing effect. It establishes documentation a consumer would read on the change; it never establishes a surface change the diff does not show.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the contract and its usage — who depends on the surface, and the existing reference docs the diff leaves untouched. It establishes whether a separate consumer exists and where the documentation would live. It never supplies the note the change failed to write.
4. A linked wiki document the change references, when it was materialised as a `.md` file under `context/docs/`: its body may hold the documentation consumers need. Cite its file path together with the quoted or closely paraphrased sentence relied on; a bare URL is not evidence that the document says it. When the change points at a specific document that was not materialised for you, the documentation may live there: report a collection gap and record no observation, never an undocumented surface.
An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.

## Grounding
Cite the diff lines of the observable surface change in every answer about it, and the contract or usage that establishes the separate consumer. For documentation that ships with the change, quote the documenting text and its file. For documentation that omits the changed element, quote the documentation and the changed element it omits. A NO about documentation rests on absence: cite the surface change and name the boundary searched — the surface's doc-comment, the changelog and docs in the diff, the description, and any materialised wiki document. For a symbol whose boundary cannot be settled, name the question. Never invent a symbol, an export marker, a changelog or a clean bill you did not see. Never assert the compile or runtime correctness of the surface, and never impute intent or care; describe the documentation practice on the observable artifact only.

## Defer
The pull request's general what-and-why narrative belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; whether a design decision's rationale is recorded belongs to `records-significant-decisions-with-rationale`. A thin description or an unjustified choice is not an observation here. Here only: is the public-surface change documented for its consumers?

questions.title: The change alters a surface a separate consumer uses
questions.question: Does the diff alter a PUBLIC or SHARED surface that a SEPARATE consumer depends on and compiles or integrates against? The kinds are those The standard lists: a library's exported symbols, a published package's API, a documented HTTP or RPC contract, a persisted or wire schema, an error or response shape callers branch on, a config default a consumer sets. Establish the separate consumer from the captured contract or usage, never from package type alone; an application can expose endpoints or wire formats without publishing a library. Internal types, private signatures, local refactors, app-only fields and generated churn alone do not count. If no change plainly alters such a surface, and the diff, description and checkout cannot settle whether a changed symbol has a separate consumer, leave the answer open and name what would settle it.
questions.yes: e.g. a renamed query parameter on a documented REST endpoint, a removed exported function of a published package, or a changed response field clients branch on.
questions.no: The changed symbols are internal types, private signatures, local refactors or app-only fields with no separate consumer.

questions.title: A breaking surface change has no documentation
questions.question: Does the change make a breaking change to a public or shared surface — a removed or renamed symbol, route or field, a narrowed type, a changed default — with no documentation anywhere: no doc-comment on or above the surface, no changelog or docs addition in the diff, no description sentence naming the consumer-facing effect, and no linked wiki document materialised as a `.md` under `context/docs/` that says it? If the change points to a specific document that was not materialised, leave the answer open: the documentation may live there.
questions.yes: e.g. the `user_id` field is renamed to `userId` in a response consumers parse, and nothing in the diff, description or linked document mentions it.
questions.no: Every breaking surface change is documented somewhere a consumer reads, or the change breaks nothing.

questions.title: Each surface change ships with documentation
questions.question: Does every public or shared surface change carry, in the same diff or in the description, documentation a consumer could read to adapt: a doc-comment on or above the surface, a changelog line or docs addition, an updated reference, a description sentence naming the consumer-facing effect, or a linked wiki document materialised as a `.md` under `context/docs/`? A generated API specification or reference counts when its authoritative source and meaning are captured; irrelevant generated output does not, and a bare URL does not. Look in every one of these places before answering NO. If the change points to a specific document that was not materialised, leave the answer open: the documentation may live there.
questions.yes: e.g. the new endpoint has a doc-comment and `CHANGELOG.md` gains 'Added GET /v1/reports'.
questions.no: A surface change ships with nothing a consumer could read: no doc-comment, changelog, docs, description sentence or linked document.

questions.title: The documentation names what moved
questions.question: Does the documentation that ships with each public-surface change name the specific changed parameter, field, route or default a consumer must adapt to, rather than only the area in general (for example 'updated the API')?
questions.yes: e.g. 'The `limit` parameter of `GET /items` now defaults to 50 instead of 100.'
questions.no: The documentation never names the changed element, e.g. 'Refactored the items API' for a renamed parameter.

rules.reason: The changed symbols are internal, with no separate consumer depending on them.
A breaking public-surface change ships with no documentation, so consumers get no migration note.
A public-surface change ships with nothing a consumer could read to discover or adapt to it.
The documentation never names the specific parameter, field, route or default that changed.
The public-surface change ships with documentation that names what moved.

practices.name: Keep linked wiki docs consistent with the change
practices.whyItMatters: A wiki that contradicts the code is worse than no wiki: teammates act on documented behaviour that no longer holds, and the drift compounds silently until someone is burned by it.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: When a change alters something the team's design or reference doc describes, the same PR brings the doc along, so the wiki keeps telling the truth about the system.
practices.holdsAs: The wiki moves with the change it describes
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: the captured linked document and changed behavior agree on the same contract, setting or operational step.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when this pull request changes a documented behaviour — a config default, a public API or wire contract, a CLI flag, an error or return code, an operational step — AND a linked wiki document describes that same behaviour, does the document still agree with the code, or has the diff left it contradicting reality? Work in two stages, in order. (1) From the hand-written diff, identify a concrete behaviour, contract or config the change alters. (2) Only if a materialised document describes that same thing, check whether the document now asserts something the code contradicts: an old default, a removed flag, a renamed field, a changed status code, a superseded step. The signal is a genuine contradiction between a specific document passage and a specific diff hunk — never staleness in the abstract, and never "the code changed, so the document is probably old". The presence or absence of a wiki link is never itself the observation; a change with no relevant document is not a weakness.

## Sources
1. The description (`context/description.md`) and each linked issue (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`): which wiki documents the change references, and any sentence saying the document was updated. They establish that a document is in scope; they never establish what the document says. A bare URL is not evidence of a document's content. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
2. The materialised documents (`context/docs/<collection>/<document>.md`): the passages that describe the behaviour. They establish what the wiki asserts today. Read the file before concluding anything about it.
3. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, with `work/change/files.json`): the hand-written hunks that alter a behaviour, contract or config, and any documentation the same change updates. It establishes what the code now does; it never establishes what the wiki says.
4. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): context for what a changed symbol, flag or step means. It never supplies a document passage.

## Grounding
For a contradiction, cite both sides: the exact added or removed `[L<n>]` diff line that changes the behaviour, and the verbatim sentence from the materialised `.md` document that still asserts the old behaviour, with its `context/docs/...` file path. If you cannot point to a specific document passage the diff makes false, there is no contradiction: never infer one you cannot cite, and never fabricate a document quote. For a document that agrees, cite the diff line of the changed behaviour and the document line (in the diff or in the materialised file) that now agrees with it. A NO about a document reference rests on absence: cite the complete description and every adopted linked issue you read. A document is available to you only when the pull request references it and its body was materialised as a `.md` file under `context/docs/`; no linked issue and no document reference in the complete description needs no Outline capture. If an adopted linked issue was not captured or cannot be read, report a collection gap and record no observation unless the missing issue cannot change the answer: a captured contradiction may stand on its own, but an answer that no relevant document exists needs every adopted reference that could change it. When the pull request references a specific document that a reader would expect to describe the behaviour this diff changes, and that document was not materialised, you cannot tell whether it now contradicts the code: report a collection gap and record no observation. An unreadable diff is the same collection gap. Never claim a build or test ran, and never impute intent or care; describe what the document says and what the code does.

## Defer
Whether a change was documented at all, in any surface, belongs to `documents-public-api-and-behaviour-changes`. Whether the WHY of a decision is recorded belongs to `records-significant-decisions-with-rationale`. Here only: does a specific linked wiki document now contradict the code?

questions.title: The pull request references a wiki document
questions.question: Does the complete pull request description (`context/description.md`), or any captured linked issue (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`), reference a wiki document? Read the whole description and every adopted linked issue before answering NO. A bare URL shows that a document is referenced, never what it says. If an adopted linked issue was not captured and the description references no document, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: e.g. the description links 'Deployment runbook' in the team wiki, or linked issue #12 references the 'Auth API' document.
questions.no: Neither the complete description nor any captured linked issue references a wiki document.

questions.title: The diff changes what a linked document describes
questions.question: Does the hand-written diff alter a concrete behaviour, contract or config (a config default, a public API or wire contract, a CLI flag, an error or return code, an operational step) that a referenced wiki document materialised as a `.md` file under `context/docs/` describes? Read the document file before answering. An empty diff, or one that touches nothing the document describes, answers NO. If a referenced document that would be expected to describe the changed behaviour was not materialised, leave the answer open; never answer NO about a document you could not read.
questions.yes: e.g. the diff changes the default `timeout` from 30 to 10 seconds, and `context/docs/ops/config.md` describes `timeout`.
questions.no: The diff is empty or changes nothing the materialised document describes.

questions.title: A linked document still asserts the old behaviour
questions.question: Does a specific passage of a materialised linked document (`context/docs/<collection>/<document>.md`) still assert something a specific hunk of this diff makes false — an old default, a removed flag, a renamed field, a changed status code, a superseded step? A genuine contradiction between a quoted passage and a quoted hunk is required: never staleness in the abstract, and never "the code changed, so the document is probably old". A document that the same pull request updates, or that already reflects the new behaviour, does not contradict the code.
questions.yes: e.g. the diff sets `timeout = 10`, and the document still says 'Requests time out after 30 seconds'.
questions.no: The document already reflects the new behaviour, is updated in the same pull request, or holds no passage the diff makes false.

questions.title: Readers would act on the stale passage
questions.question: Would a reader who trusts the passage this diff makes false act on it wrongly: a wrong documented default or limit, a removed API or flag the document still offers, or a changed auth, security or data-handling step? A stale minor or internal-facing detail is NO. When unsure, answer NO.
questions.yes: e.g. the runbook still offers a removed --legacy-mode flag, or still describes the old token-exchange step.
questions.no: The stale passage is a minor or internal-facing detail, or nothing is stale.

rules.reason: Neither the description nor any linked issue references a wiki document.
The diff changes nothing that the referenced wiki document describes.
A linked wiki document still offers a default, limit, flag or step that this change made false, and readers would act on it.
A linked wiki document still states a default, flag or behaviour that this change made false.
The linked wiki document agrees with the behaviour this change makes.

practices.name: Say what else you considered
practices.whyItMatters: A decision record that names only the winner tells the next person what was done, not what it cost. When a constraint later changes — a library is deprecated, the traffic grows, the team shrinks — the first question is always "what else did we look at, and does that reason still hold?". If the alternatives were never written down, that question can only be answered by redoing the whole investigation, and usually it is not answered at all: the decision quietly becomes something nobody feels able to revisit.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A record that names the two or three options that were genuinely in play and gives each one a sentence saying what ruled it out — the constraint it failed, the cost it carried, the thing the team was not willing to trade. Written for someone who arrives a year later with a changed constraint, so they can tell in a minute whether the decision still stands.
practices.holdsAs: Decisions say what else was considered and why not
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: the decision record names considered alternatives and their rejection reasons, or explains the evidenced absence of feasible alternatives.

## The standard
Judge whether a decision record says what else was seriously considered and why those options were not chosen. A record that states only the chosen option records an outcome; a later reader needs the reasons the others lost, because that is the only part that tells them whether the decision still holds once a constraint changes. The standard is met when the document names at least one alternative that was genuinely on the table and gives a reason it was not chosen — a constraint it failed, a cost it carried, a trade-off the team was unwilling to make — and that reason is about that alternative specifically. A reason that only restates the chosen option's merits says nothing about why the others were worse and does not count. No template or heading name is required: a document that gives the reasons in prose satisfies this as fully as one with a headed section.

## Sources
1. The document body (`context/document.md`): the whole authored text. It establishes whether an alternative is named and whether a reason is given for it. It never establishes whether the decision was right, whether the rejected options deserved rejection, or whether the document is still current.
2. The document metadata (`context/document.json`): the title. It establishes only whether the title names a decision, for the occasion. It never establishes what the body says.
Judge the text in front of you and nothing else. An image you cannot open: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. Two cases are not absence: a record that defers its options discussion to another document you were not given, and a body that visibly breaks off before any options section. If either reflects incomplete capture, report a collection gap and record no observation. If the complete authored document itself ends without discussing alternatives, judge that omission; do not mistake unfinished writing for missing capture.

## Grounding
For an alternative with its reason, cite the exact lines naming the alternative and its reason; for a record with no genuine alternative, the lines establishing why none existed. For whether the document is a decision record, cite the title, status line or heading that names the decision, or the lines that show the document's kind. A NO about alternatives rests on absence: cite the decision statement and the boundary you searched — the whole body, including any options or alternatives section quoted or stated to be empty. Never claim the decision was correct or incorrect, never claim a rejected alternative deserved its fate, and never claim the document is or is not up to date. Describe what the record says; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether a pull request records the decisions it makes belongs to `records-significant-decisions-with-rationale`. Whether the decision was right, whether the alternatives deserved rejection, and whether the document is current are not judged by any practice here. Here only: does the record name what else was considered and why it lost?

questions.title: The document is a decision record
questions.question: Is the document recognisably a decision record: it names a single decision and takes a position on it? Signals: a title or heading naming a decision; a status line (proposed, accepted, superseded); a section headed with words like decision, context, consequences, options, alternatives, trade-offs. A design overview, a runbook, a how-to guide, a meeting note, an index page, or a specification that decides nothing is not one.
questions.yes: e.g. 'ADR 7: Store events in PostgreSQL', with 'Status: accepted' and a Decision section.
questions.no: e.g. a runbook 'Restarting the worker', a meeting note or an index page: it decides nothing.

questions.title: An alternative is named with why it lost
questions.question: Does the document name at least one alternative that was genuinely on the table and give a reason specific to that alternative for not choosing it — a constraint it failed, a cost it carried, a trade-off the team was unwilling to make? No template or heading name is required: reasons given in prose count as fully as a headed section. Not enough: alternatives listed with no reason any of them lost (a bare bullet list of technology names); a reason that only restates the chosen option's merits, which says nothing about why the others were worse; a section headed "Alternatives considered" that is empty or contains only "none". Read the whole body. If the record defers its options to another document you were not given, or the body visibly breaks off before any options section, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: e.g. 'We considered Kafka, but running a cluster costs more operations time than the team has.'
questions.no: e.g. the record states the choice and its benefits only, or lists 'Kafka, RabbitMQ' with no reason either lost.

questions.title: The record explains why no alternative existed
questions.question: Does the document explain the constraint that left no genuine alternative to the chosen option — for example a platform, contract or regulation that admits only that option? An "Alternatives considered" section that is empty or says only "none", without such an explanation, does not count.
questions.yes: e.g. 'The app store only accepts in-app purchases through StoreKit, so there was no other payment option.'
questions.no: The document gives no constraint that ruled out every other option.

rules.reason: The document is not a decision record: it takes no position on a single decision.
The decision record names no alternative together with a reason specific to why it was not chosen.
The decision record names what else was considered and why it lost, or why no alternative existed.

groups.name: Disciplined delivery and version control
groups.description: Keep your delivery clean. Make each commit one self-contained change, leave generated and build files out of the diff, and branch from the shared integration branch so your work stands on its own.

practices.name: Keep each commit to one logical change
practices.whyItMatters: Mixing unrelated changes in a commit makes selective review, reverts and backports harder. Keeping changes separable makes the history more useful; clear commit subjects help a reader understand that intended separation.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Separate commits for separate ideas, such as 'Fix off-by-one in pagination' in one and 'Rename helper for clarity' in another, so each can be reviewed, reverted, or backported on its own.
practices.holdsAs: Each commit holds one logical change and no more
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: how the pull request's commits are partitioned — each commit one cohesive logical change, as its authored subject and body describe it and its own files show.

## The standard
Judge one thing: whether the commits are SPLIT so each one captures a single logical change, rather than one commit tangling separable work into a bundle a reviewer cannot follow, revert, or cherry-pick on its own. One logical change is one piece of work with everything it needs: a feature with its model, view, view model, test, asset, the manifest entry for the package it uses and the navigation that reaches it; a fix with its test; a diagram with the README line that embeds it; one document's sections revised for one reason. That is one concern however many clauses or files name it ("parse the header and validate it"). Two concerns are two pieces of work that each make sense alone: two features or user stories, two unrelated fixes, behavioural work beside a chore (a reformat or lint sweep, a rename or move sweep, a dependency bump, tooling or editor settings), or code beside an unrelated document or course deliverable. Several cohesive commits in one pull request is fine here, and a chore or a revert in its own commit is the partition working, not a tangle. A pull request with one authored commit is judged the same way: that commit is the whole partition, and it can hold one logical change or a bundle. Decide what is separable as an experienced reviewer would; there is no fixed word list. This is a workflow practice about how the history is partitioned, never a code-defect claim.

## Sources
1. The commits (`context/commits.json`): each subject, full body, `parents` and the `files` it touched against its first parent, with status and line counts. They establish the author's partition — what each commit says it holds and what it actually touched. A commit whose files carry a second piece of work its subject does not name — a new screen or a database migration under a typo-fix subject, a project-wide reformat under a feature subject — is a tangle the subject hides; the supporting files of the work it does name never are. A body that lists what its commit holds is read line by line, like the subject. A commit whose `files` were not captured, and whose patch `git show` cannot produce, is unread, never shown to be clean. `git show <sha>` in the checkout gives its patch when the file list is not enough.
2. The per-file changed-line spread of the whole change (`work/change/files.json`, `work/change/diff.patch`): the overall breadth the commits together cover.
Read subjects, bodies and each commit's files together and judge conservatively. The precomputed leads below these criteria list every authored commit as one row — its subject's shape (bare, a repeat, joined clauses, cut off), how many files it only moved, and the files it edited with their line counts — as places to look, never verdicts: joined clauses are punctuation, not a count of concerns. If `context/commits.json` is unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation; uncollected subjects are never authored silence and never an open answer.

## Grounding
Cite the commit record behind every answer. For a commit that holds two concerns, quote the deciding subject verbatim with its short SHA, name the two pieces of work, and name any path from that commit's `files` that shows a concern its subject does not name. For a series you accept as cohesive, cite the subjects whose partition you accepted, each with its short SHA; a NO that rests on absence must have read every authored commit's subject, body and `files`. For the merge-commit question, cite the commits and their `parents`. Never claim a per-commit file mapping you cannot observe. Cite the corresponding subject, SHA and file entries in the captured `context/commits.json` artifact. Never cite a diff line for this practice, and never leave an answer open because the subjects have no line of their own to cite. Describe the observable split; never impute intent or character, and never frame a tangle as a defect in the code.

## Defer
Overall pull request size, and a pull request carrying several features in separate commits, belong to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; a large but cohesive partition can be a strength here. Subject wording belongs to `commit-subjects-explain-each-change`; a vague subject alone establishes neither cohesion nor a tangle. A generated or editor file swept into a commit (`.idea/`, `.DS_Store`, a regenerated `Info.plist`) belongs to `excludes-generated-and-build-artifacts`. Here only: does each commit hold one logical change?

questions.title: An authored non-merge commit exists
questions.question: Does `context/commits.json` list at least one authored commit that is not an automatic merge commit? A merge commit has two or more entries in `parents` (`parent_count` of 2 or more) or a subject beginning "Merge ...". A single authored commit counts: it is judged like any other and can itself be cohesive or bundled.
questions.yes: At least one commit has a single parent and a subject of its own, e.g. 'Add password reset' (a1b2c3d).
questions.no: Every listed commit is an automatic merge commit, e.g. only 'Merge branch main into feature', so no authored split exists.

questions.title: A commit names two separable pieces of work
questions.question: Read every authored commit's subject and its whole body. Does any one commit name two or more SEPARATE pieces of work, each making sense alone: two features or user stories, two unrelated fixes, a fix beside a feature, a refactor beside an API sweep, behavioural work beside a chore (a reformat or lint sweep, a rename or move sweep, a dependency bump, tooling or editor settings), or code beside an unrelated document? A body that lists several such pieces counts as much as a subject that names them. The parts of one piece of work are one concern however they are joined ('and', commas, '+', bullets): a feature with its model, view, test, asset, manifest entry and navigation; a fix with its test; one document's sections revised for one reason.
questions.yes: A quoted subject or body line names two separable pieces of work, e.g. 'Add CSV export and fix the login crash' (d4e5f6a), or a body listing a new screen, a reworked parser and a lint sweep.
questions.no: Every subject and body describes one piece of work, even where it lists that work's parts, e.g. 'Add the profile screen, its view model and tests'.

questions.title: A commit's files carry work its subject hides
questions.question: Does any authored commit's `files` list (or `git show <sha>` patch) carry a second piece of work its subject and body do not name — e.g. a database migration under a typo-fix subject, or a project-wide reformat, rename sweep, dependency bump or tooling settings under a behaviour subject? The named work's supporting files never count (model, view, test, asset, manifest entry, navigation), nor does a swept-in generated or editor file. A broad commit is not a tangle by breadth alone. Leave the answer open, naming what would settle it, when a commit's `files` were not captured and `git show` fails — never answer NO for files you could not read — or when a vague subject ('wip', 'update') and its files cannot settle whether it holds one piece of work or two.
questions.yes: A commit's files show work its subject does not name, e.g. 'Fix typo in onboarding copy' (c3d4e5f) also adds `db/migrations/0042_add_orders.sql`.
questions.no: Every authored commit's files were read, and each holds the work its subject names and that work's supporting files.

questions.title: The tangle runs through the history
questions.question: Do two or more authored commits each bundle separable work, together holding most of the change, so a reviewer cannot follow or revert one concern at a time? A single bundling commit, including the only commit of a one-commit pull request, is NO. When unsure, answer NO.
questions.yes: Bundles dominate the history, e.g. most commits pair a feature with a formatting sweep or with a second feature.
questions.no: Bundled work, if any, sits in a single commit, or it is a small part of the change.

rules.reason: Every commit in the pull request is an automatic merge commit, so there is no authored split to judge.
Bundled commits run through the history, so a reviewer cannot follow or revert one concern at a time.
Commits throughout the history carry work their subjects do not name, so no concern can be reverted alone.
A commit names two separable pieces of work that could each be reviewed and reverted on their own.
A commit's files carry a second piece of work that its subject does not name.
Each authored commit holds one logical change, as its subject, body and files show.

practices.name: Track generated artifacts only when justified
practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer catches the most problems in the hand-written lines they can read closely, and a committed build output or editor config buries that source under machine noise nobody reviews. Leaving generated files out keeps the diff to the change a person can actually check, and spares everyone the odd conflict in a file no human wrote.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Build outputs, logs and editor files stay out of the repository. Deliberately tracked generated artifacts follow the documented generation workflow; intentional regeneration can be appropriate even without a simultaneous source edit.
practices.holdsAs: Tracked artifacts follow the repository generation policy
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: tracked generated or build artifacts are justified by captured repository policy or the source-to-artifact workflow.

## The standard
Judge one thing: does the change include generated or build artifacts only where the repository's captured policy or its source-to-artifact workflow justifies tracking them? This is a repository-hygiene practice about what gets committed — never a code-defect claim about a file's contents, and generated output is not itself the defect. Judge from the file paths in the diff. Machine noise being reviewed as if it were source has a recognisable shape across any stack or language — a location or a banner that says "a tool wrote this": a build-output directory, an editor or OS cruft file, a coverage dump, a vendored or cached blob, a minified single-line bundle, or a tracked generated file someone hand-edited instead of regenerating. These are open examples, not a closed list. A repository may deliberately version-control some generated sources — a committed OpenAPI spec, a generated client, an ERD, a route tree. When such a tracked artifact moves in step with the hand-written change that drives its regeneration, that is intended, regeneration-consistent movement: do not flag it. An intentional regeneration may be appropriate without a simultaneous hand-written edit. Flag only output that is not meant to be tracked, or a tracked generated file left hand-edited or stale relative to its source.

## Sources
1. The file spread (`work/change/files.json`) and the per-file headers of the diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the paths. They establish which paths changed and where they sit — the primary evidence. A path never establishes compile, build or runtime behaviour.
2. The patch body (`work/change/diff.patch`): open it only to confirm a flagged path is machine-emitted when the path alone is ambiguous — a "DO NOT EDIT", "@generated" or "auto-generated" banner, a minified single line. The evidence is the path plus that confirming line, never a line-by-line review of the file's contents.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the ignore rules, the documented generation workflow, and whether an artifact is tracked and which source drives it. It establishes whether tracking a generated file is intended. It never establishes manual editing or stale generation from an unchanged source file alone.
If the policy or source evidence a flag needs was not acquired, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
For a path you call machine output that should not be tracked, or a generated file hand-edited or stale, name each offending path verbatim and, for a generated-file claim, quote the confirming banner or name the tracked artifact and its driving source, together with the ignore rule or workflow line that shows how the repository treats it. If you cannot name an offending path, there is nothing to flag; do not invent one. Cite a line of the flagged file from `work/change/diff.patch` (`scm.pull-request.diff`, the pinned `context/change.json`): `work/change/files.json` is derived here and is not citable; a flagged file the diff shows without numbered lines (binary, or renamed without edits) is cited through the `path` line of its entry in `context/commits.json`. A NO that rests on absence must have walked every changed path: evidence.search records the boundary and the citations quote it — `changed_files` in `context/metadata.json` (`scm.pull-request.core`) and the paths you walked, listed in the rationale. Describe the observable fact ("this path is machine-emitted") and the next step (ignore it and drop it, or regenerate from source). Never assert compile, build or runtime behaviour from a path; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether a dependency change was deliberate or justified belongs to `changes-dependencies-deliberately`; a lockfile moving in step with its manifest is its concern. Do not infer that a lockfile was hand-edited merely because its manifest did not change — an intentional resolution refresh may update a lockfile alone. Here only: does the diff carry machine output that should not be tracked?

questions.title: The change touches at least one path
questions.question: Does the change add, modify, delete or rename at least one file, per `work/change/files.json` and the per-file headers of `work/change/diff.patch`? A change whose files are all generated still counts: its content can be reviewed.
questions.yes: At least one path changed, e.g. `src/App.swift` or `build/output.js`.
questions.no: The change is empty: no file is added, modified, deleted or renamed.

questions.title: The change carries machine output it should not
questions.question: Does a changed path carry machine output the repository should not track, or a tracked generated file hand-edited or left stale against its source? Output whose path or banner says 'a tool wrote this' — a build-output directory, an editor or OS cruft file, a coverage dump, a vendored or cached blob, a minified single-line bundle — is flagged by that shape unless the captured repository policy deliberately tracks it. A generated source a repository may deliberately track (a committed API spec, a generated client, an ERD, a route tree, a 'DO NOT EDIT' or '@generated' file) is flagged only when the captured policy or workflow shows it should not be tracked, or shows it hand-edited or stale; an unchanged source file alone shows neither. Never flag source, tests, docs, hand-written config or a lockfile. When the path, banner, patch and captured policy cannot tell, leave the answer open and name what would settle it.
questions.yes: A path is output the repository does not mean to track, e.g. `build/app.js`, `.DS_Store`, `coverage/lcov.info`, or an '@generated' client edited by hand.
questions.no: Every changed path is authored or a tracked generated artifact whose regeneration the workflow justifies.

questions.title: A whole output directory or a hand-edited generated file
questions.question: Does the change commit a whole build-output or dependency directory (a `build/`, `dist/` or `node_modules/` tree), or a tracked generated file hand-edited where the captured policy or workflow shows it should have been regenerated from its source? Stray cruft files, however many, do not count, and a deliberately tracked generated artifact whose regeneration the workflow justifies never counts. When unsure, answer NO.
questions.yes: e.g. a committed `dist/` tree, or a 'DO NOT EDIT' generated client with edits its source does not produce.
questions.no: The leak is one or more stray files, such as editor or OS cruft, and no generated file was hand-edited instead of regenerated.

rules.reason: The change is empty, so it commits no paths to review.
The change commits a whole build-output or dependency directory, or hand-edits a generated file instead of regenerating it.
The change commits machine output the repository does not mean to track, or a generated file out of step with its source.
Every changed path is authored or a generated artifact the repository's workflow means to track.

groups.name: Tracking work from issue to merge
groups.description: Plan and track the work so a maintainer can route it and watch it progress, and keep the issue and the change that answers it linked: split genuinely large issues into trackable sub-tasks, triage each one, name the issue the change implements, and confirm the issue's outcome when the change lands.

practices.name: Break large work into trackable subtasks
practices.whyItMatters: A big ask written as one wall of text is either 0% or 100% done, with no way to see progress or split the load. Breaking it into checkable steps turns a daunting job into pieces people can pick up and finish one at a time.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A genuinely large issue split into a task list or linked sub-issues, such as 'design the schema', 'add the endpoint', and 'wire up the UI', so progress is visible and pieces can be worked in parallel.
practices.holdsAs: Large work arrives split into trackable pieces
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: a trackable breakdown of work that is large enough to need one — checkable sub-units a maintainer can watch reach done, rather than one monolithic ask.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: when the issue describes genuinely LARGE or multi-part work, is that work broken into explicit, trackable sub-units, rather than left as a single undivided block? Trackable means the parts are individually checkable or addressable: a task list of checkboxes that name work to do, a tracked sub-issue tree, or enumerated child or tracking issues the body frames as parts. Reason like a senior reviewer scanning a backlog: a big ask written as one block is either 0% or 100% done with no visible progress; a decomposed one lets pieces be picked up in parallel and tracked to done. What counts as LARGE is a judgment, not a word count: the signal is two or more SEPARABLE deliverables that could ship or be assigned independently, or an explicit epic, initiative, meta or tracking framing the issue itself chose. Two or more such deliverables joined by commas or "and" in one sentence — a rename, a new tab, a theme, a changed default — are large work by this test however short the body is; the body's length is never the test. Sequential steps of ONE cohesive flow described as a journey are a single deliverable, not several parts. A checklist of verification items is not a work breakdown unless it also names concrete implementation sub-steps.

## Sources
Your context is the issue only; there is no diff or code.
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`context/description.md`): every section, checklist and enumerated list. It establishes whether the work is large (separable deliverables, epic framing) and whether a checklist or a set of framed child issues breaks it down. It never establishes largeness from title length or tone alone.
2. The labels and the sub-issue rollup (`context/metadata.json`): a label such as epic or tracking, and the `sub_issues_total` / `sub_issues_completed` figures. A non-zero rollup is a tracked sub-issue tree. The labels establish the framing the issue chose; they never by themselves establish that a breakdown exists.
3. The comments (`context/comments.json`): a later comment can supply the breakdown or the child issues. They establish a breakdown on that surface; they never establish one the text does not show.
An image in the body: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. Before concluding that no breakdown exists, scan ALL three surfaces. If the body or the comments were not captured, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
Every answer that the work is large quotes the exact span: a label name, a body sentence naming each separable deliverable, or the epic or tracking framing. To answer that a breakdown exists, quote the checklist lines, the `sub_issues_total` / `sub_issues_completed` figures or the framed child references. A NO on the breakdown rests on absence: scan the body, the rollup and the comments, and name all three as the boundary searched. To answer that there is no deliverable, quote the question or discussion, or say the body is empty, title-only or an unmodified template. Never invent largeness, never fabricate a breakdown you did not see. Never assert technical feasibility, hour estimates or design correctness, and never grade the reporter as a person; describe the observable artifact state only.

## Defer
Whether the work SHOULD have been one concern belongs to `issue-scoped-to-single-concern`; treat a multi-part ask as legitimately large work needing a breakdown, and do not re-judge its scope. Whether acceptance criteria or a Definition of Done are present belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`; do not re-flag a verification checklist here. Here only: is large work DECOMPOSED into trackable parts?

questions.title: Asks for a concrete deliverable in quotable text
questions.question: Does the issue ask for a concrete deliverable in body text you can quote? It does not when it is a pure question, a support request or an open discussion with no concrete deliverable, or when the body is empty, title-only or an unmodified template, so nothing is quotable.
questions.yes: The body asks for something to build or fix, e.g. 'design the schema, add the endpoint and wire up the UI for saved searches'.
questions.no: A question, a support request, a discussion, or an empty, title-only or unmodified-template body.

questions.title: Work is large or multi-part
questions.question: Is the work large or multi-part: two or more separable deliverables that could ship or be assigned independently, or an epic, initiative, meta or tracking framing the issue itself chose? Two such deliverables joined by commas or 'and' in one sentence count however short the body is. One focused deliverable (one feature, one bug) is not large, and neither are the sequential steps of one cohesive flow. Length, title and tone never decide. Do not judge whether the work should have been one issue. If the text cannot settle whether its parts are one journey or separate deliverables, leave the answer open and say what would settle it.
questions.yes: Separable deliverables or an epic framing, e.g. 'add CSV export, a print view and an email digest to the reports page'.
questions.no: One focused deliverable, or the steps of one cohesive flow, e.g. 'let users reset their password by email'.

questions.title: Work is broken into trackable parts
questions.question: Is the work broken into trackable sub-units in the body, the comments, or the labels and rollup in `context/metadata.json`? These count: a task list of checkboxes naming work to do, a non-zero `sub_issues_total`, or child issues the body or a comment names as parts. These do not: a checklist of verification items only; a plain bulleted or prose list of deliverables with no checkbox or issue per part; an epic label alone; sibling issues in the inventory that this issue never names. Scan all three surfaces. If none carries a breakdown and `sub_issues_total` is null, the provider's rollup was not captured and child issues may exist: leave the answer open.
questions.yes: A trackable breakdown is quotable, e.g. '- [ ] design the schema', '- [ ] add the endpoint', or 'sub_issues_total: 4'.
questions.no: Body and comments carry no checklist of work or named child issues, and the captured rollup is zero.

questions.title: Issue frames itself as an epic or tracker
questions.question: Does the issue itself frame the work as an epic, initiative, meta or tracking issue, through a label such as 'epic' or 'tracking' or through its own title or body ('Epic: …', 'Tracking issue for …', 'Meta: …')?
questions.yes: The issue chooses that framing, e.g. the label 'epic' or the title 'Tracking: offline mode'.
questions.no: Neither the labels nor the text frame the issue as an epic, initiative, meta or tracking issue.

rules.reason: The issue holds no concrete deliverable in quotable text: it is a question, a discussion or an empty template.
The issue asks for one focused deliverable, which needs no breakdown into subtasks.
The issue is framed as an epic or tracking issue, yet nothing is tracked under it.
The issue asks for several separable deliverables without a task list or sub-issues to track each.
The large work is broken into trackable parts through a task list, sub-issues or framed child issues.

practices.name: Classify the issue the way the project classifies issues
practices.whyItMatters: A label kind the project filters and groups by — type, priority, size — routes the issue to the board column, the person and the sprint it belongs to. An issue outside that scheme is the one nobody's filter shows, so it waits.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: The issue carries the labels, native type, owner or milestone required by the documented project policy for its kind; fields that the policy does not require may remain unset.
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: the issue satisfies the classification requirements of the documented project policy applicable to it.

## The standard
Judge whether this issue follows the labelling convention the project actually keeps, not whether every metadata field is filled. A convention must be established by an explicit documented project policy applicable to this kind of issue. Label frequency, a list of labels in use or another issue's assignment does not establish a requirement. Compare the captured issue with that policy: require only the label kinds, native type, ownership or milestone it actually mandates. A native issue type can satisfy a corresponding label kind. Never demand a classification the project does not use. Current automated capture does not supply project classification requirements, so this practice is unavailable for automated review. In a manual review, use the documented policy; failed acquisition of required policy or metadata is a collection gap. One observation per review, over the whole issue.

## Sources
1. The documented project classification policy supplied to the manual review: applicable label kinds, native issue types, ownership and milestone requirements. It establishes what this issue is required to carry, not how often metadata happens to occur elsewhere.
2. The issue metadata (`context/metadata.json`): native type, labels, assignees and milestone. It establishes what this issue carries.
3. The title and body (`context/description.md`): the issue kind and any explicit routing request. A request alone does not establish a project-wide rule.

## Grounding
Quote the applicable documented requirement and this issue's metadata. Never infer a normative convention from label frequency, labels in use, ownership on other issues or the number of people in a project. Never assess whether the work is worth doing.

## Defer
Problem framing belongs to `issue-states-an-actionable-problem`, scope to `issue-scoped-to-single-concern`, and the definition of done to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Here only: is the issue classified the way this project classifies its issues?

questions.title: A project policy classifies this kind of issue
questions.question: Does a documented project policy supplied to the review set classification requirements for this kind of issue: label kinds, a native type, an owner or a milestone? Answer NO only when a captured policy states that no requirement applies to this kind of issue. A missing policy is not evidence that there is no convention: leave the answer open and name the policy that would settle it.
questions.yes: A quoted policy sets classification requirements for this kind of issue.
questions.no: A quoted policy states that this kind of issue needs no classification.

questions.title: The issue carries what the policy requires
questions.question: Does the issue's metadata satisfy every classification requirement the applicable policy sets? A native issue type can satisfy a corresponding label kind. Do not require a field the policy does not mandate.
questions.yes: Every requirement the policy sets is satisfied, e.g. the policy asks for a type label and the issue carries 'type: bug'.
questions.no: A requirement the policy sets is not satisfied; quote it and the metadata that lacks it.

rules.reason: The project policy sets no classification requirement for this kind of issue.
The issue lacks a classification the project policy requires for it.
The issue carries every classification the project policy requires for it.

insufficiencyReason.description: Hephaestus captures the issue metadata, but not the project classification requirements that establish which labels, owners or milestones this issue should carry. Labels used elsewhere do not establish a required convention. A person with the project policy can assess this practice.

practices.name: Confirm the outcome before closing the issue

insufficiencyReason.description: Hephaestus reads an issue as it stands when the review runs, after the close. Its checklist, sub-issue progress and comments can all change after the close, and the issue can be reopened and closed again, so what Hephaestus reads cannot show what was still open when it was closed. Whether the outcome was confirmed at that close needs a person who saw it.

practices.whyItMatters: Closing an issue tells the whole team it is handled. Closing it with a checklist item still unticked or sub-issues still open drops that work quietly, and someone hits the gap later expecting it to be done.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Before closing, every acceptance item is checked and every tracked sub-issue is finished, or a comment says plainly what is being dropped and why, so 'closed' honestly means done.
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: evidence dated to the close accounts for the issue's stated outcome, through confirmed completion or an explained remainder.

## The standard
When an issue is closed as done, judge whether its own stated definition of done was confirmed at that close — every checkable acceptance item ticked and every tracked sub-issue finished — or whether a remainder was named at the close. Assess this single closure decision only, never the work: an empty checkbox may simply never have been ticked while the work was genuinely done. A closing comment that says plainly what is being dropped or deferred and why accounts for the remainder. The question is about the record as it stood at the close, and only evidence dated to that close can answer it. The current `state_reason`, body and rollup describe the latest state, not this close; never decide from them, whichever way they point. Never assert compile, runtime or correctness behaviour; there is no diff or code here. One observation per review, on the single at-close question. Do not infer a longitudinal or developer-wide pattern from this one issue.

## Sources
1. The issue record (`context/metadata.json`): state, `state_reason`, `closed_at`, labels and the sub-issue rollup. `closed_at` dates the close and nothing else. The body, labels and rollup are their values when the review read them, which is after the close; they never show their values at the close.
2. The title and body (`context/description.md`): the current text. A checkbox can be ticked, unticked or added after the close, and the issue can be reopened and closed again, so a current checkbox is not a checkbox at the close.
3. Comments (`context/comments.json`): `created_at` dates when a comment was written, not its present text, which may since have been edited; a comment written after the close is never a disposition at the close.
4. The workspace inventory (`context/project_inventory.json`): state the overlapping or closing artifact you found, quoted as `#number "title" (state)`, or that you scanned it and found none.
When the comments or the issue record were not captured, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
Every claim cites an exact quoted span and says what dates it: the state or `state_reason` value, the `closed_at` timestamp, and the at-close evidence of each item an answer relies on. An answer left open quotes what was read and states that it is dated after the close. State the inventory result in every observation. Describe only observable state — "closed as done with '<quoted line>' still unchecked at the close" — never a charge against the closer. Never fabricate a checklist, a clean bill or a disposition.

## Defer
Whether a new or open issue defines a checkable outcome belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Here only: was the stated outcome confirmed at the close?

questions.title: The issue was closed as done
questions.question: Does evidence dated to this close show the issue was closed as done? Answer NO only when evidence dated to the close shows it was closed as not planned, wontfix, duplicate, superseded or deferred. The current `state_reason` describes the latest state, not this close: when nothing dated to the close settles it, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: Evidence dated to the close shows the issue was closed as done.
questions.no: Evidence dated to the close shows it was closed as not planned, a duplicate, superseded or deferred.

questions.title: The issue stated checkable done-items
questions.question: Did the issue, as it stood at this close, state checkable done-items: acceptance or Definition-of-Done lines, a task list, or tracked sub-issues? Answer from evidence dated to the close. The current body and rollup were read after it, so when only they speak to it, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: Evidence dated to the close shows done-items, e.g. an acceptance checklist of three lines.
questions.no: Evidence dated to the close shows the issue stated no checkable done-item, only prose.

questions.title: A done-item was still open at the close
questions.question: Does evidence dated to this close show a done-item still open at it: an unchecked acceptance or Definition-of-Done line, or a sub-issue rollup short of complete? The current body and rollup were read after the close; when only they speak to it, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: Evidence dated to the close shows an item still open, e.g. '- [ ] export handles empty results' unchecked at the close.
questions.no: Evidence dated to the close shows every checkable item ticked and every tracked sub-issue complete.

questions.title: An acceptance condition was open
questions.question: Is an item open at the close an acceptance or Definition-of-Done condition, rather than only an open sub-issue in the rollup? Answer NO when no item was open at the close.
questions.yes: An acceptance or Definition-of-Done line was still unchecked at the close.
questions.no: No item was open, or only sub-issues in the rollup were open.

questions.title: The close names the remainder
questions.question: Does a comment written at or before the close say plainly what is being dropped or deferred and why? A comment written after the close does not count.
questions.yes: A comment dated to the close names what is dropped or deferred and why.
questions.no: Nothing dated to the close names where the open remainder went.

rules.reason: The issue was closed as not planned, a duplicate, superseded or deferred, not as done.
The issue stated no checkable done-item for the close to confirm.
The issue was closed as done with an acceptance condition open and nothing at the close accounting for it.
The issue was closed as done with tracked sub-issues still open and no remainder named.
The close confirmed every stated outcome or named where the remainder went.

practices.name: Link the change to the issue it implements
practices.whyItMatters: A change that names the issue it answers can be read against what was asked, closes that issue when it lands, and leaves a trail anyone can follow later. One without it makes the reviewer guess what the work was for, and leaves the issue open or closed by hand.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: The title, the description or the branch names the issue by number, with a closing keyword in the body when the change completes it, so the issue closes with the merge and the two stay linked.
practices.holdsAs: Every change names the issue it implements
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: the pull request names the issue it implements, so the work can be read against what was asked and the issue can close with the merge.

## The standard
Judge one thing: does this pull request say which issue it implements, in a way the platform links? A link is the issue's number in the title (`#12: …`), a closing reference in the body (`Closes #12`, `Fixes #12`, `Resolves #12`, or the provider's equivalent), a branch created from the issue (`12-add-login`), or a captured linked work item. A link makes the issue readable from the review; only a provider-recognized closing relationship can close it when the change merges; a change with none of these stands alone. Judge the presence of the link, never the quality of the issue it points to or whether the change fulfils it.

## Sources
1. The title, source branch and body (`context/metadata.json`, `context/description.md`): the number references and closing keywords as written. They establish the link the author made. They never establish that the issue exists or that the change fulfils it.
2. The linked work items (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`, and `context/linked_work_items.json` with `how` per item) when captured: the items the platform resolved from those references, and for each whether the provider records it as a closing candidate for this change (`how: closesOnMerge`) or the text merely mentions it (`how: mentions`). A provider-recorded closing link is the link, whatever the text says; a mention is only a mention. Their absence establishes nothing when no reference was written.
3. The inventory (`context/project_inventory.json`): whether the project tracks issues at all, and, for a change with no reference, whether an open issue plainly describes this work — quote its `#number "title"` if you find one, or say you scanned it and found none.
4. The commits (`context/commits.json`): a further place an issue number may appear. They establish a reference the author left in history, nothing more. The precomputed leads below these criteria list every number referenced, where it was written, and whether the inventory or the linked items hold an issue of that number with its title and state.
If the record or the inventory is unavailable for a change with no reference, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
To answer that the change names an issue, quote the reference as written in the title, body, branch name or commit subject, or the linked item's `#number "title"`. To answer that a reference does not hold, quote it and name the fact that breaks it: the number absent from the inventory and the linked items, or the issue's title against the change's work. A NO on naming an issue rests on absence: scan the title, body, branch, commits and linked items, and name every source scanned. For the open-issue answer, quote the inventory's `#number "title"` or say you scanned it and found none. Never invent an issue number, and never claim an issue's content from its number alone.

## Defer
Whether the change fulfils the issue's acceptance criteria belongs to `honours-linked-issue-acceptance-criteria`; the description's what and why belong to `describe-what-and-why`. Here only: is the change linked to the issue it implements?

questions.title: Project tracks its work in issues
questions.question: Does this project track work in issues: does `context/project_inventory.json` list at least one issue, or does a captured linked work item resolve to an issue of this project? A captured inventory that lists no issues means the repository tracks none.
questions.yes: The project has issues, e.g. the inventory lists '#12 "Add login" (OPEN)'.
questions.no: The captured inventory lists no issues at all.

questions.title: Change answers no issue by convention
questions.question: Is this change of a kind that answers no issue by convention: a release or version bump, a dependency update from a bot, a revert, or a merge of one long-lived branch into another? A change a person made to the product (a feature, a fix, a refactor, a docs or configuration change) is not such a change, even when it names no issue.
questions.yes: The change is e.g. 'Release 2.3.0', a Dependabot dependency update, 'Revert "Add login"', or 'Merge develop into main'.
questions.no: A person changed the product, e.g. 'Add CSV export to the reports page'.

questions.title: Change names an issue by number
questions.question: Does the title, body, source branch, a commit message or a captured linked work item name an issue by number? These count: the number in the title ('#12: …'), a closing reference in the body ('Closes #12', 'Fixes #12', 'Resolves #12' or the provider's equivalent), a branch created from the issue ('12-add-login'), a number in a commit message, or an item in `context/linked_work_items.json`. A number that appears only in template example text left in the description ('e.g. Closes #N') does not count. The precomputed leads list every number and where it was written. Scan every source before answering no.
questions.yes: A reference is written, e.g. 'Closes #12' in the body, or the branch '12-add-login'.
questions.no: No title, body, branch, commit or linked item names an issue, apart from template example text.

questions.title: A written reference does not hold
questions.question: Does an issue reference this change writes fail to be what it claims? That is the case when the number resolves to no issue in the inventory or the linked items, or when the reference claims to implement an issue whose captured title and body clearly concern different work. A deliberate cross-project issue link can satisfy traceability and is not broken. Judge only the reference, never the quality of the issue or whether the change fulfils it. If nothing is referenced, nothing is broken. If the inventory was not captured and no linked item resolves the number, it could be a pull request as well as an issue: leave the answer open and say what would settle it.
questions.yes: A written reference breaks, e.g. 'Fixes #40' where #40 is not an issue of this project, or '#12' claimed for login work while #12 is 'Dark mode'.
questions.no: Every written reference resolves to an issue of this project about this work, or to a deliberate cross-project issue, or nothing is referenced.

questions.title: The reference is in a form the platform links
questions.question: Is the issue named in a form the platform links: the title, a closing keyword in the body, a branch created from the issue, or a captured linked item? A number only in a commit message does not count.
questions.yes: e.g. 'Closes #12' in the body, the title '#12: Add login', or the branch '12-add-login'.
questions.no: The issue number appears only in a commit message, e.g. 'Fix #12 crash' as a commit subject.

questions.title: A closing link targets different work
questions.question: Does a closing keyword ('Closes #12', 'Fixes #12', 'Resolves #12') or a provider-recorded closing link (`how: closesOnMerge` in `context/linked_work_items.json`) name an issue whose captured title and body clearly concern different work, so the merge would close an issue this change does not fulfil? A mention without a closing relationship does not count. A change that delivers part of the issue, prepares for it, or works on the same feature is not different work. When unsure, answer no.
questions.yes: e.g. 'Closes #12' where #12 is 'Dark mode' and the change adds CSV export.
questions.no: No closing keyword or closing link names an issue about different work.

questions.title: No issue in the project covers this work
questions.question: Having scanned every issue in `context/project_inventory.json`, open or closed, is there none that this change's work could belong to? Compare titles and bodies with the change. If any issue might describe this work, answer no and quote its '#number "title"'.
questions.yes: No issue in the inventory concerns this work.
questions.no: An issue might describe this work, e.g. '#31 "Export reports as CSV" (OPEN)' for a change that adds CSV export.
