The change is a release, bot dependency update, revert or branch merge, which answers no issue by convention.
A closing reference in the change would close an issue about different work.
The issue reference the change writes resolves to no issue of this project, or to one about different work.
The change names its issue only where the platform does not link it, such as a commit message.
The change is product work, yet it names no issue and no issue in the project covers it.
The change names no issue, although the project tracks its work in issues.
The change names the issue it implements by number.

practices.name: Confirm the linked issue's outcome
practices.whyItMatters: A linked issue with its outcome unconfirmed tells the next person little about what was delivered. After a change merges, ticking what landed and naming what moves elsewhere keeps the tracker true.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: After a change merges, its linked issue accounts for what landed: delivered items are ticked or a closing sentence names them and says what moves elsewhere, and the issue's state matches.
practices.holdsAs: The linked issue accounts for merged work
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: for merged work, the captured record confirms the linked issue's stated outcome — its checkable items ticked or the remainder named — so the tracker accounts for what was delivered.

## The standard
Judge one thing about this merged pull request: does the captured record bring the linked issue's own definition of done into line with what landed? The merge establishes the occasion; this review assesses confirmation in the capture, not the issue body at merge time. An issue that stated a checkable outcome (an acceptance checklist, a Definition of Done, a Given-When-Then block, tracked sub-issues) is confirmed when the items the change delivers are ticked and any remainder is named — in the issue, in the pull request body, or in a closing comment. Assess only this bookkeeping act, never whether the work is correct: an unticked item may describe delivered work, and a ticked one may not. A closing sentence that says plainly what is done and what is deferred confirms the outcome as well as ticks do; a sentence that names the feature ("added CSV export") without naming the items confirms nothing.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): `state` and `merged_at`. It establishes that and when the change merged. It never establishes the issue's state.
2. Each linked item (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`: number, title, state, body; `how` in `linked_work_items.json` says whether the provider records it as a closing candidate): the checkable outcome as written, with its ticks as captured. It establishes what was stated and which items are ticked. Confirmation captured after the merge counts. A missing confirmation describes this capture; it does not establish that confirmation never happened or that it was missing at merge time. Its body is the text as mirrored at capture, and its opening and closing dates are not when any line of it was written. A closed state alone confirms nothing; the ticks or the words do.
3. The body (`context/description.md`) and the discussion (`context/general_comments.json`): a done/deferred mapping or a closing sentence. They establish what the author said was delivered. They never establish that it was.
4. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): read only to ground a heavier severity when a named item is plainly not touched. It never establishes that an item is met.
If the linked item's body or the record's merge time is unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
Quote the outcome items from the linked item as written, the tick state, the merge time from the record, and any closing sentence. To answer that the outcome is accounted for, quote the ticked items, the checked mapping or the sentence. A NO rests on absence: read the linked item's body, the description and the discussion, and name them as the boundary searched. Never claim an item is met or unmet from the code; never infer a tick that is not in the capture; never read a closed state as a tick. Credit a tick or a sentence in the item's body or the description as captured; say it was there before, at or after the merge only when independently dated evidence establishes that, since the creation date of a body, a description or a comment alone does not date text edited later. A later capture that confirms the outcome does not undo an earlier observation that read it unconfirmed; each stands for the capture it read.

## Defer
Whether the change fulfils the acceptance criteria belongs to `honours-linked-issue-acceptance-criteria`; the issue's own closing decision, when someone closes it by hand, belongs to `issue-closed-with-unmet-outcome`. Here only: does the captured record confirm the linked issue's outcome for the merged work?

questions.question: Is the pull request merged: does `context/metadata.json` record state merged with a `merged_at` time?
questions.yes: The record shows the merge, e.g. 'merged_at: 2026-05-02T10:14:00Z'.
questions.no: The pull request is open or was closed without merging.

questions.title: A linked issue states a checkable outcome
questions.question: Does an item this change explicitly implements state a checkable outcome you can quote: a task list, an acceptance or Definition-of-Done block, a Given-When-Then block, or a non-zero sub-issue rollup? An item counts when it is a closing candidate (`how: closesOnMerge` in `linked_work_items.json`) or partial work this change explicitly delivers part of. A mention alone does not count, and neither does a number that appears only in template example text left in the description ('e.g. Closes #N'). A user story without a task list, an outcome heading or sub-issues is no checkable outcome, however plainly the diff delivers it. The precomputed leads list each item with its outcome items and ticks.
questions.yes: e.g. '#12 "CSV export"' (closesOnMerge) lists '- [ ] export downloads a valid CSV' and '- [ ] an empty result shows a message'.
questions.no: No item this change implements states a checkable outcome, e.g. only a plain user story, a mention, or a template example.

questions.title: Linked issue was abandoned
questions.question: Was the linked item that states the outcome closed as not planned, duplicate or superseded, so its outcome was deliberately abandoned? A close as completed is not abandonment.
questions.yes: e.g. the item's state reason is 'not planned' or 'duplicate'.
questions.no: The item is open or was closed as completed.

questions.title: The record accounts for the outcome
questions.question: Does the captured record account for the linked item's stated outcome? It does when every outcome item is ticked; when a checked mapping or a sentence in the item, the pull request body or a comment names which items were delivered and where the rest moves; or, for partial work on an issue that stays open, when the delivered items are ticked and the rest left open. Generic template checks do not count, a sentence naming the feature without the items confirms nothing, and a closed state alone confirms nothing. Confirmation captured after the merge counts. Judge the recorded mapping, never whether the code delivers the items. If the complete text leaves the mapping genuinely ambiguous, leave the answer open and name the deciding question.
questions.yes: e.g. every item is ticked, or a comment says 'CSV download and empty-state message done; print view moves to #19'.
questions.no: Items are unticked with no word naming them, or the only sentence names the feature loosely, e.g. 'added CSV export'.

questions.title: Most of the outcome goes unaccounted
questions.question: Is most of the linked item's stated outcome unticked and unmentioned in the capture while the item is closed, or is the captured item still open with nothing said about the outcome? One or two unticked items, or a sentence that names the outcome even loosely, is less than that. When unsure, answer NO.
questions.yes: e.g. the closed issue has five of six items unticked and no sentence about them, or the issue is still open with no word after the merge.
questions.no: Only one or two items are unticked, or a sentence names the outcome, or everything is accounted for.

questions.title: An unaccounted item is plainly not in the change
questions.question: Is at least one unticked, unmentioned outcome item one that `work/change/diff.patch` plainly does not touch, with no changed file or line related to it? Read the diff only for this. An item about process rather than files (a review, an approval, a merge, a workflow step) is not one a diff can touch and does not count. When the diff could deliver the item, or you cannot tell, answer no.
questions.yes: e.g. 'an empty result shows a message' is unticked and unmentioned, and no changed line touches empty-result handling.
questions.no: The diff could deliver every unticked item, the open items are process steps, or you cannot tell.

No issue this change implements states a checkable outcome to confirm.
The linked issue was closed as not planned, duplicate or superseded, so its outcome was abandoned.
After the merge, most of the linked issue's outcome is unaccounted for, including an item the change plainly does not touch.
After the merge, the linked issue's outcome items are neither ticked nor named, so the tracker does not show what landed.
The linked issue's outcome items are ticked, or a sentence names what was delivered and what moves elsewhere.

practices.name: Track the review asks you defer
practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer's ask answered with 'later' and nothing else is a promise that evaporates at the merge. Turning a deferred ask into a tracked issue, or getting the reviewer's explicit agreement to drop it, keeps the review's value after the thread is resolved.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Every review ask the author does not address in the change is either turned into an issue the thread links, or explicitly waived by the reviewer; nothing is resolved with a bare 'will do later'.
practices.holdsAs: Deferred review asks become tracked issues
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: a review ask the author defers rather than addresses is turned into tracked work or explicitly waived by the reviewer, never resolved on a bare promise.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when a reviewer asked for something in a thread and the author did not do it in this change, what happened to the ask at the merge? A deferral is tracked when the thread, the body or a comment names an issue for it (`#number`, a link, "tracked in …") or the reviewer explicitly agrees to drop it ("fine to skip", "not needed", a reviewer statement accepting the author's stated reason). An approval given on the condition that the ask be done later ("approving, as long as the test lands in your next pull request") keeps the ask alive: it is a deferral that needs a tracked item, never a waiver. A deferral is bare when the ask is resolved or the change merged with only "later", "next PR", "will do" or silence. Judge only asks the author deferred; an ask the author addressed in the diff, or answered with a reason the reviewer accepted, is not a deferral.

## Sources
1. The inline review comments (`context/comments.json`: `path`, `line`, `body`, `author`, `created_at`) and the conversation (`context/general_comments.json`): every ask and every reply, with authors and dates. They establish which asks were made, which were answered, and with what words. The threads (`context/review_threads.json`) carry each thread's path, line and resolution and no words; a resolution by the author establishes nothing about the substance, and a resolution by the reviewer after the author's stated reason is the reviewer accepting it. The precomputed leads below these criteria list every comment by someone other than the author, one row each, with whether the change touches its file, whether the author replied, whether the reviewer had a later word on the thread or approved after it: decide every row that asks something.
2. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): whether an ask was addressed in the change — the file and line the thread anchors to, read as changed or not. It establishes addressed versus not; it never establishes a waiver.
3. The body and the discussion (`context/description.md`, `context/general_comments.json`): a follow-up list, an issue reference for the deferral, or the reviewer's agreement. They establish tracking or a waiver when quotable.
4. The linked work items (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`) when captured: an issue that names the deferred ask. It establishes the tracking; its absence establishes nothing when a comment names an issue by number.
If the change merged but the threads are absent or truncated, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
Quote the reviewer's ask and the author's reply verbatim with their authors and dates, and the issue reference or waiver when there is one. To answer that an ask was addressed, cite the changed line that addresses it; never claim an ask was addressed without it. A NO on tracking or waiver rests on absence: read the thread, the body, the conversation and the linked items, and name them as the boundary searched, noting silence where the author never replied. Never infer a waiver from an approval alone.

## Defer
Whether the author replied to comments at all belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`; a thread left unresolved at the merge belongs to `merged-past-unresolved-review-threads`. Here only: where did the deferred asks go?

questions.title: Pull request is merged
questions.question: Is the pull request merged: does `context/metadata.json` record state merged with a `merged_at` time?
questions.yes: The record shows the merge, e.g. 'merged_at: 2026-05-02T10:14:00Z'.
questions.no: The pull request is open or was closed without merging.

questions.title: A reviewer ask was left undone
questions.question: Did someone other than the author ask for a change in this pull request that the change does not make? The author is the `author` login in `context/metadata.json`; the precomputed leads list every other login's comment, one row each. Decide each against the diff. An ask is addressed by a changed line anywhere in the change that does what was asked; an unchanged anchor alone does not show it was not. A half-addressed two-part ask leaves one part undone, and a RESOLVED mark decides nothing. Not undone: an ask answered with a reason the reviewer explicitly accepted; a question that requests no change ('what is this for?'); a remark aimed at later work ('worth keeping in mind next time'). If you cannot tell whether the change addresses an ask, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: e.g. a reviewer wrote 'please add a test for the empty list' and no test for it appears in the diff.
questions.no: Every reviewer ask is addressed in the diff or answered with a reason the reviewer accepted, or no ask was made.

questions.title: A deferred ask was left on a bare promise
questions.question: Was a reviewer ask that this change does not make left with only 'later', 'next PR', 'will do' or silence? That means no issue is named for it (`#number`, a link, 'tracked in …') in the thread, the body, a comment or a linked item, and no reviewer explicitly waived it. A waiver is the reviewer agreeing to drop the ask: 'fine to skip', 'not needed', accepting the author's stated reason, or a reviewer's own 'ignore' or 'fine' on an ask, theirs or a bot's. These are not waivers: an approval conditioned on doing the ask later, a later approval without such words, a resolution by the author. If the last word could be a waiver or a deferral and the approval carries no comment, leave the answer open and name what would settle it.
questions.yes: e.g. the author replied 'will do in the next PR', resolved the thread, and the change merged with no issue named.
questions.no: Every deferred ask names an issue ('tracked in #42') or the reviewer explicitly waived it ('fine to skip'), or nothing was deferred.

questions.title: A correctness, safety or test ask went untracked
questions.question: Is one of the untracked, unwaived asks about correctness, safety or tests: a bug, a crash or data-loss risk, a security concern, a missing or broken test? A rename, a comment, a style point or a nit is not. When unsure, answer no.
questions.yes: e.g. 'this can throw on a null user, please guard it' was answered 'later' and merged with no issue.
questions.no: Any ask left untracked is small, such as a rename, a comment or a nit, or none is left untracked.

Every reviewer ask was addressed in the change or answered with a reason the reviewer accepted.
A correctness, safety or test ask was deferred on a bare promise and the change merged without tracking it.
A review ask was deferred on a bare promise, with no issue tracking it and no reviewer waiver.

practices.name: Merge only after someone else approved
practices.subject: MERGER
practices.whyItMatters: A change merged before anyone approved it skips the one check the team agreed on: a second pair of eyes before the code is everyone's. It is also how a reviewer's outstanding request for changes gets buried. Waiting for the approval, and re-requesting it after a rework, is what keeps the review real.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: The person who merges does so after an approval from someone other than the author that is still current — no later request for changes, no dismissal — and after a rework asks for the approval again before merging.
practices.holdsAs: Nothing merges without a current approval from someone else
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: the merge happens after a current approval from someone other than the author, and never over an outstanding request for changes.

## The standard
Judge one thing about the moment this pull request merged: was there, at that moment, an approval from another person — an account other than the author's whose decision is not marked `bot` — that still stood? An approval stands when it was submitted before the merge and nothing later withdrew it — no dismissal, no revocation (`UNAPPROVED`) and no request for changes by the same reviewer after it. A request for changes stands when it was submitted before the merge and no later approval by the same reviewer replaced it. A decision marked `bot` is an automated account's recorded act, never another person's review: its approval is not an approval here, and its request for changes does not stand against another person's approval. A complete bounded event record with no dismissal, revocation or later request for changes establishes no recorded withdrawal within that boundary. A latest-state snapshot alone does not establish complete historical event coverage. Merging with a standing approval and no standing request for changes is the practice; merging with none, or over a standing request for changes, is the lapse. Judge the decisions as recorded, never whether the review was thorough — that belongs to the review practices. That the author presses the merge button on their own pull request is the ordinary course in most teams and is never the lapse here; the only lapse is merging without another person's standing approval. The subject is the person who merged, whether or not that person authored the change.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): `merged_at`, `merged_by`, `author`. It establishes who merged and when. When `merged_by` is absent, record no observation: the review cannot name the merger. A different recorded merger is still the subject.
2. The review decisions (`context/review_threads.json`, `reviewDecisions` oldest first: `state`, `author`, `submittedAt`, `body` when one was written, `dismissed`) and the threads: each decision with its author and time. Dated events establish which approvals and requests stood at the merge. A current `DISMISSED` state or `dismissed` flag with no withdrawal time establishes only the state at capture, not whether dismissal preceded merge. A `truncated` record is a collection gap for this practice. The precomputed leads below these criteria list the merge and one row per decision with `beforeMerge`, `isAuthor`, `dismissed` and `bot` computed, and each reviewer's last decision apart: decide from the rows, and quote the decision and the merge from the record.
3. The inventory (`context/project_inventory.json`): whether other people work in this project, for the occasion only.
If `merged_at` or the decisions are unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
Quote `merged_at`, `merged_by` and each decision as recorded with its `author`, `state` and `submittedAt`. To answer that an approval or a request for changes stood, quote that decision and the merge time; to answer that none stood, quote the decisions that existed, or state that the complete record holds none. Identity is the login as recorded, compared as text: the same login is the same account. Whether an account is automated is the captured `bot` marker, never the login's shape or a display name; a decision without the marker counts as its reviewer's own. Never infer that a reviewer is the author from a display name, a repository path or a namespace; never infer an approval from a comment or a thumbs-up; never treat the author's own approval as one.

## Defer
Whether review threads were resolved belongs to `merged-past-unresolved-review-threads`; whether the pipeline was green belongs to `ready-and-traceable-handoff`, which reads `head_checks`. Here only: did another person approve before the merge?

questions.no: The pull request is open or was closed without merging.

questions.title: Project plainly works without review
questions.question: Does the repository plainly work without review here: no reviewer was requested on this pull request, no review decision (including one marked `bot`) or review thread exists on it, AND `context/project_inventory.json` shows a single-person project? A requested reviewer, any review decision or any review comment on this pull request means review is in play. If the inventory was not captured and nothing on this pull request shows review in play, leave the answer open and name the inventory.

questions.no: A reviewer was requested, a review decision or review comment exists, or other people work in the project.

questions.title: Another person's approval stood at the merge
questions.question: At `merged_at`, did another person's approval stand? That is an APPROVED decision by a login other than the `author`'s, not marked `bot`, submitted before `merged_at`, and not followed before the merge by a dismissal, a revocation (`UNAPPROVED`) or a request for changes from the same reviewer. The author's own approval never counts, an approval marked `bot` never counts, and a comment or thumbs-up is no approval. Who pressed merge does not matter. Decide from the precomputed rows (`beforeMerge`, `isAuthor`, `dismissed`, `bot`). A complete bounded event record with no withdrawal establishes none; a latest-state snapshot alone does not. If a deciding event has no usable time, including a `dismissed` flag with no dated withdrawal, leave the answer open.
questions.yes: e.g. 'APPROVED by bob at 09:02', merged by alice at 10:14, with no later decision by bob.
questions.no: No other person's approval stood at the merge, e.g. no decisions at all, only the author's own, or only one marked `bot`.

questions.title: A request for changes stood at the merge
questions.question: At `merged_at`, did another person's request for changes stand? That is a CHANGES_REQUESTED decision by a login other than the author's, not marked `bot`, submitted before `merged_at`, with no later approval by the same reviewer replacing it and no dismissal dated before the merge. A request for changes marked `bot` never stands against another person's approval. A request that carries a `dismissed` flag with no dated withdrawal may have been withdrawn before the merge: leave the answer open.
questions.yes: e.g. 'CHANGES_REQUESTED by carol at 08:40', not dismissed, and no later approval by carol before the 10:14 merge.
questions.no: No other person's request for changes stood at the merge.

questions.title: An approval was dismissed and not renewed
questions.question: Was an approval by another person (not marked `bot`) dismissed or revoked by a dated event before `merged_at`, with no renewed approval from that reviewer before the merge? A current dismissed flag with no withdrawal time does not date the dismissal.
questions.yes: e.g. bob's 09:02 approval was dismissed at 09:30 after a push, and bob did not approve again before the 10:14 merge.
questions.no: No approval by another person was withdrawn before the merge without being renewed.

The pull request was merged over another person's standing request for changes.

practices.name: Record the plan before the first commit
practices.whyItMatters: A tracked issue written before the first recorded commit gives reviewers a prior statement of the work. Commit timestamps provide a recorded ordering, not proof of when someone actually started thinking or coding.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: The tracked issue this change implements has an opening timestamp no later than the earliest captured commit author timestamp. The record names both times without inferring intent or unrecorded work.
practices.holdsAs: The issue exists before the first recorded commit
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: the tracked issue this change implements exists no later than the earliest captured authored commit, without inferring actual work-start or motive.

## The standard
Judge one thing: did the issue this pull request implements exist no later than the first recorded commit? The earliest captured commit author date (`context/commits.json`, `authoredAt`) is the recorded timing proxy. It does not establish when actual work began, and the pull request creation time is a handoff time, not a substitute for it. The issue's opening is its `createdAt` in the linked work item. An issue opened before the first captured commit precedes that recorded step; an issue opened after it follows that step. Neither timing establishes the author's intent or the order of unrecorded work. Judge only the recorded order of the two dates, never the quality of the issue or of the change.

## Sources
1. The linked work item (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`, its opening line `Opened <time>`, and `linked_work_items.json`, `createdAt`): when the issue was opened. It establishes the plan's date.
2. The commits (`context/commits.json`, `authoredAt`): author dates of recorded commits. Require a usable author date for every captured commit and compare the earliest; neither a commit date nor a handoff timestamp substitutes for missing author dates. These dates do not establish actual work-start.
3. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): the identity of the reviewed work, never a substitute start time.
4. The precomputed leads below these criteria: each candidate issue, how it was named, its opening time, the earliest commit's author date and the hours between them, computed; read the two dates from it and check them against the sources above.
Failed or missing required linked-work-item or commit capture is a collection gap and produces no observation. Successfully captured records with missing native dates leave the timing unsettled: name the missing date.

## Grounding
Cite the linked item's `Opened <time>` line and the reviewed pull request record; cite the earliest usable author date and SHA from the captured `context/commits.json` artifact. To answer that a date is missing, name the commit or the issue number that lacks it, and for an issue among the `unresolvedReferences` never claim it exists, predates the work or closes. To answer that the change implements no issue, quote the description's wording or state that the leads list no candidate. Never infer an order from issue and pull request numbers; never read a commit date where an author date exists.

## Defer
Whether the change names its issue belongs to `links-the-change-to-its-issue`; whether the issue states a checkable outcome belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Here only: did the issue exist before the first recorded commit?

questions.title: Change implements a named issue
questions.question: Do the precomputed leads list an issue that this pull request implements? A candidate counts when it is this repository's closing candidate (`how: closesOnMerge`, including a link made in the provider's UI), or is named by a closing keyword, the title, the branch or the author's own 'Related to #N'. A 'Related to' counts only when the description or the issue shows this change delivers part of that issue's work. One among the `unresolvedReferences` named this way still counts. None counts when the description rules it out ('Not related to #N'); when the number sits only in a quotation, code, an HTML comment or template example text; when it is another project's; or when the change is a release, a bot dependency update or a revert.
questions.yes: e.g. the body says 'Closes #12', or the branch is '12-add-login', and the leads list #12.
questions.no: No listed candidate is an issue this change implements, or the change is a release, a bot dependency update or a revert.

questions.title: The issue predates the first commit
questions.question: Was the issue this change implements opened no later than the earliest captured commit's `authoredAt`? The precomputed leads give the issue's `createdAt`, the earliest author date across all captured commits, and the hours between them; check them against the sources. When several plausible issues fall on the same side, use the one a closing candidate names, else the title, else the branch, else the 'Related to'. Never infer an order from issue or pull request numbers, and never use a commit date or the pull request's creation time in place of an author date. Leave the answer open, and name what would settle it, in three cases. First, `context/commits.json` is empty or a commit has no usable `authoredAt`. Second, the issue has no opening time here: it is among the `unresolvedReferences`, or its linked item has no `createdAt`. Third, plausible issues fall on both sides and nothing settles which one this change implements.
questions.yes: e.g. #12 opened 2026-04-28T09:00:00Z; the earliest commit was authored 2026-04-30T15:02:00Z.
questions.no: e.g. the earliest commit was authored 2026-04-30T15:02:00Z; #12 opened 2026-05-01T08:00:00Z.

groups.name: Building iOS apps well
groups.description: Write SwiftUI the way it is designed to be written: views that describe the screen from state they are handed, state owned where it belongs, concurrency that is structured, an interface everyone can use, a preview for every screen, and permissions declared truthfully. These practices run only on changes that touch Swift code.

practices.name: Keep networking and persistence out of views

precondition.skipReason: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: A SwiftUI view that fetches, decodes or saves is a view nobody can preview, test or reuse, and its logic is invisible to the next screen that needs the same data. Keeping that work in a model or store is what lets the view stay a description of the screen.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Views describe the screen from state they are handed; requests, decoding and file or preference access live in a model, store or service the view talks to through a method or a binding, and SwiftData is used through its own view-side idiom.
practices.holdsAs: Views render the state they are handed and never fetch or persist
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: added SwiftUI view code delegates I/O appropriately or uses the framework's supported view-side persistence idiom.

## The standard
Judge one thing about the SwiftUI code this change adds: does a `View` type perform I/O itself? I/O in a view is a `URLSession` or `URLRequest` call, `JSONDecoder`/`JSONEncoder` use, `UserDefaults` or `FileManager` access, `Data(contentsOf:)`, a Core Data fetch request, or a `fetch`/`load`/`save` implemented inside a `struct … : View` — in `body`, a modifier closure (`.task`, `.onAppear`, a button action) or a method of the view. A view that calls a model's method (`store.load()`, `viewModel.save(item)`) or passes a `Binding` is not performing I/O, and the framework's own view-side storage — SwiftData's `@Query` and `modelContext.insert`/`delete` through `@Environment(\.modelContext)`, Core Data's `@FetchRequest`, and SwiftUI's `@AppStorage` and `@SceneStorage` — is the framework's designed use of a view, not I/O the view took on. The judgement is about where the work lives, never about the architecture's name.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added lines and the type each hunk lies in, read from the hunk header and the surrounding declaration. It establishes which added lines are inside a view type and which call I/O. It never establishes what unchanged code does.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the enclosing type of a hunk when the diff context does not show it, and whether a called method belongs to a model or store. Read it only to place a line; it never adds an I/O call the diff does not show.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the I/O calls it found inside view types, as leads to inspect, never as conclusions.
If the diff of a Swift file is truncated where a view type is edited, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
For an added line that performs I/O, quote the `[L<n>]` line and the `struct … : View` declaration it lies in. For view code that performs none, cite the added view code and its enclosing declaration, include a delegating call when relevant, and record the diff as the source searched: every added line inside a view type was read. For whether the change adds view code at all, cite an added line with its enclosing view declaration, or the declarations that place every added hunk outside a view. For a line whose enclosing type cannot be placed, quote it and name the declaration that would settle it. Never claim I/O from a method name alone (`load()` may be a model call); never claim a type is a view without its declaration; never count a SwiftData `modelContext` call or a `@Query`, `@FetchRequest`, `@AppStorage` or `@SceneStorage` declaration as I/O.

## Defer
Duplicated logic across views belongs to `removes-duplication-instead-of-copy-pasting`; oversized view bodies to `keeps-functions-small-and-single-purpose`. Here only: does the view do I/O itself?

Added lines inside a view type count whether or not they perform I/O. A model-only, service-only, test-only or non-Swift change does not count.

questions.no: The added lines lie only in models, services, tests or non-Swift files.

questions.title: An added view line performs I/O itself

Not I/O by the view: calling a model's method (`store.load()`, `viewModel.save(item)`), passing a `Binding`, and the framework's view-side storage — `@Query`, `modelContext.insert`/`delete`, `@FetchRequest`, `@AppStorage`, `@SceneStorage`. Never infer I/O from a method name alone; `load()` may be a model call.

A single read inside one view (a `UserDefaults` read, a decode) does not count, nor does I/O in a small preview-only or prototype view. When unsure, answer NO.

practices.name: Own SwiftUI state at the right level

precondition.skipReason: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: State declared in the wrong place is the root of the bugs that make SwiftUI feel unpredictable: a model recreated on every render, a value copied into two views that drift apart, a derived value stored and forgotten. Declaring each piece of state where it is owned keeps the screen a function of its data.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Value state a single view owns is `@State`; a shared model is `@Observable` and injected through the environment or passed down, never recreated in a child; a child that edits a parent's value takes a `Binding`; a derived value is computed, not stored.
practices.holdsAs: Each piece of state lives at the level that owns it
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: each piece of SwiftUI state declared where it is owned — view-local values as `@State`, shared models observed and injected, edits through `Binding`, derived values computed rather than stored.

## The standard
Judge the state declarations this change adds to SwiftUI views against four rules. (1) A value one view owns and mutates is `@State` (or `@AppStorage` for a persisted setting); a `let` or plain `var` that the view mutates is a lapse. (2) A model shared by more than one view is one object: `@Observable` (or `ObservableObject`) created once by its owner and reached through `@Environment`, `@Bindable` or a passed reference — a child view that creates its own instance of a shared model (`@State private var store = Store()` in a child, `StateObject` for a model the parent already holds) is a lapse. (3) A child that edits a parent's value takes a `Binding` (`@Binding`, `$value`), not a copy it mutates. (4) A value derivable from other state (a count, a filtered list, a formatted string) is a computed property, not a second stored variable kept in sync by hand. Judge declarations and how they are wired, never naming or file layout.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added declarations and the wiring that hands state between views (`init` arguments, `.environment(…)`, `$` bindings). It establishes what was declared where. It never establishes what unchanged views hold.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether a model type is `@Observable`, whether a parent already owns an instance a child recreates, and whether a stored value is derivable from other declared state. Read it to place a declaration; it never adds a declaration the diff does not show.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the declarations it found inside view types, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where a view's declarations are edited, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
For a declaration that breaks a rule, quote the `[L<n>]` declaration and name the rule; for a shared model recreated in a child, also quote the parent's declaration of the same model; for a derived value, name the state it derives from. For declarations that follow the rules, quote the one you accepted as the representative and record that every added state declaration in the diff was enumerated. For whether a model is shared, name the type and the views that hold it, or the fact that would settle it. Never claim a model is shared without a second view that holds it; never claim a value is derivable without naming the state it derives from.

## Defer
I/O inside views belongs to `keeps-views-free-of-networking-and-persistence`; concurrency belongs to `uses-structured-concurrency-safely`. Here only: is the state declared where it is owned?

questions.title: The change adds state to a SwiftUI view
questions.question: Does the change add a state declaration or state wiring to a SwiftUI view: an added `@State`, `@Binding`, `@Environment`, `@Bindable`, `@AppStorage`, `@Observable`, `ObservableObject`, `StateObject`, `ObservedObject`, or a mutable stored property inside a view type, or added wiring that hands state between views (`init` arguments, `.environment(…)`, `$` bindings)? A change to a view's layout alone does not count.
questions.yes: e.g. `[L14] @State private var query = ""` or `.environment(store)` added to a view.
questions.no: The change touches view layout, models outside views, or non-view code only.

questions.title: A child recreates or copies its parent's state
questions.question: Does an added declaration split state a parent view owns? Either (a) a child creates its own instance of a model a parent already owns (`@State private var store = Store()` or a `@StateObject` in the child) — quote both declarations; or (b) a child mutates a copy of a parent's value that the parent reads, and nothing hands the edit back (no `Binding`, callback or model method). A draft returned through a save callback is not a split; reaching a model through `@Environment`, `@Bindable` or a passed reference is right. If a view creates a model instance and neither the diff nor the checkout shows whether a parent owns one too, leave the answer open and name what would settle it.
questions.yes: e.g. `[L18] @State private var store = LibraryStore()` in `BookRow` while `LibraryView` already owns one; or a child `var isOn: Bool` toggled where the parent's flag was meant to change.
questions.no: Children reach shared models through the environment, `@Bindable` or a reference, and hand edits back through a `Binding` or callback.

questions.title: View-local or derived state is misdeclared
questions.question: Does an added declaration misplace state a view keeps for itself: a `let` or plain `var` stored property that the view mutates, where `@State` (or `@AppStorage` for a persisted setting) belongs; or a stored value kept in sync by hand with other declared state it could be computed from (a count, a filtered list, a formatted string)? For a derived value, name the state it derives from and the code that copies it across; a value fetched, typed by the user or edited as a draft is not derived. Judge declarations and wiring, never naming or file layout.
questions.yes: e.g. `[L9] var count = 0` mutated in a button action, or `@State var filtered: [Item]` reassigned whenever `items` changes.
questions.no: Values the view mutates are `@State` or `@AppStorage`, and derived values are computed properties.

rules.reason: The change adds no state declaration or state wiring to a SwiftUI view.
A child view recreates or copies state its parent owns, so the two can silently reset or drift apart.
A view keeps mutable state outside `@State`, or stores a value it could compute from other state.
Each added piece of state is declared where it is owned: local `@State`, injected models, bindings, computed values.

practices.name: Make the UI accessible by default

precondition.skipReason: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: A control a screen reader cannot name, a label that cannot grow with the user's text size, an image that says nothing — each locks a group of people out of the screen, and each is a line the author could have written when the view was made. Accessibility added later is the expensive kind.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Every icon-only control and meaningful image has a label; text uses semantic fonts so Dynamic Type works; nothing is fixed to a size that clips at larger text; colour is never the only signal.
practices.holdsAs: Every control carries a label and text scales with the user
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: the added SwiftUI interface is usable with a screen reader and at large text sizes — icon-only controls and meaningful images labelled, text sized semantically, layout free of size caps that clip.

## The standard
Judge the interface code this change adds against a closed list of accessibility facts. (1) An icon-only control — a `Button`, `Toggle`, `Link` or tappable `Image` whose visible content is an `Image(systemName:)` or an asset image with no text — carries an `accessibilityLabel` (or a `Label` with a text title). (2) A meaningful image (an asset that carries information) carries a label or is marked `.accessibilityHidden(true)` when decorative. (3) Text, and an SF Symbol shown with it, use a semantic font (`.font(.body)`, `.headline`, `.title2`, …) or a scaled custom font, not `.font(.system(size: 14))` or a fixed-size custom font — a symbol sized in points stays small when the text around it grows. (4) No text container is capped in height (`.frame(height:)`, `.lineLimit(1)` on body copy) in a way that clips at larger text. (5) A state shown by colour alone (red for error, green for done) is also shown by text, an icon or a trait. Judge added lines only; an existing lapse the change did not touch is not this change's.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added interface lines and the modifiers attached to them in the same expression. It establishes what each control and text carries. A modifier on the same view chain counts; one on a distant ancestor does not establish a label for an inner icon.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether an asset image is decorative or informative, and whether a custom font is scaled with `relativeTo:`. Read it to classify; it never adds a control the diff does not show.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the icon-only controls, fixed-size fonts and height caps it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where a view body is edited, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
For an added item that breaks the list, quote the `[L<n>]` line of the control, image, font or cap and name the fact it breaks; for a missing label, cite the view chain you read. For an interface that keeps every fact, quote a representative labelled control or semantic font and record that every added control, image and text line in the diff was enumerated. For an image whose role is open, name the asset. Never claim a label is missing without reading the whole view chain the control sits in; never claim clipping from a `.frame` on a non-text container.

## Defer
Localisation of the strings belongs to no practice here; magic numbers in layout to none. Here only: can everyone use what was added?

One unlabelled icon or one fixed-size font on a secondary element does not count. When unsure, answer NO.

practices.name: Use structured concurrency safely

precondition.skipReason: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: An unstructured task that outlives its view, UI state mutated off the main actor, a fire-and-forget request that cannot be cancelled — these are the crashes and stale screens that appear only on a slow network. Swift's structured concurrency prevents them when it is used the way it is designed.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: View-lifecycle work runs in `.task` or another effective cancellation lifecycle. A synchronous user action can start a Task whose lifetime fits the operation; UI state stays correctly isolated and needed results or failures are handled.
practices.holdsAs: Async work is scoped to its view and cancelled with it
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: async work tied to the lifetime that owns it, UI state mutated on the main actor, and no fire-and-forget task where structure was available.

## The standard
Judge the concurrency code this change adds against a closed list. (1) View-lifecycle work belongs in `.task { }` or an equivalent observed cancellation lifecycle. A `Task { }` in a synchronous button action is a native bridge to asynchronous work, not a defect by itself. Judge whether its lifetime and cancellation fit the operation: work that must stop with the view has an effective cancellation path, while a user-initiated operation can legitimately complete after the view disappears. A stored handle or a written reason can establish intent but is not mandatory when the captured code already establishes the lifecycle. (2) State the UI reads is mutated on the main actor: a type that holds view state is main-actor isolated — by `@MainActor`, by being a SwiftUI `View`, or by the target's default actor isolation (`SWIFT_DEFAULT_ACTOR_ISOLATION = MainActor` in the build settings or `project.yml`) — or the mutation is `await MainActor.run`; a mutation of `@Published`/`@Observable` UI state from a background context is a lapse. (3) Detached work and dispatch queues have an evidenced need for their independent execution or scheduling; the captured code may establish that need without a redundant comment. (4) A result needed by the operation is consumed; a task can perform a side effect without its handle being stored, and whether a thrown failure is handled belongs to the practice named under Defer. Judge added lines; existing concurrency the change did not touch is not this change's.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added concurrency constructs and where they sit (a view modifier, a model method, a service). It establishes what was written. It never establishes the actor a type is isolated to when that declaration is outside the diff.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the declaration of the type a mutation lands in (`@MainActor` or not) and the target's default actor isolation, and whether a `Task` handle is stored. Read it to place a construct; it never adds one.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the `Task {` blocks, `.onAppear` with async work, detached tasks and dispatch queues it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where async code is added, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
For an added construct that breaks the list, quote the `[L<n>]` construct and name the item it breaks; for an actor lapse, also quote the declaration of the type mutated. For constructs that follow the list, quote a representative one and record that every added concurrency construct in the diff was enumerated. For an isolation that cannot be read, name the type. Never claim a mutation is off the main actor without the type's isolation and the target's default isolation; never claim a task is fire-and-forget when a handle is stored in the same hunk.

## Defer
Swallowed errors in async code belong to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; crash-shaped constructs to `avoids-unsafe-panics-and-chosen-crashes`. Here only: is the concurrency structured?

(2) UI state mutated from a background context in a type that is not main-actor isolated. (3) `Task.detached` or a `DispatchQueue` with no need the code shows. (4) A needed result never awaited or read; a dropped thrown error belongs to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`. Added lines only; a call into an unchanged method is judged as a call. If nothing else breaks an item and a mutated type's isolation (annotation or the target's default) cannot be read, leave the answer open and name it.

Claim an off-main mutation only with the type's declaration and the target's isolation setting in hand. A lifecycle mismatch on a short local operation does not count. When unsure, answer NO.
