questions.no: The lapse is a short local operation, a detached task or queue without need, or an unread result.

rules.reason: The change adds no concurrency: no async code, task, actor, main-actor annotation or dispatch queue.
A network task that nothing cancels writes view state, or UI state is mutated off the main actor.
Added async work outlives its view, runs detached or on a queue without need, or never reads a result it needs.
The added async work is scoped to its owner, UI state stays on the main actor, and needed results are used.

practices.name: Ship a preview with each new view

precondition.skipReason: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: A SwiftUI view without a preview is a screen nobody can see without running the whole app to it, and the first thing the next person deletes when it breaks. A preview with representative data is the cheapest verification a view can have, and the way a reviewer sees what changed.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Every new view type ships a `#Preview` that renders it with representative sample data — including an empty or error state when the view has one — so the screen can be seen and checked without launching the app.
practices.holdsAs: Every new view ships with a preview that renders it
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: a `#Preview` (or `PreviewProvider`) arriving with each new SwiftUI view type, rendering it with representative data.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when this change adds a new SwiftUI view type, does the same change ship a preview for it? A preview is a `#Preview` block or a `PreviewProvider` that constructs the view; it is representative when it hands the view sample data of the shape it renders (a filled model, a non-empty list) rather than defaults only, and it is complete when a view that has an empty, loading or error state previews that state too. A preview that constructs the view with a fresh or live view model and no sample shows only the view's first state — a spinner, an empty list, a prompt — and a live fetch inside a preview is not sample data; such a preview exists but is not representative. A preview for an existing view the change edits is welcome but not required. Judge presence and representativeness of the preview, never its layout or naming.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with the file list (`work/change/files.json`): the added `struct … : View` declarations and the `#Preview`/`PreviewProvider` blocks in the same change. It establishes which new views have a preview and what data the preview passes. It never establishes that a preview renders.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): a preview that lives in another file of the same change, or sample-data helpers the preview uses. Read it to find the preview; it never supplies one the change did not add.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the new view types and the previews it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where a new view is declared, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
For each new view, quote the `[L<n>]` `struct … : View` declaration. For a preview, quote its `#Preview` or `PreviewProvider` line and the data it passes, and name what it lacks when that data is not representative. A claim that a new view has no preview rests on absence: quote the declaration and say what you scanned — every Swift file in the diff. For a preview found only in the checkout, name its file. Never claim a preview renders or compiles.

## Defer
How to verify the change as a whole belongs to `states-how-to-verify-the-change`; tests for logic to `ships-tests-with-the-change`. Here only: can the new screen be seen?

questions.title: The change adds a new SwiftUI view type
questions.question: Does the change add a new SwiftUI view type: an added `struct … : View` declaration in a non-test file? Every added view type counts, `private` and file-scoped ones included. An edit to an existing view, a model-only change or a preview-only change does not count.
questions.yes: e.g. `[L3] struct BadgeView: View {` added in `Views/BadgeView.swift`.
questions.no: No new `struct … : View` is declared outside tests; the change edits existing views, models or previews only.

questions.title: A new view has no preview
questions.question: After scanning every Swift file in the diff, is there a new `struct … : View` type (in a non-test file, `private` and file-scoped ones included) that no `#Preview` block or `PreviewProvider` in this change constructs? A preview may live in another file of the same change. A parent's preview does not preview the child: a small helper view (a row, a badge) needs its own. A preview of the view that exists only in the checkout, where the diff cannot show whether this change added it, is not an absence: when no other new view plainly lacks a preview and a new view's only preview is found in the checkout, leave the answer open and name what would settle it.
questions.yes: e.g. `[L3] struct BadgeView: View` is added and no `#Preview` or `PreviewProvider` in the change constructs `BadgeView`.
questions.no: Every new view type is constructed by a `#Preview` or `PreviewProvider` in the change.

questions.title: A new view's preview lacks representative data
questions.question: Does a preview of a new view render it with nothing representative, or omit a state the view plainly has (an empty, loading or error branch in its body)? Not representative: an empty list for a list screen, a model holding only defaults, a fresh view model whose initializer loads nothing (the preview shows only a spinner, an empty list or a prompt), or a live fetch in place of sample data. Read what the constructed model holds before calling it empty: a model whose initializer fills sample data is representative, and a view that takes no data is representative once constructed. If that initializer cannot be read, leave the answer open and name it.
questions.yes: e.g. a preview passing a fresh view model whose initializer starts with an empty array, or a list view with an error branch no preview shows.
questions.no: Each new view's preview shows it with sample data of the shape it renders, or the view takes no data, and its empty, loading or error states are previewed.

rules.reason: The change adds no new SwiftUI view type outside tests.
A new SwiftUI view ships without a preview, so nobody can see it without running the app.
A new view's preview renders it without representative sample data, or skips a state the view has.
Every new view ships with a preview that renders it with representative data.

practices.name: Declare permissions truthfully and ask at the point of use

precondition.skipReason: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: A capability the app requests without a usage description crashes on the device; one with a boilerplate description fails App Review and the user's trust; one requested at launch instead of at the moment it is needed is denied and never asked again. The declaration and the ask are part of the feature.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: When a change adds a capability that needs the user's permission, the `Info.plist` usage description arrives in the same change, says truthfully what the app does with the access, and the permission is requested where the feature needs it, not at launch.
practices.holdsAs: Permissions say truthfully why and are asked for in use
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: a capability that needs the user's permission arriving with a truthful usage description and a request made where the feature needs it.

## The standard
Judge the permission-bearing capabilities this change adds against three facts. (1) Declaration: when the platform requires usage-description keys for the access actually requested, the matching keys are present in `Info.plist`, `project.yml` or the target's build settings. Determine the keys from the actual authorization API and deployment target, not an import or one fixed key per framework. For example, modern EventKit full or write-only calendar access uses the corresponding `NSCalendarsFullAccessUsageDescription` or `NSCalendarsWriteOnlyAccessUsageDescription`; legacy calendar APIs differ. Notification authorization needs no usage-description key, and the system photo picker needs no full-library authorization. (2) Truth: the description names what the app does with the access, not a placeholder ("needed", "for the app", an empty string). (3) Point of use: the authorization request (`requestWhenInUseAuthorization`, `requestAuthorization`, `PHPhotoLibrary.requestAuthorization`, …) is made from the feature that needs it, not from app launch or a root view's `onAppear`. Judge added capabilities; an existing one the change did not touch is not this change's.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with the file list (`work/change/files.json`): the added capability code, authorization requests, and usage-description keys in `Info.plist`, `project.yml` or `*.pbxproj`. It establishes what was added where. It never establishes what the app already declared.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the existing `Info.plist`/`project.yml` for a key the change relies on but did not add, and the call site of the request. Read it to complete the picture; a key present there satisfies the declaration.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the capabilities, requests and usage keys it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where the capability is added, or the project's plist is unreadable, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` capability or request line and the plist or project key as written. A claim that a key is missing rests on absence: state the files scanned — the change, the checkout's `Info.plist` and `project.yml`, and the target's build settings. Never claim a request site is launch without the call chain that reaches it. For a description you call a placeholder, quote it. For a capability that needs no key, name the platform exemption. For keys that may live where the checkout cannot show, name the build setting or generated file.

## Defer
Over-broad permissions and insecure defaults belong to `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions`. Here only: is the permission declared truthfully and asked for at the point of use?

questions.title: The change adds a permission-bearing capability
questions.question: Does the change add a permission-bearing capability: added permission-requiring access through `CoreLocation`, direct photo-library APIs, `AVFoundation` capture, `UserNotifications`, `EventKit`, `Contacts`, `HealthKit`, `AppTrackingTransparency`, or an added authorization request? `SwiftUI`'s `PhotosPicker` or `PHPickerViewController` alone needs no full-library permission and does not count; an import alone does not establish restricted access; an existing capability the change did not touch does not count.
questions.yes: e.g. `[L20] manager.requestWhenInUseAuthorization()` or `EKEventStore().requestFullAccessToEvents` added.
questions.no: The change adds no restricted access and no authorization request, e.g. only a `PhotosPicker` or an import.

questions.title: A required usage-description key is missing
questions.question: Does an added capability require a usage-description key that is present nowhere: not in the change, the checkout's `Info.plist` or `project.yml`, or the target's build settings (`INFOPLIST_KEY_…` in `*.pbxproj`)? Derive the required keys from the actual authorization API and deployment target, as fact (1) of The standard says, not from an import; notification authorization and the system photo picker need none. A key present in the checkout satisfies the declaration. Answer YES only after reading every place the key could live; if one of them was not captured or cannot be read, leave the answer open and name it.
questions.yes: e.g. `requestWhenInUseAuthorization()` is added and no `NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription` exists in `Info.plist`, `project.yml` or the build settings.
questions.no: Every key the added access requires is present in the change or the checkout, or the access needs none.

questions.title: Permission is requested at launch
questions.question: Is an added authorization request (`requestWhenInUseAuthorization`, `requestAuthorization`, `PHPhotoLibrary.requestAuthorization`, …) made at app launch — the `App` type, the app delegate's launch, or the root view's `onAppear` or `.task` — for a feature the user has not reached? A root view that is itself the feature, such as a one-screen map app asking for location, asks at the point of use. Claim a launch site only with the call chain that reaches it.
questions.yes: e.g. `[L12] .onAppear { CLLocationManager().requestWhenInUseAuthorization() }` on `ContentView`, the root, while the map lives two screens deep.
questions.no: Every added request is made from the feature that needs it, or from a screen near it, not at launch.

questions.title: A usage description is a placeholder
questions.question: Is the usage-description string for an added capability, in the change or the checkout, a placeholder rather than a statement of what the app does with the access: "needed", "for the app", an empty string, or similar text that names no use?
questions.yes: e.g. `NSCameraUsageDescription` = "Camera needed" or an empty string.
questions.no: Each description says what the app does with the access, e.g. 'Scans receipts to add expenses'.

questions.title: Permission is requested before its feature
questions.question: Is an added authorization request made from a screen other than the feature that needs it — for example one screen before it — while not at app launch and not from the root view?
questions.yes: e.g. the notification request runs when the settings list opens, one screen before the reminder screen that uses it.
questions.no: Every added request is made from the feature that needs it, or at launch.

rules.reason: The change adds no capability that needs the user's permission.
An added capability needs a usage-description key that neither the change nor the project declares.
Permission is requested at launch, before the user reaches the feature that needs it.
A usage description is a placeholder that does not say what the app does with the access.
Permission is requested from a screen before the feature that needs it, not at its point of use.
Each added capability has a truthful usage description where required and is requested where it is used.

practices.name: Use adaptive colors so every appearance works

precondition.skipReason: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: A screen built from literal colors is right in one appearance and wrong in the other: white text vanishes on a light background, a hard-coded card stays white in Dark Mode, and every screen has to be revisited when the palette changes. Semantic and asset colors adapt on their own, and the whole app follows one palette.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Text, backgrounds and fills use semantic colors (`.primary`, `.secondary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`), materials, the accent color or named asset colors with light and dark variants; a literal is used only where the color is part of the content, such as text over a fill the same view sets.
practices.holdsAs: Colors adapt to light and dark appearance alike
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: the added interface takes its colors from the system's semantic set, materials, the accent color or asset colors with both appearances, not from literals that hold one appearance.

## The standard
Judge the color choices the change adds to SwiftUI views against a closed list. A literal is `Color.white`, `Color.black`, `.white` or `.black` as a foreground, background or fill, `Color(red:green:blue:)`, `Color(hex:)` or a hex-parsing initializer, `UIColor(red:)`, `Color(uiColor: .white/.black)`, and a color from `.gray`/`.systemGray` when it stands for text on a background. An adaptive color is a semantic one (`.primary`, `.secondary`, `.tertiary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`, `.secondarySystemBackground`, `.label`), a material (`.ultraThinMaterial`, `.regularMaterial`), the accent (`.accentColor`, `.tint`) or a named asset color (`Color("Card")`, `Color(.card)`) — an asset color is adaptive when its colorset carries a dark appearance. A literal is not a lapse where the color is the content: text or a symbol over a fill or image the same view sets, a brand color deliberately constant, a shadow or a translucent scrim over an image. Judge the added lines only.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: each added color expression and the modifier chain it sits in — what it colors (text, background, fill) and what fill the same view sets around it. It establishes the literal and its role. It never establishes an unchanged view's colors.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the asset catalog (`*.xcassets/<name>.colorset/Contents.json`) for a named color's appearances, and a color extension (`Color+App.swift`) a name may resolve to. Read it to classify a name; a `Color("x")` whose colorset has only one appearance is a literal in disguise.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the literal and adaptive color lines it found and, for each named asset color, whether its colorset has a dark appearance, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where a view body is edited, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Grounding
For a literal you call a lapse, quote the `[L<n>]` color line and, when the role matters, the fill or background line of the same view. For an asset color, cite the colorset's appearances from its `Contents.json`, or the definition a name resolves to. For colors that adapt, quote a representative adaptive color and record that every added color expression in the diff was enumerated. For a named color whose appearances cannot be read, name the asset. Never call a color a literal without its line; never call a named color adaptive without its colorset or its definition.

## Defer
Labels, fonts and colour-only state belong to `makes-ui-accessible-by-default`. Here only: does the color hold in both appearances?

questions.title: The change sets a color in a SwiftUI view
questions.question: Does the change set a color in a SwiftUI view: an added `.foregroundStyle`, `.foregroundColor`, `.background`, `.fill`, `.tint`, `.shadow(color:` or `Color`/`UIColor` expression inside a view type? Added color lines count whether or not they carry a lapse.
questions.yes: e.g. `[L20] .background(Color(.secondarySystemBackground))` or `.foregroundStyle(.white)` added.
questions.no: The change adds no color expression inside a view type.

questions.title: An added literal color holds one appearance
questions.question: Does an added color that holds one appearance sit where the interface adapts: text on a system or adaptive background, a screen or card background, or a fill the rest of the interface adapts around? One appearance: the literals listed in The standard, and a named color whose colorset has no dark appearance. Not a lapse: an adaptive color as The standard lists them; a literal that is the content (text or a symbol over a fill or image the same view sets, a shadow, a scrim over an image); a chromatic brand color kept constant, such as a custom blue button fill. A white, black, gray, near-white or near-black literal used as a background or as text is never a brand color, though it may be content. If nothing else holds one appearance and a named color's colorset or definition cannot be found, leave the answer open and name it.
questions.yes: e.g. `[L20] .background(Color.white)` on a card, or `.foregroundColor(.black)` on text over the system background.
questions.no: Every added color adapts or is content, e.g. `.foregroundStyle(.white)` over a `Color.blue` fill the same view sets, or a constant custom-blue button fill.

questions.title: A screen background or main text is hard-coded
questions.question: Is a color found above that holds one appearance, and is not content or a constant brand color, added as a screen or card background, or as the primary text color of a screen? One such color on a secondary element does not count. When unsure, answer NO.
questions.yes: e.g. `ScrollView { … }.background(Color.white)` for the whole screen, or the screen's title and body set to `.black`.
questions.no: Any literal colors a secondary element; screen and card backgrounds and the main text adapt.

rules.reason: The change sets no color in a SwiftUI view.
A screen or card background, or a screen's primary text, is hard-coded to one appearance.
An added literal color fixes text or a fill to one appearance where the interface around it adapts.
Every added color adapts to light and dark appearance, or is a literal only where it is the content.

groups.name: Communicating in the open
groups.description: How you talk to teammates in shared channels: ask questions someone can actually answer, give answers people can act on, and keep others informed about where the work stands and what is blocking it. This is about the clarity of the exchange, not the correctness of the code being discussed.

practices.name: Ask questions a teammate can answer
practices.whyItMatters: A vague question forces the person helping you to stop and ask what you actually mean before they can even start, turning a one-message answer into a slow exchange. A question that carries its own context gets answered on the first reply.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A question that says what you are trying to do, what you already tried, and exactly where it broke, so a teammate can answer it in a single reply without asking you anything first.
practices.holdsAs: Questions carry the goal, the attempt and the error
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: a question posed in the captured exchange carries enough context — the goal, what was tried, what happened — for a teammate to answer it in one reply.

## The standard
Judge whether a question raised in this conversation gives a teammate enough to answer it in a single reply, rather than forcing a round of clarifying questions first. A well-formed ask names the concrete goal, what was already tried, and what actually happened or is blocking. A bare "it doesn't work" or "how do I do this?" with no context makes the responder guess. Judge only the observable way the question is posed; never whether the underlying problem is real, hard or worth solving. Use judgment about how much context the question genuinely needs: a quick clarification among people who plainly share the context is not a defect. The review is about one participant: judge only the questions in their turns (marked `"underReview": true`); the other turns are context.

## Sources
1. The turn that poses the question (`context/conversation_thread.json`): its stated objective, what was tried, the exact behaviour seen or the specific point of confusion. It establishes how the question is posed. It never establishes whether the problem is real or worth solving.
2. The surrounding turns of the same thread (`context/conversation_thread.json`): earlier turns may supply the context the question leans on; a later reply that has to ask what was meant shows what the responder had to extract first. They establish what context was shared inside the captured thread and nothing outside it.
An image or attachment in a turn: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. When the thread begins mid-conversation, so you cannot tell whether what the question leans on was supplied in a turn you never saw, report a collection gap and record no observation; that is neither an absence nor an open question.

## Grounding
Quote the exact turn you assessed. To answer that the question can be answered where the surrounding turns supply the context, quote those turns too. A NO rests on absence: read the whole captured thread and show the question and that boundary, with no turn supplying the goal, the attempt or the observed behaviour. To answer that a turn is not a question, quote it. Describe the observable gap — "the question names no goal and no attempt" — never laziness or intent. Never invent missing context, grade an exchange you cannot quote, or claim the problem is or is not real.

## Defer
Whether the reply moves the asker forward belongs to `gives-actionable-answers`. Here only: does the question, as posed, let a teammate answer it in one reply?

questions.title: The thread poses a question
questions.question: Does a turn of the participant under review (marked `"underReview": true` in `context/conversation_thread.json`) actually ask a question — for help, information or a decision? A statement, an acknowledgement or social chat is not a question.
questions.yes: A turn asks something, e.g. 'How do I get the staging deploy to pick up the new env var?'.
questions.no: None of their turns is a question: they hold statements, acknowledgements or social chat, or there is no settled conversation.

questions.title: Question can be answered in one reply
questions.question: Could a knowledgeable teammate answer the question in one reply, from its turn and the surrounding turns of the thread, without first asking what the asker means, tried or expected? The goal, the attempt and the observed behaviour are what a thin question lacks, not a checklist: a question needs only what its answer depends on, and a quick question between people who plainly share the context needs no more. A later reply that has to ask what was meant shows the context was missing. Judge how the question is posed, never whether the problem is real or hard. If what it lacks may sit in an attachment or link whose content was not captured (a screenshot of the error, a linked log), leave the answer open and name it.
questions.yes: e.g. 'Deploying to staging, I set FOO in the dashboard and redeployed, but the app still logs FOO=undefined — where else is it read?'.
questions.no: The question is too thin to answer without asking what was meant, tried or expected, and no turn supplies it, e.g. 'the deploy doesn't work, help?'.

questions.title: Question needs a full round of clarifications
questions.question: Is the question, as written and read with every surrounding turn, impossible to answer without a full exchange of clarifications first — a responder cannot begin to help until they learn what the author means? A question that a little more detail would merely sharpen, and that a teammate could already start on, is not. When unsure, answer NO.
questions.yes: e.g. 'it's broken again, any idea?' with no turn saying what is broken, what was tried or what happened.
questions.no: A teammate could already start on the question; a little more detail would only sharpen it.

rules.reason: No turn in the conversation is a question; it holds statements, acknowledgements or social chat.
The question gives no goal, attempt or observed behaviour, so it cannot be answered without a round of clarifications.
The question leaves out part of its context, such as what was tried or what happened, that a responder needs.
The question, with its thread, carries enough context for a teammate to answer it in one reply.

practices.name: Give answers people can act on
practices.whyItMatters: When someone asks for help, a reply that only gestures at the problem leaves them exactly as stuck as before and burns another round of messages. An answer with a concrete next step lets them get moving right away.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A reply that either solves the question outright or points to the exact next step or place to look, so the person who asked can act on it immediately instead of asking again.
practices.holdsAs: Answers give the next step, not another question
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: a reply to a question in the captured exchange gives the asker something to act on now — the answer, the exact place to look, or the next step.

## The standard
Judge whether a reply to someone's question actually moves them forward, rather than leaving them where they started. A useful answer either resolves the question directly or names a concrete next step the asker can take. A reply that only restates the problem, points vaguely at "the docs", or answers a different question does not. A short answer can be fully actionable; length is not the signal. Judge only the observable helpfulness of the reply as written, never whether its technical content is ultimately correct. Use judgment about what the asker needed. The review is about one participant: judge only the replies in their turns (marked `"underReview": true`); the other turns, the question among them, are context.

## Sources
1. The question turn (`context/conversation_thread.json`): what was asked and what the asker needed. It establishes the question the reply is measured against. It never establishes whether the problem is real or hard.
2. The reply turn (`context/conversation_thread.json`): the answer given, the place named, the step proposed. It establishes what the asker can do next. It never establishes that the answer is technically right.
3. The surrounding turns (`context/conversation_thread.json`): whether the exchange is still in progress, and whether the answer had already been given elsewhere in the thread. They establish the state of the exchange inside the captured thread and nothing outside it.
An image or attachment in a turn: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing; judge the reply by its own words. When a real question and its reply are both in front of you but the thread begins mid-conversation, so you cannot tell whether the answer had already been given elsewhere in it, report a collection gap and record no observation; that is neither an absence nor an open question.

## Grounding
Quote the question and the reply you assessed. To answer that the reply can be acted on, quote the answer, the place named or the step proposed, or the other turn that already gave the answer. A NO rests on absence: read the surrounding captured turns and show the question, the reply and that boundary, with no other turn supplying the answer. To answer that a turn answers no question or is a partial step, quote the turns that show it. Describe the observable gap — "the reply names no place to look and no step" — never dismissiveness. Never fabricate an answer the reply did not give, and never claim the reply's content is correct or incorrect.

## Defer
Whether the question itself carried enough context to be answerable belongs to `asks-answerable-questions`. Here only: does the reply, as written, let the asker move forward?

questions.title: A genuine question has a reply
questions.question: Does a turn of the participant under review (marked `"underReview": true` in `context/conversation_thread.json`) reply to a genuine question someone else asked, whether or not the reply helps? A reply that sidesteps the question or answers a different one still counts. There is none when no question was asked, when none of their turns replies to one, or when there is no settled conversation to read.
questions.yes: e.g. 'Where is the retry limit configured?' followed by a teammate's reply, helpful or not.
questions.no: None of their turns replies to a question someone else asked, or no question was asked.

questions.title: Reply is a partial step in an ongoing exchange
questions.question: Is the reply a reasonable partial step rather than the reply meant to settle the question: it asks for something the answer depends on (the full error, the version, what was tried), or the surrounding turns show the exchange continuing past it toward the answer? A request for needed detail counts even when the thread ends without the asker supplying it.
questions.yes: e.g. 'can you paste the full error?' in reply to 'the build fails', whether or not the asker answered.
questions.no: The reply is the response meant to settle the question.

questions.title: Asker can act on the reply now
questions.question: Could the asker act on the reply now because it gives the answer, the specific place to look, or the exact next step? An answer another turn of the thread already gave counts. A link to a specific page, file, ticket or line is a place to look; you cannot read it, so judge only whether it names a specific place, while a bare 'check the docs' does not. Length is not the signal. A reply that only restates the problem or answers a different question does not move the asker forward. Judge helpfulness as written, never technical correctness. If the reply admits incompatible readings, quote the ambiguity and say what would settle it.
questions.yes: e.g. 'It's `RETRY_LIMIT` in `config/jobs.yml`, line 12.'
questions.no: The reply leaves the asker still stuck, e.g. 'check the docs' or 'yeah that's a known thing'.

questions.title: Reply gives nothing to act on
questions.question: Does the reply give the asker nothing to act on at all — no answer, no place to look, no step — rather than nearly landing the answer and missing one pointer? When unsure, answer NO.
questions.yes: e.g. 'hmm, weird' or 'it depends' in reply to a concrete question.
questions.no: The reply is actionable, or nearly so: one pointer would land it, e.g. 'it's somewhere in the jobs config'.

rules.reason: The conversation holds no genuine question with a reply from someone else.
The reply is a reasonable partial step in an exchange that is still in progress.
The reply to a genuine question gives no answer, no place to look and no next step.
The reply points toward the answer but stops one concrete pointer short of something the asker can act on.
The reply gives the answer, the place to look or the next step the asker can act on.

practices.name: Post clear status and blocker updates
practices.whyItMatters: When work stalls quietly, the people depending on it keep waiting without knowing anything is wrong, and a blocker someone else could have cleared in minutes sits for days. A plain update on where things stand and what you need keeps the team moving.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: An update that says where the work stands and, when you are stuck, names the blocker and what would unblock it, so teammates can plan around it or step in to help.
practices.holdsAs: Updates say where the work stands and what blocks it
practices.criteria:
REVIEW FOCUS: an update about ongoing work says where things stand and, when stuck, names the blocker and what would clear it.

## The standard
Judge whether an update about ongoing work tells the team where things stand and, when the author is stuck, names the blocker plainly along with what is needed to clear it. A clear update lets teammates plan around the work or step in to unblock it; an update so vague no one can tell whether help is needed leaves the team guessing. Judge only the observable clarity of the update, never whether the work itself is on track. Use judgment about how much an update needs to say: a brief "still on it, no blockers" among teammates already in sync is fine, and a real update made clear by its surrounding context is a good update, not a missing one. The review is about one participant: judge only the updates in their turns (marked `"underReview": true`); the other turns are context.

## Sources
1. The update turn (`context/conversation_thread.json`): what it says about the current standing, whether it reports being blocked, what it names as the blocker and what it asks for. It establishes the clarity of the update as posted. It never establishes whether the work is actually on track or whether the blocker is real.
2. The surrounding turns of the same thread (`context/conversation_thread.json`): earlier turns may already establish the standing an update omits, or show that the teammates are in sync; a later turn that has to ask what is needed shows what the update left unsaid. They establish what was shared inside the captured thread and nothing outside it.
An image or attachment in a turn: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. When an update IS posted but the thread begins mid-conversation, so you cannot tell whether the standing it omits was already established, report a collection gap and record no observation; that is neither an absence nor an open question.

## Grounding
Quote the update you assessed. To answer that the standing or the ask is clear where the surrounding turns supply it, quote those turns too. To answer that something is vague or missing, quote the vague line and the turns you read around it, which bound the search. To answer that a turn is not an update, quote it. Describe the observable gap — "the update says it is blocked and names no blocker" — never avoidance or intent. Never invent a blocker the author did not mention, and never claim the work is or is not on track.

## Defer
Whether a question posed in the thread carries enough context to answer belongs to `asks-answerable-questions`; whether a reply moves the asker forward belongs to `gives-actionable-answers`. Here only: does the update tell the team where things stand and what would unblock them?

questions.title: The thread holds a status update
questions.question: Does a turn of the participant under review (marked `"underReview": true` in `context/conversation_thread.json`) give a status update about in-flight work or a blocker — what they are doing, how far along it is, or that they are stuck? There is none when none of their turns reports on ongoing work (a question, an acknowledgement, social chat), when there is no in-flight work or blocker to report, or when there is no settled conversation to read.
questions.yes: e.g. 'Payment webhook: handler done, waiting on the sandbox keys to test it.'
questions.no: None of their turns reports on ongoing work or a blocker.

questions.title: Update makes clear where the work stands
questions.question: Does the update, alone or with the surrounding turns of the same thread, make clear where the work stands? A brief 'still on it, no blockers' among teammates already in sync is clear, and earlier turns may already establish the standing an update omits. It is not clear when the update is so vague that no one can tell how the work is going or whether help is needed. Judge only the observable clarity of the update, never whether the work is on track. When the meaning genuinely admits incompatible readings, quote the ambiguity and say what would settle it rather than guessing.
questions.yes: e.g. 'handler done, tests next, should open the PR tomorrow', or 'still on it, no blockers' among teammates in sync.
questions.no: e.g. 'working on stuff, some things came up' with no turn saying how far the work is.

questions.title: A reported blocker goes unnamed
questions.question: Does the update say the work is stuck, blocked or waiting, yet name neither what is blocking it nor what would unblock it, with no surrounding turn saying? A mention of issues the author says they are handling ('hit a few snags, sorting them out') reports no blocker; its vagueness is a matter of standing. Never invent a blocker the author did not mention. If the blocker may be named in an attachment or link whose content was not captured, leave the answer open and name it.
questions.yes: e.g. 'kind of stuck on the webhook, will see' with no turn naming the cause or what would help.
questions.no: No blocker is reported, or the update or a surrounding turn names what is blocking.

questions.title: What would clear the blocker is unclear
questions.question: Does the update name a blocker but leave unclear what is needed to clear it — no concrete ask, decision, or person or thing it waits on — with no surrounding turn supplying it? A blocker whose name already says what clears it (waiting for a named review, for CI to finish) is clear. A later turn that has to ask what is needed shows the update left it unsaid. An update that reports no blocker does not count.
questions.yes: e.g. 'blocked on the sandbox environment' with no word on what is needed, and a teammate replying 'what do you need from us?'.
questions.no: No blocker is reported, or the update says what would clear it, e.g. 'need the sandbox API keys from Dana'.

rules.reason: No turn in the conversation is a status update about in-flight work or a blocker.
The update signals that the work is stuck but names neither the blocker nor what would clear it.
The update names a blocker but not what is needed to clear it.
The update is too vague to tell where the work stands or whether help is needed.
The update says where the work stands and, where it is blocked, what would unblock it.
